item.title: [CBS Sports] The state of the outfield position heading into 2027: Pete Crow-Armstrong leads a talented but thin field
item.dc:creator: Chris Towers

item.content:encoded:
There were 13 outfield-eligible players worth at least $20 in the FanGraphs Player Rater in 2026, just two fewer than the first base spot. If you remember that you only need to start one first baseman (and potentially a corner infielder and DH) while you might need to start as many as five outfielders at a time, well, you can see why this is problematic.
That's not to say the outfield is somehow a wasteland for Fantasy right now. First base was unusually strong in 2026, but in 2025, there were three times as many $20 players with outfield eligibility as at first base. And it's worth noting that the 13 $20 outfielders in 2026 are actually a few more than 2025's nine.
On the whole, I look at outfield as a position with a decent amount of depth in a three-outfielder, 12-team league. You should be able to draft a full lineup without feeling too bad about your outfield options in that formula.
Once you start getting into five-outfielder leagues, and especially deeper leagues with 15 teams, it starts to feel a lot more thin. That's to be expected, of course, but it's important to keep that in mind when you're preparing for the 2027 season. You don't have to make the position a priority in every draft, but if you aren't cognizant of it, you could end up with a real weakness in those deeper leagues.
For more on the state of the outfield position, .
2026 Outfield Review
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, CHC: .280 - 119 - 45 - 107 - 41
- Yordan Alvarez, HOU: .316 - 105 - 42 - 106 - 1
- Fernando Tatis Jr., SDP: .289 - 96 - 25 - 83 - 38
- Randy Arozarena, SEA: .281 - 113 - 26 - 79 - 26
- Jordan Walker, STL: .269 - 97 - 29 - 102 - 22
- James Wood, WSN: .265 - 106 - 30 - 77 - 21
- Jackson Chourio, MIL: .291 - 96 - 25 - 75 - 23
- Alec Burleson, STL: .279 - 89 - 26 - 116 - 4
- Jake McCarthy, COL: .291 - 80 - 15 - 83 - 32
- Michael Harris II, ATL: .294 - 79 - 26 - 87 - 12
- Jackson Merrill, SDP: .254 - 86 - 26 - 87 - 27
- Bryce Harper, PHI: .269 - 93 - 29 - 87 - 7
- Jake Bauers, MIL: .266 - 93 - 26 - 86 - 11
- Seiya Suzuki, CHC: .270 - 96 - 26 - 86 - 3
- Carson Benge, NYM: .282 - 86 - 20 - 65 - 22
- Andy Pages, LAD: .274 - 75 - 23 - 85 - 13
- Corbin Carroll, ARI: .239 - 91 - 22 - 78 - 21
- Oneil Cruz, PIT: .280 - 65 - 20 - 67 - 30
- Daylen Lile, WSN: .246 - 81 - 22 - 89 - 15
- Jac Caglianone, KCR: .289 - 72 - 23 - 75 - 7
- Bryan Reynolds, PIT: .261 - 102 - 17 - 72 - 9
- Chandler Simpson, TBR: .306 - 66 - 0 - 38 - 46
- Riley Greene, DET: .280 - 79 - 21 - 75 - 3
- Ceddanne Rafaela, BOS: .285 - 67 - 16 - 70 - 17
"Marginal player signs with the Rockies and has a Coors Field-inflated career season" used to be a pretty reliable archetype. Still, the Rockies have given Fantasy players little to get excited about in recent years. Jake McCarthy stands out as a notable exception, as his contact-and-speed profile proved to be a perfect fit for Coos Field. We're talking about relatively easy career-best production across the board, in a way that feels relatively obvious in retrospect. I don't have a ton of faith that this would prove replicable in any other ballpark — the gap between his .321 expected wOBA and his .349 actual mark was the 20th biggest in baseball — but it works there. As long as he isn't traded, McCarthy is a good bet to replicate his 2026 success.
I also want to highlight Harris and Merrill, because it feels very natural to group them together. They're both younger than you might realize – Harris will turn 26 shortly before his sixth MLB season in March, while Merrill won't even be 24 on Opening Day. They're also both linked by the combination of plus athleticism and bat speed, plus pretty poor approaches at the plate. They are, on the whole, capable of overcoming their poor swing decisions with outlier outcomes when they make contact, but that isn't always the case for either. Hence, the lengthy slumps that have held both back in recent years. They both got the good end of their range of outcomes in 2026, and we saw how high the ceiling can be for both. But drafting either for their 2026 outcome will carry inherent risks until they show some growth in their plate discipline.
Biggest Breakout from 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
How could it be anyone else? Crow-Armstrong went from being a talented but deeply flawed hitter to arguably the best player in baseball, and he did it in-season. Early on, he looked more or less like the same guy he had always been, walking just nine times in 128 plate appearances through the end of June; he walked at least 12 times in each of the final five months of the season, something he had never done in any of his previous 13 months. He did that without sacrificing the pull-side power that has long been a key part of his game, and it turned him into one of the most dominant hitters in the game. Expecting all of those gains to carry over into 2027 might be asking a bit much — sometimes guys just get super locked in for a while — but he's clearly a much-improved hitter, and one who should be the first player taken in every single Roto league in 2027. And he shouldn't go much later in points leagues, where he was also the top player in 2026.
Honorable Mention: Jordan Walker, Cardinals
Okay, so if it were going to be anyone but Crow-Armstrong, it would be Walker, who went from being one of the biggest prospect busts in recent seasons to one of the best players in Fantasy. Walker still had pretty bad plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues, but he overcame that by being more aggressive early in the count and by doing more damage when he did make contact. The plate discipline issues and a late-season swoon — his expected wOBA dropped from .374 to .290 from the first half to the second — hint at the kind of risk involved in buying fully into what he did in 2026, and I suspect I'll be a little lower on him than the consensus. On the other hand, those were the exact reasons I cited to avoid Crow-Armstrong before the season, and look how that turned out. There's something to be said for just betting on the young, super-talented players when they show it.
Biggest Bust from 2026
The overall numbers don't show it, but Judge looked more or less like himself before he started dealing with that rib injury. In March and April, he posted a .450 xwOBA, right in line with his typical mark, but then things went downhill even before he ultimately went on the IL with a fractured rib. Was his downturn because of the injury? If so, then I think you can still make the case for him as a top-five pick in any league. But we're talking about a guy who will be 35 early next season, coming off a largely lost season that also came with an apparent decline in the underlying skill level, and that's a lot of red flags to overlook in a top-five pick. I might end up with Judge ranked that way come the spring, but it won't feel good.
Honorable Mention: Kyle Tucker, Dodgers
Maybe you don't think he was worth the contract the Dodgers gave him. Fair enough; you won't be alone in holding that opinion. But anyone who tells you there was any way to see this kind of disaster coming from Tucker is just lying to you. A 29-year-old went out and posted the worst batting average, on-base percentage, and slugging percentage of his career, and in two of those cases, it wasn't even close. Tucker had the combination of bat speed, athleticism, and plate discipline that should protect him against this kind of drop-off. Maybe the lights in L.A. were too bright for him. Maybe the pressure of the contract got to him. But I don't believe Tucker has just completely lost the ability to be an impact player, and he's still in what should be one of the best lineups in baseball, so I'll buy the bounce-back at what should be a steeply discounted price. The fact that he put together an excellent September and a very good postseason run certainly makes that an easier story to tell, of course.
Biggest rankings movers from 2026 to 2027
Up: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs; Yordan Alvarez, Astros; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Jake Bauers, Brewers
As maybe the biggest Yordan Alvarez believer in the entire Fantasy industry coming into 2026, I do worry there's going to be a big overcorrection on him in 2027. We didn't learn anything new about Alvarez. If you think 2026 was a breakout season of some sort for him, I'm sorry, but you just weren't paying attention; he's just always been this good. His .442 xwOBA was higher than his career average, sure, but it was also not even the highest of his career, and he had a separate season with a .436 mark, too. The skills have always been there, but the difference is that he stayed healthy in 2026 after a bunch of injuries in previous seasons. I'm thrilled that he stayed healthy, and the fact that he did it in a season when his standing among Fantasy players was never lower is a good reminder that the Fantasy community isn't nearly as good at predicting who will and won't stay healthy as we think. But that will also be true in 2027: He'll be a top-five pick in most leagues despite the injury risk not being substantially different than it was last season. That's not to say he shouldn't be a top-five pick, of course; it's to say that he should have been a lot closer to a top-five pick last season than he was.
You could make a case for Bauers as the biggest breakout at outfield, because he was viewed as an even bigger afterthought than Walker was. He was a 30-year-old platoon specialist, after all! That he somehow went out in 2026 and put up a .901 OPS against lefties and had the best season of his career by a mile came completely out of nowhere, and it's going to be very interesting to see what the market for him as a free agent looks like this offseason. I buy a lot of what he did in 2026, and I suspect there will be enough skepticism around it to keep his price pretty reasonable. But betting on age-30 breakouts is historically a pretty bad idea, so you'll have to get a pretty big discount on what he did in 2026 to make him worth the risk, I think.
Down: Ronald Acuna, Braves; Kyle Tucker, Dodgers; Wyatt Langford, Rangers; Brent Rooker, Athletics
I wanted to make Langford one of the biggest bust picks, if only to highlight the fact that he has almost certainly been the least profitable pick in Fantasy over the past three years. He has struggled to stay healthy and just hasn't been the impact player you'd expect from a guy who had the kind of prospect pedigree he did — not to mention the benefit of the doubt the Fantasy community has continued to give him. I suspect that will come to an end in 2027, and … it kind of makes me more excited about buying into him this season. Because, for as frustrating and disappointing as he's been as a big-leaguer, his per-162 game pace for his career is pretty terrific: 90 runs, 24 homers, 24 steals, and 77 RBI. If he just does that in 2027, isn't that worth something like a fifth-round pick? And I don't think that's the ceiling for Langford, who has put up those numbers at a very young age while playing through a variety of injuries and has certainly flashed a higher ceiling at times. I'm not trying to excuse his poor performance; I'm just pointing out that all he has to do is stay healthy to be a very good Fantasy option. That's usually a good player to buy into at a discount.
The notoriously frugal A's are surely feeling some degree of buyer's remorse on Rooker's contract, but that contract should assure that he continues to play every day for them. His disappointing season came to an end after just 48 games, but he was on pace for another 30-homer season despite the injury. The .200 average is a tough look, as was the career-worst 32% strikeout rate, and the big drop off as a 31-year-old will rightly lead to plenty of skepticism around the potential of a bounce back. But that will also mean Rooker will come at a huge discount, potentially with a price outside the top 200 in many drafts. I'll buy that dip, personally. If you can buy him as a very cheap bench bat, there's no downside.
Offseason preview
Who needs an upgrade most?
A bunch of these teams are straddling the line between trying to go for it and needing to rebuild. The Reds could very well be in the market for a big upgrade in the outfield, or they could decide to move Elly De La Cruz and hit the reset button (again). The Astros could decide to give it one more run with this core, or they could move Alvarez and pivot to the future. The Phillies seem most likely to try to take a big swing, if only because Dave Dombrowski only knows how to take big swings. However, the Cardinals loom as a team that is ascending and could decide to get involved in the free-agent market with their core of cost-controlled position players.
Top impending free agents
- Randy Arozarena
- Seiya Suzuki
- Ian Happ
- Jake Bauers
- Trent Grisham
- Daulton Varsho
- Luis Robert
- Ramon Laureano
- George Springer
Arozarena is such a fascinating free agent. He's coming off a perfectly timed career-best season, but he'll be 32 before Opening Day and has rated out as a pretty terrible defender for several years running. There's probably no chance he gets anything more than a five-year contract in free agency, and he might need to agree to a move to DH as soon as 2027, two things that might be a tough pill to swallow. But having the best season of his career in the toughest offensive environment in baseball is no small thing, and nobody can deny his flair for the dramatic would be a great fit for a team with championship aspirations. The underlying skill set doesn't look so different from previous seasons, but his price will likely be higher than ever, making him one of the more obvious players to avoid in drafts for 2027, no matter where he lands.
Suzuki and, to a lesser extent, Happ look like players who will carry pretty solid value in Fantasy no matter where they land, but everyone else looks pretty context-dependent. Varsho's pull-heavy swing (and elite center field defense) would be a perfect fit for the Yankees, for example, but would be a much less interesting profile elsewhere. Stay tuned.
Trade candidates 
- Yordan Alvarez, Astros
- Jarren Duran, Red Sox
- Steven Kwan, Guardians
- Byron Buxton, Twins
- Brent Rooker, Athletics
- Jake McCarthy, Rockies
Alvarez feels like the biggest wild card here. The Astros won the AL West, but with just a .500 record, and they had such a poor showing in a two-game Wild Card round loss to the White Sox that the hometown crowd showered them with boos along the way. The Astros have lost their long-held edge over the competition, and while Alvarez's contract isn't expiring, he only has two years left on a relatively below-market deal. So this might be their last chance to maximize their return for him. The Astros are in flux in a lot of ways after firing Dana Brown, so they might not be positioned to make a big, franchise-altering move, but they would probably be best served trying to get off the treadmill of mediocrity sooner rather than later.
It increasingly looks like the Red Sox should have traded Duran at least a year ago, if not longer. All of a sudden, he's a 30-year-old corner outfielder who probably shouldn't play every day against lefties, and while he'll likely still earn a below-market salary in arbitration, he no longer looks like a real bargain. His skill set still has plenty of value for Fantasy (20 homers, 21 steals will always play), and I'd bet on him improving on last year's .207 average, but this isn't an early-round profile anymore.
Top rookies to know for 2026
- Josue De Paula, Dodgers
- Walker Jenkins, Twins
- Eduardo Quintero, Dodgers
- Theo Gillen, Rays
- Mike Sirota, Dodgers
- Zyhir Hope, Tigers
- Edward Florentino, Pirates
- Eric Hartman, Braves
- Drew Burress, Athletics
- Josiah Hartshorn, Cubs
- Lazaro Montes, Mariners
Jenkins is probably the most likely player here to be in an Opening Day lineup – I'm not sure what would have to happen for him not to be there, absent injury. He didn't take the league by storm in his first 26 games, but he was actually pretty great once he got adjusted, hitting .385/.400/.615 with just three strikeouts over his final 10 games. He has power, speed, and an excellent approach at the plate and should be a popular breakout candidate for 2027.
But not as popular as De Paula could be. I say "could" because, well, there's no obvious place for him to play. It's definitely not going to be in right field or DH, and slotting De Paula in at left field would require finding somewhere for Teoscar Hernandez and his large salary to go. Center field is the biggest hole in the Yankees outfield, but De Paula hasn't played there since 2023, and … well, you see the problem here. De Paula destroyed Double-A and very much passed the eye test in 11 MLB games, earning not-totally-unfair comparisons to Juan Soto and Yordan Alvarez for his approach at the plate. He could be an absolute star, but given the roster crunch and the fact that he's only 21 and hasn't played at Triple-A yet, this might be a situation like Junior Caminero's a few years back – remember, he debuted toward the end of the 2023 season but wasn't an everyday player until August of 2024. I hope it doesn't take that long, but we'll have to at least consider the possibility that it will.

item.dc:creator: Jon Conahan

item.content:encoded:
Jacob Misiorowski is incredible, but meet Rays' Junior Caminero, who is the best in baseball at hitting a 100 MPH fastball originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Looking at the World Series matchup, the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays have a great opportunity to win this.
The Brewers are a great team from top to bottom and don't make many mistakes, while the Rays keep winning with elite starting pitching, timely hitting, and a superstar in Junior Caminero.
Caminero might be one of the better players in Major League Baseball, but unfortunately, outside of fans who truly follow the game, he doesn't get as much hype as he deserves.
As weird as that might sound for a guy who hit 42 home runs this season and 45 last year, it feels like Caminero doesn't get the respect he deserves.
Misiorowski is well known, even to casual fans, because of how hard he throws. He's a guy who's going to consistently throw 100-plus miles per hour.
But here's the thing: Caminero is arguably the best hitter in Major League Baseball on high-velocity pitches. According to BaseballThings.com, he's hitting .358 with a ridiculous .580 OPS on pitches 96-plus miles per hour.
Baseball fans are in for a treat when these two meet, as Misiorowski will toe the rubber in Game 1.
They've gone at it before, and Misiorowski has struck Caminero out twice in three at-bats, with the Rays slugger failing to get a hit. Caminero keeps proving he can step up in big moments, so it wouldn't be surprising to see him get Misiorowski this time around.

item.title: [mlb.com] Our experts make their World Series predictions

item.content:encoded:
The Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were a franchise record, navigated a tight NL Division Series against the Padres before clobbering the two-time reigning champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series sweep. It’s just the second World Series appearance in their history and their first since 1982.
Meanwhile, the Rays swept the division rival Yankees in the ALDS before handling the Guardians in six games in the ALCS. They’re back in the Fall Classic for the third time and the first since 2020.
Both teams do a little bit of everything right on the diamond, making for what should be a thoroughly exciting World Series. Here’s how our group of MLB.com experts see it playing out.
Rays vs. Brewers
The pick: Brewers (43 of 51 votes, 84.3%)
Why they’ll win
Any time you take down the back-to-back reigning champs, and do so in a sweep, it’s going to make noise. But really, this is nothing new for the 2026 Brewers. They owned the best regular-season record with a roster that just gets the job done across the board.
The Brewers can play small ball, but they can slug when it matters most, too. In fact, Milwaukee has been more homer-dependent in October than it was all year. But the club can still work a deep count and get on base in many ways. Just ask Jake Bauers.
On the mound, it’s no secret that the bullpen is the Brewers’ strength. One of the best groups in the regular season is only doing more of the same in October, with a 1.33 ERA in eight games. Lefty Aaron Ashby is leading the charge during a historically good run. And then there’s that Jacob Misiorowski guy, who has been good enough in the playoffs but could unleash a new, dominant level in the World Series.
What they’re saying
“There's something about this Brewers club. Maintaining the league's best record all summer and barely giving an inch so far in the postseason, they're looking pretty unstoppable with the right mix of clutch hits, key performers and an absolutely lockdown bullpen. It might finally be the Crew's moment in the spotlight.” -- Adrian Garro, editorial producer
“The Brewers have been knocking on this door for years and are firing on all cylinders following their impressive sweep of the Dodgers. They are smart and hard-nosed enough not to let the long layoff affect them negatively.” -- Andrew Werle, supervising editor, content operations
“Walking off Mason Miller. Sweeping the 2-time defending champion Dodgers. These Brewers may just be a team of destiny, with their final obstacle being the American League's top-seeded Rays.” -- Kyle Boris, supervisor, media operations
The dissenting view
The Brewers have been dominant, but so have the Rays. They have a clear edge in starting pitching, with Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez firing on all cylinders. The Tampa Bay bullpen, while not as overpowering as the Brewers’, is still strong and has lockdown closer Bryan Baker waiting in the wings.
The key for the Rays likely lies in their lineup, where Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda appear to be heating up at the right time. Much like Milwaukee, the Rays will put together quality at-bats, get on base and then cause havoc on the basepaths. Perhaps no one is more adept at doing so than Chandler Simpson.
“The Rays' ‘small ball’ doesn't slump, and they've been pressing all of the right pitching buttons.” -- Jonathan Mayo, national reporter, prospects
“With their Big 3 of Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero breaking out at the end of the ALCS -- plus a slight edge over the Crew in starting pitching -- I believe the Rays are going to steal Game 1 vs. The Miz and ride that to a World Series title. Third time is a charm.” -- Brian McGrath, supervising editor, content operations
Series predictions
Brewers (6 games): 23 votes
Brewers (7 games): 14 votes
Brewers (5 games): 5 votes
Rays (7 games): 4 votes
Rays (6 games): 3 votes
Rays (5 games): 1 vote
Brewers (4 games): 1 vote
There may have been an overwhelming majority of our group predicting the Brewers to win the World Series, but that doesn’t do justice to how close these two teams seem to be. This will: 44 of 51 voters see the series going at least six games.
Who will be named World Series MVP?
Jackson Chourio (MIL): 16 votes
William Contreras (MIL): 13 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL): 6 votes
Yandy Díaz (TB): 5 votes
Brice Turang (MIL): 5 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL): 1 vote
Jake Bauers (MIL): 1 vote
Junior Caminero (TB): 1 vote
Trevor Megill (MIL): 1 vote
Drew Rasmussen (TB): 1 vote
Chandler Simpson (TB): 1 vote
It’s not hard to see why Chourio was our experts’ favorite to take home the World Series Most Valuable Player Award. Still just 22 years old, Chourio already leads Brewers franchise history with six career playoff home runs. He’s already shown he can rise to the occasion this year with a walk-off single against Mason Miller in the NLDS and a massive homer against Blake Snell in the NLCS. But Chourio’s overall production this October has been quiet (6-for-35). It might just be a matter of time before he breaks out.
“Chourio is due to break out in the World Series. While he hasn't done much in the playoffs so far, his two homers were impactful -- a go-ahead shot and a game-tying blast. He's ready to let it rip.” -- Kelsie Heneghan, senior coordinator, social media editorial, MiLB
“He's a legend in the making. This is the start of his Hall of Fame case.” -- Will Leitch, senior columnist
Who will be on the mound when the series ends … and what happens?
Trevor Megill (MIL), final out: 24 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL), final out: 10 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), final out: 6 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL), final out: 6 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), walked off: 3 votes
Drew Rasmussen (TB), final out: 1 vote
Ian Seymour (TB), final out: 1 vote
Megill has been lights-out as the Brewers’ closer, so it’s easy to envision him shutting things down at American Family Field in Game 6 or 7. But don’t be surprised if it’s Ashby continuing his fireman role -- or The Miz coming in for a clutch relief appearance.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Oct 2026, 04:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Benny Sieu)
MILWAUKEE -- The Milwaukee Brewers will be looking for hard-throwing Jacob Misiorowski to regain his dominant regular-season form against the visiting Tampa Bay Rays on Friday in the opening game of the World Series.
Misiorowski, who often tops 100 mph with his fastball, will be opposed by veteran right-hander Nick Martinez in a matchup of teams that have not won the World Series. It is the first meeting of two teams without a World Series title since the Philadelphia Phillies topped the Kansas City Royals in six games in 1980.
Milwaukee, which won a franchise-record 103 games during the regular season, advanced with a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, while the Rays ousted the Cleveland Guardians in six games in the American League Championship Series.
The Brewers' only other World Series appearance was in 1982 when they were in the American League. The charismatic 'Harvey's Wallbangers' lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive seventh game.
The Rays will be making their third World Series appearance. They lost to Philadelphia in five games in 2008 and in six games to the Dodgers in 2020.
Misiorowski, considered the favorite for the NL Cy Young Award, was 16-5 with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. The latter two stats were best in the majors.
But the 24-year-old right-hander did not make it through five innings in either postseason start, although the Brewers rallied to win both games. They topped the San Diego Padres 3-2 in Game 1 of the National League Division Series and the Dodgers 2-1 in the NLCS opener.
'I feel good. I feel like the first one might have been a little under what I expected, but the second one was pretty much right where I wanted to be,' Misiorowski said.
Misiorowski worked out of trouble in his postseason starts, allowing three runs on nine hits in 8 1/3 innings with 11 strikeouts and four walks.
'He hasn't been as crisp,' Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. 'I don't think people are up there thinking it's going to be 104 (mph), and I think they're elated if it's anything less than that. They're obviously looking at an area. They're trying to exploit everything. He's exposed, like all these guys get at some point.'
At the back end, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed six runs over 40 2/3 innings for a 1.33 ERA in the postseason. Closer Trevor Megill has four saves after collecting 30 in the regular season.
Milwaukee was last in the NL in home runs (154) during the regular season but leads all teams in the postseason with 10 homers in eight games. The Rays have hit seven in nine games.
Catcher William Contreras batted .367 with three homers and five RBIs over the Brewers' first two series. Outfielder Jackson Chourio hit .171, but he had two homers and a team-high seven RBIs.
Jake Bauers, who reached the majors with the Rays in 2018, was named the NLCS Most Valuable Player after hitting .286 with one homer and six RBIs against the Dodgers. Bauers set career highs with 26 homers and 86 RBIs during the regular season.
The 36-year-old Martinez pitched in the postseason with San Diego in 2022 and the Cincinnati Reds last season, but he will be making his World Series debut Friday. Ace Drew Rasmussen will start Game 2 with an extra day's rest, with former Brewers ace Freddy Peralta to follow in Game 3.
'It's exciting,' Martinez said Thursday. 'I think as a team, as a staff, we're confident in whoever we call up for the mound. It fell on me, and my job is just to rack up as many outs as we can and keep us in this ballgame.'
Martinez picked up the win in Game 4 of the ALCS when the Rays evened the series with a 7-3 victory at Cleveland. He allowed one run on two hits in 5 1/3 innings.
'He was pitching in pretty cold weather in Cleveland,' said Rays manager Kevin Cash, who was also at the helm for the 2020 World Series. 'Made some adjustments, he got the strike throwing where he wanted, the cutter gone, and the changeup. I don't even know, somebody told me he changed his grip in between innings, between the first and second. I'm glad I didn't know that in the moment.'
Martinez also started Game 3 in the Rays' ALDS sweep of the New York Yankees. He gave up two runs in 3 2/3 innings in an eventual 4-3 Tampa Bay victory.
Martinez is 0-1 with a 4.44 ERA in 12 regular-season games (seven starts) against Milwaukee. He has a 2.93 ERA in eight games at American Family Field.
Rays closer Bryan Baker, who tied for the MLB lead with 41 saves, has five saves in five postseason chances, pitching in seven of the nine games.
Third baseman Junior Caminero, whose 42 homers were second in the AL, has just one hit in 33 at-bats in the postseason.
--Jim Hoehn, Field Level Media

item.title: [mlb.com] Rays-Brewers World Series position-by-position breakdown
item.dc:creator: Mike Petriello

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to a most fantastically interesting World Series, in which focusing on the size of the markets involved completely misses the forest for the trees. It’s a No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchup, just the sixth time in the past 30 years that’s happened. It’s a pair of fanbases who have never won before, which marks the first time since 1980 (Royals vs. Phillies) that’s happened, and thus only the second time in more than a century, since the previous time had been 1920.
It’s a matchup of teams that have more than a few connections. Note that Tampa Bay’s top two starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, each came up with Milwaukee, and were teammates on the 2020-21 Brewers. Note, also, that NLCS MVP Jake Bauers made his debut with Tampa Bay back in 2018, and that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold spent nine years in the Tampa Bay front office before moving to Wisconsin.
It's more than just that. Depending on how you view your baseball aesthetics, it's a delightfully throwback sort of on-field style. It’s not that these teams eschew analytical thinking -- exactly the opposite, really -- but no team struck out less than the Rays, each team finished in the top five in steals and the bottom 10 in homers, and the bunt hits leaderboard goes “Tampa Bay first, Milwaukee second.”
Throw in a pair of excellent defenses, and you know what you’re going to get here, which is excellent baseball played by a pair of teams that actually look a whole lot like one another. We know what else we're going to get, too: an incredibly interesting series. Which side has the edge?
Catcher
William Contreras, over the past five years, has a pretty solid argument to make as being the best all-around catcher in the National League. While his bat over the last two seasons (110 OPS+) isn’t quite what it was at his peak from 2022-24 (129 OPS+), it’s reliably solid, and then of course he’s been fantastic in eight playoff games, posting a 1.157 OPS with three homers. It’s hard to overstate how important the midseason acquisition of Liam Hicks (129 OPS+ in 41 games for Tampa Bay) was, really helping to lengthen a top-heavy lineup, though he hasn’t done much with the bat in the playoffs. Given relatively similar defensive value, we’ll give a small edge based on track record.
Advantage: Brewers
First base
It's a tale of two winding paths here, as Jonathan Aranda finally had his breakout last season, a decade after he signed as an amateur free agent with Tampa Bay, and of course Jake Bauers' long road to get to this point has been well-chronicled. Bauers has the offensive edge both in terms of power and getting on base, and neither are terribly strong defensive players, so given the mild 2026 regular-season advantage and also the superior performance in October, it’s hard not to choose Bauers on this. Great stories, both.
Advantage: Brewers
Second base
Brice Turang is the best all-around second baseman in the game, pairing excellent defense with a more recently found power stroke, popping 21 homers and driving in 100. The Rays have certainly found some ways to get value out of their second-base duo of Richie Palacios and Ben Williamson, but it’s a relatively below-average spot for Tampa Bay and, either way, we’re comparing to Milwaukee’s best-in-class superstar. This one is probably the biggest mismatch of any pairing on the list.
Advantage: Brewers
Shortstop
Here’s how you know how well-regarded Taylor Walls is on defense: The Rays continue to play him every day despite a near-total lack of offense from the position, as he’s posted all of a .381 OPS this month, and even that was juiced a little by the inexplicable three walks that Cleveland issued him in ALCS Game 6. It’s not just a small-sample thing, either, as Walls has been a routinely ineffective hitter for the entirety of his career.
There’s no doubt that Milwaukee’s Cooper Pratt is a stronger offensive force, though that’s been more good than great, with a league-average line as a rookie and a mostly singles-based approach in the playoffs. While he’s expected to be a quality shortstop as his career progresses, a number of important miscues in the postseason tilt this one to the more surehanded Walls.
Advantage: Rays
Third base
If there’s some argument that this series features more depth than true superstars, then that case falls apart a little at third, where Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero posted his second consecutive 40-plus homer season on his way to, most likely, some high placement on AL MVP ballots. It’s true that prior to his ALCS Game 6 homer, his bat had been relatively quiet in October, but we’re also talking about all of eight games against some of the best pitching the sport has to offer. (The average fastball he’s seen? 96.8 mph.) There’s an obvious speed-and-defense edge for Milwaukee in David Hamilton and Joey Ortiz, but not quite so much that you’d take either or both over Caminero, or that it’s really close at all.
Advantage: Rays
Left field
This is actually the most fun comparison, because who do you like more, the 22-year-old power-and-defense superstar in Jackson Chourio -- the only player in history to have three 20-20 seasons through age-22 -- or the 25-year-old elite speed-and-contact guy in Chandler Simpson, who improved his defense to the point that both were named Gold Glove finalists last week? It’s yet another reminder that there’s more than one way to provide value, and certainly both teams are very pleased with their situations here. It’s hard, though, not to default to Chourio, who might already be a top-20 position player in the sport. If both can run and field, and only one has any power, then the advantage writes itself.
Advantage: Brewers
Center field
In Garrett Mitchell and Jonny DeLuca, you have two very strong defensive center fielders, though you’d probably give the slight edge here to DeLuca. (Cedric Mullins also carries a good glove, though this spot has belonged to DeLuca all month.) The question about their bats is what shape of production you prefer, in that Mitchell struck out considerably more than DeLuca, but he also had an on-base percentage 54 points higher, thanks in large part to a walk rate three times as high. While we’re not weighing postseason performance too much here, it’s worth noting that Mitchell has had some huge hits, while DeLuca mostly has not. This is about as razor-thin as we’ll see here, but even if Mitchell’s glove isn’t as good, it’s still good, and he gets on base. Edge, Milwaukee. A small one, anyway.
Advantage: Brewers
Right field
For everything that Sal Frelick has done for the Brewers over his four seasons with the team -- and he has done quite a bit -- this was not a terribly strong season for him, posting a career-worst 70 OPS+, and he’s managed only three singles and a few walks in the playoffs. That’s not to say that he can’t help the team win in other ways, because he can and does, but Tampa Bay’s Victor Mesa Jr. has been one of the team’s breakout stars, putting up not only a 127 OPS+ but also some truly elite defensive metrics, in just half a season. You’re already familiar, anyway, with his absolute cannon of a throwing arm. Mesa Jr. wasn’t on the Opening Day roster and didn’t even join the Rays for good until late May. He might just be one of the most important players in the World Series, though.
Advantage: Rays
Designated hitter
It would be hard to find two players who mean more to their respective teams than veterans Yandy Díaz (in his eighth season with Tampa Bay) and recently appointed Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich (in his ninth season as a Brewer). Neither plays the field much anymore, nor is either at or near their peak of offensive performance these days. But Díaz far outperformed Yelich during the regular season (124 OPS+ to 91 OPS+, where again, 100 is average), and that’s held true in the postseason, too, where Yelich has been held out of certain games against tough lefties in favor of Andrew Vaughn. At DH, literally the only thing that matters is “dangerous bat,” and that’s Díaz still, after all these years.
Advantage: Rays
Starting pitchers
If we’re talking about each team’s top three starters, which represent the bulk of a postseason rotation, then it’s Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser for Milwaukee, and Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez for Tampa Bay. Those six pitchers, so far in the playoffs, have combined for a 1.87 ERA. They’re not that good, obviously, with every underlying metric saying that the strikeout rate has been just average, and that they’ve been bailed out to some extent by excellent defense and relief pitching.
Still: When Misiorowski -- the presumptive NL Cy Young winner, the most dominant per-batter pitcher of the moment -- has the highest postseason ERA of these six, you know how strong each team is here. You really can’t look at full-season stats, either, because it goes without saying that the Tampa Bay version of Peralta is a very different pitcher than New York version we saw prior to the Trade Deadline. Misiorowski is the best of the six, but is he that much better than Rasmussen right now, himself an ace? Maybe not.
These are two strengths, but we like Tampa Bay ever so slightly more for one reason: depth. No Milwaukee starter, not even the top ones, has managed to get past five innings in the playoffs so far, which puts a lot of pressure on the bullpens. (There’s a particularly interesting angle here if Tampa Bay’s high-contact, flat-swing hitters can foul off enough Misiorowski pitches to wear him out, as has already happened to him this month.) If you look past the top three, you’d probably take Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour to get outs a little more than Milwaukee’s Shane Drohan and Dustin May.
They’re both good, obviously. They’re World Series starting rotations. We’d give the ever-so-slight edge to Tampa Bay in a best of seven.
Advantage: Rays
Relief pitchers
If Milwaukee’s starters have been more good than great this month, then their relievers have more than picked up the slack, as you’ve almost certainly heard the note that in 40 2/3 postseason innings, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed all of six earned runs. While most of the focus there lands on Aaron Ashby or closer Trevor Megill, realize that JoJo Romero has a 47% strikeout rate this month, and that Abner Uribe, Antonio Senzatela, Megill and Ashby are all averaging more than 98 mph on their heaters this month. In fact, it is the second-hardest-throwing bullpen of the pitch tracking era (since 2008) -- at 98 mph even -- and the hardest that doesn’t include Mason Miller.
It makes, then, for an ironic matchup against a Tampa Bay bullpen that is A) also very good but B) does not throw hard, comparatively, at just 93.2 mph. (That goes down slightly, if you don't include Peralta’s impressive appearance in ALCS Game 4.) Much depends on the status of Bryan Baker, their All-Star closer, who was used so heavily against Cleveland that his fastball, which averaged 96.3 mph during the regular season, sunk below 93 mph in ALCS Game 6.
He was still good, of course. All the Rays are. It’s just hard not to go with Milwaukee, given their superior depth and full rest.
Advantage: Brewers
Prediction
It should be clear by now that this is an incredibly tightly matched series between two mirror-image teams, the best in their respective leagues, and you could as easily claim “rust or rest” for Milwaukee after their layoff, no matter which narrative you’d like to go with. Milwaukee has the biggest-name pitcher in Misiorowski; Tampa Bay has clearly the biggest star hitter in Caminero; and both sides play strong defense and win in ways that aren’t just waiting for the homer.
We like that Milwaukee has the home-field advantage, and the bullpen edge, and also that their lineup just seems a little deeper; in the second half of the season, no team -- not the Dodgers, not the Cubs, not anyone -- got more production from the No. 6 through 9 spots in their lineup than Milwaukee. That’s in part because of the middle infield, where the Brewers were third best, while Tampa Bay was third weakest. There’s at least some question about what shape Baker will be in, though three days of rest before the World Series ought to help.
It won’t be a cakewalk, because there’s too much talent and similarity on both sides for that. But every small edge matters, and Milwaukee has enough of them that we expect the second World Series title in city history, and the first for the Brewers franchise. Get ready to slide, Bernie.
Brewers in seven.

item.title: [MLB.com] Por qué el choque entre Caminero y Misiorowski en el Juego 1 sacará chispas
item.dc:creator: David Adler
item.description: Misiorowski lanza más fuerte que cualquier pitcher abridor en el béisbol. Caminero hace swing con su bate más rápido que nadie. Es un enfrentamiento de alto octanaje digno del Clásico de Otoño, y lo tendremos desde el primer momento. Lanzadores abridores con mayor velocidad promedio de recta en el 2026: 1. Jacob Misiorowski: 100.6 mph 2-E. Hunter Greene: 98.3 mph 2-E. Bubba Chandler: 98.3 mph 4-E. Eury Pérez: 98.2 mph 4-E. Jared Jones: 98.2 mph Bateadores con mayor velocidad promedio de swing en
item.content:encoded:
Misiorowski lanza más fuerte que cualquier pitcher abridor en el béisbol. Caminero hace swing con su bate más rápido que nadie. Es un enfrentamiento de alto octanaje digno del Clásico de Otoño, y lo tendremos desde el primer momento.
Lanzadores abridores con mayor velocidad promedio de recta en el 2026:
1. Jacob Misiorowski: 100.6 mph
2-E. Hunter Greene: 98.3 mph
2-E. Bubba Chandler: 98.3 mph
4-E. Eury Pérez: 98.2 mph
4-E. Jared Jones: 98.2 mph
Bateadores con mayor velocidad promedio de swing en el 2026:
- Junior Caminero: 79.4 mph
- Jordan Walker: 79.3 mph
- Nick Kurtz: 78.2 mph
- Cam Smith: 78.0 mph
- Oneil Cruz: 77.7 mph
Nos encantan los enfrentamientos de "los mejores contra los mejores", y no nos vamos a quedar cortos en el Juego 1. Caminero siempre trae su mejor swing; Misiorowski siempre suelta su recta al máximo. Su batalla es sólo otra forma en la que la Serie Mundial podría decidirse por pura velocidad.
Caminero ha alcanzado una velocidad de swing de 75 mph o más --ese es el umbral de "swing rápido" de Statcast-- en el 84% de sus swings esta temporada. Dos de cada tres pitcheos que lanza Misiorowski son rectas, la mayor cantidad entre los abridores, y dos de cada tres de esas rectas superan las 100 mph. Ambos jugadores van a fondo.
Los totales en bruto son simplemente alucinantes. "Miz" ha lanzado 1,211 rectas de tres dígitos en una sola temporada. Eso es casi 500 más que cualquier otro lanzador en un año desde que se empezó a rastrear los pitcheos en el 2008 (el cubano Aroldis Chapman alcanzó los tres dígitos 723 veces en el 2016). Es casi 1,000 más que cualquier otro abridor (Hunter Greene llegó a los tres dígitos 337 veces en el 2022). Y aún no ha terminado. Disculpen si sonamos como un disco rayado, pero Misiorowski se ha pasado este año rompiendo básicamente todos los récords de velocidad que tenemos.
Caminero, por su parte, ha desatado la mayor cantidad de "swings rápidos" entre todos los bateadores con 954. Sólo tenemos datos de rastreo de bates desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas del 2023, pero esa es la mayor cifra en un año para cualquiera hasta ahora. Así que si alguien tiene la fuerza para alcanzar el fuego de Misiorowski y conectarlo con contundencia, ese es Caminero.
Y estos dos muchachos llevarán las cosas mucho más allá de simplemente "rápido". Olvídense de las 100 mph --Misiorowski ha alcanzado un máximo de 105.5 mph esta temporada, una marca que sólo el gran lanzallamas Chapman ha superado, y a la que ningún abridor se ha acercado ni a dos mph (Justin Verlander y Jordan Hicks son los únicos otros que siquiera han tocado las 103). El primer pitcheo de "Miz" en los playoffs fue a 104.8 mph, un récord en la era del rastreo de pitcheos en postemporada.
El envío más rápido realizado en la Serie Mundial desde 2008 es de 103.2 mph, logrado por Chapman en el 2016. El más rápido de un abridor es de 101.1 mph, de Noah Syndergaard en el 2015. Misiorowski podría destrozar ambas marcas para el primer inning del Juego 1 --quizás incluso contra Caminero.
¿Será el bate de Caminero lo suficientemente rápido para alcanzar el fuego extremo de Misiorowski? Bueno, ha logrado una velocidad de swing de 80 mph o más en 536 ocasiones esta temporada --más que toda la alineación de los Cerveceros junta (499). Y ya vimos lo que puede hacer ese tipo de velocidad de swing: en el jonrón de Caminero contra Cade Smith en la victoria decisiva de los Rays en la SCLA, su velocidad de swing fue de 81.2 mph. El resultado fue el primer cuadrangular que el cerrador de los Guardianes había permitido con su splitter en las Grandes Ligas.
Caminero necesitará hasta la última gota de esa velocidad de swing para devolver las rectas de Misiorowski. "Miz" ha acumulado 354 swings fallidos y 168 ponches con su recta de cuatro costuras esta temporada; ambas cifras sólo son superadas por las logradas por Gerrit Cole en 2019 (384 y 193, respectivamente) como las máximas en una campaña en la era del rastreo de pitcheos. ¿La velocidad promedio de esos ponches para Misiorowski? 101.3 mph.
Curiosamente, en la única ocasión en que Misiorowski y Caminero se enfrentaron --el 1ro de abril--, Misiorowski apenas le lanzó rectas a Caminero. Caminero vio tres rectas de cuatro costuras y cinco sliders en dos turnos al bate, y ninguna de esas rectas alcanzó los tres dígitos. Pero el slider lo dominó. "Miz" ponchó a Caminero una vez y lo hizo batear una línea en la otra.
Pero estamos bastante seguros de que en la Serie Mundial, Misiorowski soltará la recta contra Caminero --especialmente después de ver cómo los Guardianes lo atacaron con envíos altos en la SCLA. Misiorowski domina con la recta alta. Sin embargo, ha estado buscando abanicados con su bola de cuatro costuras en los playoffs, por lo que tal vez Caminero también pueda darle pelea.
La verdad, todo lo que queremos es que Caminero haga unos swings descomunales contra el fuego de Misiorowski mañana por la noche. Y esperamos verlo con total seguridad. Si el swing más rápido del béisbol conecta con la recta más veloz del béisbol, eso podría decidir el juego.

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Rays vs. Brewers 2026 World Series Picks and Player Predictions in MLB Postseason

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 World Series is going to make history. Either the Tampa Bay Rays or Milwaukee Brewers are about to claim their first championship.
So, that's what's at stake. But what should everyone expect?
According to FanDuel, the Brewers are the favorite (-172) and the Rays are the underdog (+148). Yet this is ultimately a 103-win team against a 98-win team, and both clubs play a very similar style of baseball.
It's therefore worth getting in depth with the specifics of this matchup before making any predictions. Who are the key players? What are the key matchups? What are the X-factors that will determine the series?
Let's see what we can see, and then we'll present picks for the winner of the World Series and for the World Series MVP.
World Series Schedule
1 of 6
All Games on Fox
Game 1 (Friday, October 23): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 2 (Saturday, October 24): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 3 (Monday, October 26): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 4 (Tuesday, October 27): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 5 (Wednesday, October 28)*: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 6 (Friday, October 30)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 7 (Saturday, October 31)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
*If necessary
Key Players for the Rays
2 of 6
3B Junior Caminero
Caminero has been the driving force in the Rays' lineup over the last two seasons, slamming over 40 home runs and racking up over 100 RBI in each. Yet he went cool with a season-low .772 OPS in September, and he initially struggled to snap out of it once the postseason began.
That changed in the last three games of the ALCS. The 23-year-old had hits in all three, including a home run in the clincher that he soaked in as much as possible (and then some). Is he back? It sure seems like he's back.
DH Yandy Díaz
Even if he's not as big of a power threat as Caminero, Díaz rarely fails to have a good at-bat or to hit the ball on a line. He's hit an even .300 across the last four seasons, and he led the AL in hits this year.
The 35-year-old was not the MVP of the ALCS, but he could have been. He torched the Cleveland Guardians for a 1.061 OPS and six extra-base hits, culminating in the two-run homer that iced Game 6.
RHP Drew Rasmussen
Even if he didn't get a ton of hype, Rasmussen was a ball-knower's ace in the regular season between 2022 and 2026. He posted a sub-3.00 ERA annually, and he even led the AL in WHIP this season.
Now the secret is out. The 31-year-old's three starts in the playoffs have yielded just three earned runs in 21.0 innings, with 23 strikeouts and only three walks. His changeup has been especially lethal, holding hitters to three hits in 24 at-bats.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Peralta was with the Brewers this time last year, and his journey since then has taken him to lows with the New York Mets and now highs again with the Rays. He's coming into the World Series hot off being named the ALCS MVP.
The 30-year-old doesn't offer a complicated scouting report. He's throwing his fastball about 70 percent of the time in October, daring hitters to beat him on his best pitch. They haven't, going just 8-for-39 against it so far.
RHP Bryan Baker
Baker blew his third save of the year back on May 13. He hasn't blown one since in 53 turns on the mound, along the way allowing just five earned runs in 52.0 innings.
The 31-year-old's velocity has declined throughout the year, but that has yet to translate into any kind of advantage for hitters. It could be because he uses his fastball and changeup in roughly equal tandem, using both to hold hitters to one hit in 21 at-bats thus far in October.
Key Players for the Brewers
3 of 6
LF Jackson Chourio
The Brewers signed Chourio to an $84 million contract before he had played even one game in the majors. It has paid off in the form of three straight 20-20 seasons, and all before he's turned even 23 years old.
On paper, his .171 batting average and .553 OPS say he's not having a good postseason. Yet even if the Brewers would like more consistency, they'll take the clutch gene that has delivered seven RBI, including two that snatched victory from the jaws of defeat.
1B Jake Bauers
There were 137 players who took at least 500 plate appearances this season, and only 12 of them had a better OPS+ than Bauers. Not bad for a 31-year-old who had an 84 OPS+ for his career coming into the season.
Bauers has become a menace of another sort in the playoffs. Even if he only has one multi-hit game, he's shown tremendous patience in racking up a .441 OBP and driving in six runs. He had multiple at-bats that dug the Los Angeles Dodgers' grave as he was winning MVP honors for the NLCS.
C William Contreras
Contreras has regressed a little as a regular-season performer, but you'd never know from how he's hit this postseason. He's hit safely in six of eight games, with three home runs and five RBI.
Also, don't overlook his mastery of the ABS. He challenged a league-high 185 calls from behind the plate this season, and he won 80 of them. He's kept it up in the playoffs, going 8-for-12 and winning some truly game-changing challenges.
RHP Jacob Misiorowski
After making 30 starts and pitching to a 1.80 ERA and a 5.7 K/BB ratio, Misiorowski is going to win the NL Cy Young Award. As soon as he hit 104.8 mph on his first pitch of the playoffs, he seemed ready to tap into still another gear for October.
Except, he hasn't made it past the fifth inning in either of his two assignments, consisting of nine hits and four walks in 8.1 total innings. He clearly isn't gassed, but he'll need to be better to maximize Milwaukee's chances in the World Series.
LHP Aaron Ashby
Milwaukee's entire bullpen has been incredible in the playoffs, handling 40.2 innings and allowing just six earned runs. Trevor Megill and Abner Uribe deserve their flowers, too.
Yet Ashby has simply been on another level, thus far posting 12.1 shutout innings and allowing just four hits and three walks. The next hitter who gets a knock off his curveball, changeup or slider will be the first.
Matchups That Will Define the World Series
4 of 6
Junior Caminero's Bat Speed vs. the Brewers' Velocity
What makes Caminero so dangerous? For one thing, nobody whips the bat through the zone like he does. His average swing this season was 79.5 mph, the highest of any qualified hitter.
In the World Series, though, he'll be up against a Brewers pitching staff that is averaging 98.3 mph on the fastball. That's almost a full mile per hour faster than the hardest-throwing staff of the 2025 playoffs.
Chandler Simpson's Speed vs. the Brewers' Defenders
Simpson is basically a free 90 feet in human form. He had 11 more infield hits than anyone else this season. He also stole 46 bases, and took 21 more bases on wild pitches, passed balls and the like. It all makes him a rare weapon.
The Brewers, though, could be up to stopping him. Their infield was among the very best this season with a total output of +7 Outs Above Average. More to the point, William Contreras was second in the league in caught-stealings.
Jacob Misiorowski vs. the Rays' High-Contact Offense
Misiorowski's contact rate during the regular season was a mere 65.5 percent, easily the best in baseball. Yet he hasn't been nearly as successful at avoiding contact in the postseason, where his rate has jumped to 77.4 percent.
If the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers could do that, the Rays should be able to as well. They led MLB with an 81.8 contact percentage during the regular season, and it has only gone down to 77.2 in the postseason.
The Brewers' Lefty Bats vs. the Rays' Righty-Heavy Pitching
It isn't just Jake Bauers. Milwaukee's left-handed hitters as a collective have a 122 wRC+ in the playoffs, and that's despite facing some darn good left-handed pitching. In the NLCS alone, they faced a pair of two-time Cy Young Award winners in Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
The Rays aren't nearly as synonymous with left-handed pitching, indeed carrying only three for the ALCS against Cleveland. And one of them (Ian Seymour) isn't looking so hot after carrying a heavy workload in the regular season.
X-Factors That Will Define the World Series
5 of 6
Home Cooking
The best home record in MLB during the regular season? Well, it was a tie at 55-26… between the Rays and Brewers, naturally.
Neither club has fumbled its home-field advantage in the postseason. The Brewers are 4-0 at American Family Field. The Rays are 4-1 at Tropicana Field. So on paper, both teams can claim to have an advantage on their home turf.
That said, it's the Brewers who truly stand to find out. If this series goes the distance, they'll have the honor of hosting the finale in Milwaukee on October 31.
The Three True Outcomes
For the uninitiated, the three true outcomes are strikeouts, walks and home runs. Neither the Rays nor the Brewers was necessarily synonymous with the concept during the regular season, specifically in the sense that they both ranked in the bottom 10 of the league in home runs.
They have since gone on wildly different paths in October. The Brewers' percentage of three true outcomes when on offense is at 47 percent. For the Rays, it's only 31 percent.
Both paths have ultimately arrived in the same spot, but this may be where we find out which one wins the day. Can the Brewers keep winning by racking up walks and homers? Or, will the Rays avoid enough strikeouts to gain the inside track?
Speed and Defense
Regardless of what happens in the TTO department, neither of these teams should be expected to give much away, while both should be expected to take as much as they can get.
In other words, they're both good at fielding the ball and running the bases. The Rays and Brewers each ranked in the top six for defensive efficiency this season. They were both top-five in stolen bases, and separated by just two steals in the end.
In these respects, the World Series should reward baseball purists for their attention. The result could come down to fine margins—a ball just out of reach or a tag applied just in time.
Predicting the Outcome and World Series MVP
6 of 6
For the World Series: Brewers in 6
Regarding my credentials, I had the Brewers sweeping the Dodgers in the NLCS before it happened. So, I've been right at least once in my life.
Yet whereas the Dodgers looked old, slow and generally out of sorts while trying to keep pace with Milwaukee, the Rays are cut from the same cloth as a ballclub. They're younger and more athletic, and committed to playing smart, clean baseball that emphasizes the little things to add up to one big haymaker.
One area where Milwaukee should have an edge is on offense. The Brewers have as many as five hitters you really have to worry about. The Rays really only have three, in Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda.
The Brewers' bullpen stands out as another advantage, even if they'll need more from their starters to avoid their relievers getting overexposed in a longer series. It, too, is deeper than what the Rays have to offer. And let's be real that Milwaukee relievers are simply on a heater right now.
So, congratulations in advance to the Brewers. If anything is worth a 57-year wait, it's a World Series championship.
For World Series MVP: William Contreras
This pick is partially about deferring to a hot hand. The Brewers have gotten contributions from all their hitters in the postseason, but Contreras has been a constant the whole way through. You just can't fake a 1.157 OPS.
Between his ABS challenges and his ability to control the running game, Contreras' defense also stands to be a huge factor in the World Series. He could also be a not-so-secret weapon when Freddy Peralta pitches for the Rays. If anyone knows him, it's the guy who caught him 81 times between 2023 and 2025.

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Tarik Skubal and the Next 10 Players to Sign $200 Million Contracts
item.dc:creator: Joel Reuter

item.content:encoded:
Assuming something resembling a normal MLB offseason emerges from the rubble of CBA negotiations this winter, two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal could be in line for a record-setting payday for a pitcher.
At the very least, he's a lock to exceed $200 million in his first trip to free agency. He could be eyeing a $400 million mega deal as one of the best pitchers to ever hit the open market.
There is a steep drop-off in earning power behind him in this year's free-agent class, but there are high-profile extension candidates across baseball, and more and more teams are making an early push to lock up young talent.
Ahead, we've taken a shot at predicting the next 10 players who will sign $200 million contracts, with age, production, long-term outlook and proximity to free agency all factors in building the list.
2B/SS CJ Abrams
1 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2028
Whether he is the centerpiece of a blockbuster deal or a foundational building block for the Nationals, CJ Abrams has put himself in position for a massive payday following a career year offensively.
Still only 26 years old, he posted a 127 OPS+ with 30 doubles, 33 home runs, 106 RBI and 34 steals in a 5.1-WAR season, earning his second All-Star selection in the last three years.
Despite his defensive shortcomings and a potential long-term move to second base, his age and offensive impact make him an obvious candidate for a lucrative extension and the potential headliner of the 2028-29 free-agent class.
Even as a second baseman, he will have a strong case to eclipse the seven-year, $175 million deal that Marcus Semien signed with the Rangers prior to his age-31 season.
DH Yordan Alvarez
2 of 10
Contract Status: Two years, $53.7 million remaining on contract
Teams buying out the final year or two of a superstar's contract to lock him up with a fresh long-term extension is common practice. No one is a more obvious candidate for that approach than presumptive AL MVP Yordan Alvarez.
With two years remaining on his six-year, $115 million extension, and fresh off a season where he hit .316/.432/.601 with 42 home runs and 106 RBI to make a run at AL Triple Crown honors, he is unquestionably one of the game's elite offensive talents.
His back-loaded current deal will pay him $26.8 million in 2027 and 2028, so replacing those two years with a fresh long-term deal and an AAV somewhere in the $30 million range would not actually be tacking that much onto the payroll next year.
The Astros could also decide it's time to rebuild, which would make him a blockbuster trade chip and an obvious extension candidate for any team that ponies up the prospect talent to land him.
3B Junior Caminero
3 of 10
Contract Status: Pre-arbitration, controllable through 2030
Junior Caminero will not reach arbitration for the first time until after the 2027 season. At that point, he might be in line for a record-setting payday if he continues to produce at the level he has in the last two seasons.
2025: 154 G, 130 OPS+, 45 HR, 110 RBI, 4.3 WAR
2026: 162 G, 144 OPS+, 42 HR, 101 RBI, 5.7 WAR
The Rays have never signed a player to a contract worth a guaranteed $200 million, but Caminero is a face-of-the-franchise caliber superstar worth committing a significant chunk of the payroll to for the foreseeable future.
The additional revenue that will come from their World Series trip, coupled with the potential for a salary floor to be instituted in the upcoming CBA negotiations, raises the chances of Caminero inking an extension.
The 11-year, $288.8 million extension Bobby Witt Jr. signed with the Royals is a reasonable starting point in negotiations, but we are inching closer to Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s 14-year, $500 million deal with every ball he sends into the seats.
SS Elly De La Cruz
4 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2029
The Reds have already approached Elly De La Cruz with an extension offer.
"We engaged in Spring Training of 2025 and presented an offer," Reds president of baseball operations Nick Krall told reporters in January. "The offer would have been the largest contract in Reds history. We didn't have any further conversations regarding the offer."
The current largest contract in club history is the 10-year, $225 million deal Joey Votto signed in 2012, so he has already had the opportunity to join the $200 million club and declined.
With Scott Boras as his agent and coming off the best season of his career, in which he showed improved defensive chops alongside his tantalizing power-speed combination, the likelihood of him signing an early extension is extremely low.
The Reds could eventually put him on the trade block if an extension doesn't work out. Any team acquiring him would likely want to get a long-term deal on the books. That provides multiple avenues for a huge payday in the coming years.
RHP Logan Gilbert
5 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2027
The volatility of pitchers makes mega contracts far less common, though Dylan Cease did reel in a seven-year, $210 million payday from the Blue Jays last offseason, even coming off an inconsistent contract year.
Over the last five seasons, Logan Gilbert has averaged 31 starts and 180.1 innings while posting a 3.46 ERA and 110 ERA+. That durability and consistency make him a prime candidate for a massive contract.
His 14.2 WAR over that five-year stretch ranks among the top 20 among all pitchers. Whether it's an extension from the Mariners or as the top arm in the 2027-28 free-agent class, a boatload of money is on the horizon.
The 29-year-old played on a $10.9 million salary last season. He is projected to earn $15.4 million in his final year of arbitration, which would make him an extremely attractive trade chip if Seattle decided to deal from its pitching depth.
SS Gunnar Henderson
6 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2028
In a down year by his own lofty standards, Gunnar Henderson was still a 3.2-WAR player, posting a 102 OPS+ with 57 extra-base hits and 24 home runs while starting 149 games at shortstop.
After a 6.1-WAR rookie season in 2023 and an 8.8-WAR follow-up season in which he finished fourth in AL MVP voting, he firmly established himself as one of the game's brightest young stars.
He looked like a clear long-term building block while the Orioles were on the rise, but their stalled progress toward contention led to the Adley Rutschman trade this past summer. That might not be the end of the roster turnover.
MLB insider Buster Olney made headlines in August when he said, "he's not going to sign there long term in all likelihood," while discussing Henderson's future. Whether he is the next homegrown star out the door or reaches free agency after the 2028 season, he will command big money.
1B Munetaka Murakami
7 of 10
Contract Status: One year, $17.5 million remaining on contract
Despite a prolific run in the Japanese League, Munetaka Murakami was not met with the robust market many expected last offseason due to swing-and-miss concerns. He signed a two-year, $34 million deal with the White Sox. That translated into him becoming the center of their surprising climb to the postseason.
The 26-year-old had a .207 batting average and 35.4 percent strikeout rate, but his on-base ability (16.6 BB%, .347 OBP) and power (130 OPS+, 35 HR) still made him one of the most impactful sluggers in baseball.
If he can match that performance in his second season stateside, a significantly more lucrative contract likely awaits in his next trip to free agency.
Pete Alonso got a $31 million AAV on a five-year deal ahead of his age-31 season as an elite power hitter with limited secondary value. Murakami will be four years younger when he shops for his next contract. Even if he doesn't match that AAV, a longer deal could easily push the full value above $200 million.
SS Jeremy Peña
8 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2027
At first glance, Jeremy Peña is not an obvious candidate for a $200 million deal, but never underestimate the earning power of a quality shortstop in a thin market at the position.
The 29-year-old has taken his offensive game to another level the past two seasons, logging a .291/.345/.477 line and 130 OPS+ despite missing some time to injuries. He remains a standout defender.
With 22.2 WAR over his first five seasons and a playoff track record few players his age can match, he would be an obvious extension candidate if not for the fact that he switched agents and hired Scott Boras in June 2025.
That clearly indicates he intends to test the market after the 2027 season, which could put him on the trade block this winter. Xander Bogaerts was the same age when he signed his 11-year, $280 million contract with the Padres. While he had a longer track record, Peña is a far superior defender.
LHP Tarik Skubal
9 of 10
Contract Status: Free agent
Tarik Skubal was the only 2026-27 free agent projected to earn a contract north of $200 million in my recent article predicting the 10 biggest contracts handed out in free agency this winter.
The nine-year, $324 million contract that Gerrit Cole signed prior to the 2020 season is a logical starting point, but Skubal could be aiming for a $40 million AAV given his track record and the rising cost of frontline pitching.
Barring a surprise mega-deal for Japanese League star Teruaki Sato, the odds are extremely high that Skubal will be the next free agent to lock in at least $200 million.
With a 2.42 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 655 strikeouts in 546 innings over the last three seasons, he has firmly established himself as one of the best pitchers in the sport in the prime of his career.
OF James Wood
10 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2030
One of the key return pieces from the Juan Soto blockbuster trade with the Padres, James Wood has developed into one of the best young sluggers in baseball and the face of the franchise for the Nationals.
The towering 6'6" outfielder has put together consecutive 30-homer, 3-WAR seasons. This year, he quietly developed into a more complete hitter beneath the surface of his 144 OPS+ and 30 long balls.
The 24-year-old raised his walk rate (12.3 to 16.4 percent), lowered his strikeout rate (32.1 to 28.7 percent) and added 21 steals in 25 attempts without sacrificing any of his power production.
After signing Cade Cavalli to a four-year, $47 million extension in September, the Nationals could be looking to lock up more pieces this offseason. Wood is the top candidate for a franchise cornerstone-level deal.

item.title: [NBC Sports] 2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft: Can you trust Garrett Crochet in 2027? What about Byron Buxton?
