item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will play a Suds vs. Sun World Series that will produce a first-time champion and likely baseball's first all-indoor championship.
The best-of-seven showdown between low-payroll pennant winners opens Friday night in Milwaukee. It'll be the first World Series between title-less teams since the Philadelphia Phillies defeated the Kansas City Royals in 1980 and just the second since 1910.
One city is known for the television sitcom “ Laverne & Shirley," the home of Harley-Davidson motorcycles, cheeseheads and breweries that have included Miller, Pabst and Schlitz. The other is a vacation destination featuring warm weather, beaches and art museums.
“They’re highly athletic but so are we. I’m excited to see two great teams that play the game a little differently than maybe it’s been played the last decade or so,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said after his team defeated Cleveland in six games for the AL pennant. “We’re going to use our speed. We’re going to bunt when it’s called for. We’ll try to get matchups and I can assure you they’re going to do the same.”
Just five of the current 30 teams have never won a title, with Colorado, San Diego and Seattle also ringless.
“The city is ready. I know that the fans are ready, and I know that we’ll be ready,” said Milwaukee's Jake Bauers, MVP of the four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NL Championship Series.
Milwaukee's Jacob Misiorowski heads the pitchers with his 100 mph-plus heat, and each team features a dynamic 22-year-old anchoring the lineup: Jackson Chourio of the Brewers and Junior Caminero of the Rays. Tampa Bay's Freddy Peralta and Drew Rasmussen could pitch against their former team.
“I don’t know how the people, the fans are going to take it, but I’m happy to be go there,” said Peralta, the ALCS MVP. “I have a lot of people that I love over there, people that care about me and I’m happy to be there and be able to compete together and take a lot of pictures and videos."
The Brewers started as the expansion Seattle Pilots in 1969, then were bought by Bud Selig's group in bankruptcy court and moved to Milwaukee for the 1970 season. The team's only Series trip was a seven-game loss to St. Louis in the 1982 Suds Series, back when the Brewers were in the American League.
Tampa Bay launched as the expansion Devil Rays in 1998 and dropped the “Devil” ahead of the 2008 season. The team's two Series appearances ended with losses to Philadelphia in 2008 and the Dodgers in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season.
Best face each other for 6th time in wild-card era
This will be only the sixth time since the start of the wild-card era in 1995 that teams with the top records in each league meet in the World Series after Atlanta-Cleveland (1995), New York Yankees-Braves (1999), Boston-St. Louis (2013), Dodgers-Rays (2020) and Dodgers-Yankees (2024).
Two low-payroll teams in Series for first time in 35 years
Milwaukee had MLB’s 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31. Tampa Bay was 25th.
Not since 1991 had both pennant winners been among the bottom 50% in player spending. Minnesota was 15th among 26 teams when it beat Atlanta (19th) in seven games.
Matchup with a ceiling
Tampa Bay’s ballpark has a fixed roof and Milwaukee’s is retractable — it probably will be closed with game-time temperatures predicted to be in the upper 40s or low 50s.
When all World Series games were played at retractable-roof ballparks in 2020 (Texas) and 2023 (Texas and Arizona), there were three open-air games each year.
The roofs of both ballparks came into play this postseason.
In the ninth inning of Milwaukee’s 3-2 win over the Padres in Game 1 of their NL Division Series, San Diego’s Ty France hit a high drive that appeared it might be headed over the left-field wall for a go-ahead homer until it struck a cable on the retractable roof in Milwaukee.
Two nights later, Yankees rookie Spencer Jones hit a flyball off a catwalk at Tropicana Field that was caught by Rays right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. for an out in the second inning of New York’s 5-2 loss in Game 2 of their AL Division Series.
Common ties
Greg Vaughn, Willy Adames and Matt Garza are the most prominent players with lengthy stretches on both teams, and Bauers made his big league debut with the Rays in 2018.
Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked for the Rays for nine years before Milwaukee hired him as an assistant GM in October 2015.
One of baseball's great nicknames
Those 1982 Brewers were known as Harvey's Wallbangers, a nickname given by first baseman Cecil Cooper. The Brewers led the major leagues in home runs under manager Harvey Kuenn and had a roster with five future Hall of Famers: Robin Yount, Paul Molitor, Rollie Fingers, Ted Simmons and Don Sutton.
Haunted hotel?
Various players over the years have claimed The Pfister Hotel, where many teams stay in Milwaukee, is haunted. Opened in 1893, the hotel has Romanesque Revival architecture, and players have claimed to hear spooky noises and footsteps.
If there is a Game 7, it would be played in Milwaukee on Halloween night.
Boss Man
Milwaukee's Pat Murphy, winner of the last two NL Manager of the Year awards, has two tattoos referencing Bruce Springsteen: “No Retreat No Surrender” on his left forearm and “The Boss” on his back.
He first went to a Springsteen concert in 1980 when he was in college, then another when he was coaching at Notre Dame.
“He grew up a Catholic kid in New Jersey. I was a Catholic kid from upstate New York,” the 67-year-old Murphy said. “There’s just so much that resonates with me how he speaks about things.”
Ballpark histories
The 1982 Series was played at Milwaukee County Stadium, home of the Braves from 1953-65 before they moved to Atlanta, and then the Brewers from 1970-2000. This year's championship will be played at American Family Field. Known as Miller Park from 2001-20, the ballpark is adjacent to the County Stadium site. It was host of the 2002 All-Star Game, which ended in a 7-7, 11-inning tie after both teams ran out of pitchers.
Milwaukee's ballpark is known for its Racing Sausages in the middle of the sixth inning, with the Brat, Polish, Italian, Hot Dog and Chorizo competing. It also has the Uecker Seat in the last row of section 422 in the left-field upper deck — it includes a bronze statue of Bob Uecker, the beloved funny man who broadcast Brewers games for 54 seasons until his death last year.
Tampa Bay's home, Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, is on its third name. Known as the Florida Suncoast Dome from 1990-93 and the ThunderDome from 1993-96, the stadium got its current name about 18 months before the Rays' first game in 1998.
Its only prior World Series games were in 2008, when the Rays split the first two games against Philadelphia before the Phillies won three straight at home. Tampa Bay's other Series appearance was in 2020, when due to the coronavirus pandemic the entire series was played at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas.
The Trop reopened this season after repairs to damage caused by Hurricane Milton. The Rays plan to move to a new stadium across the bay in Tampa in 2029.
Jersey watch
Milwaukee went 29-13 in cream uniforms during the regular season, 17-7 in pinstripes, 27-12 in navy blue, 9-6 in City Connect outfits and 21-21 in light blue. During the postseason, the Brewers are 4-0 in cream and 3-1 in navy.
Tampa Bay was 36-19 in home white, 32-33 in road navy, 8-2 in road Columbia blue, 12-3 in Devil Rays throwback jerseys, 6-4 in City Connect and 3-3 in road gray. In the playoffs, the Rays are 2-1 in home white, 2-0 in Devil Rays throwbacks and 3-1 in road gray.
Mirror mirror
Milwaukee was 32 for 128 (.250) and had a .347 on-base percentage in its NLCS sweep of the Dodgers, the exact same numbers Los Angeles batters had in their NLCS sweep of the Brewers last year.

item.title: [fansided.com] How many teams have never won a World Series? Either Rays or Brewers will make history
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: For the third time in franchise history, the Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series. Thanks to another brilliant outing from Freddy Peralta and more big hits from their big three, the Rays polished off the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night. Led by ex-Rays prospect and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, the Brewers swept the Dodgers en route to
item.content:encoded:
For the third time in franchise history, the Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series. Thanks to another brilliant outing from Freddy Peralta and more big hits from their big three, the Rays polished off the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night.
Junior Caminero and the Rays will now take on Jacob Misiorowski, Brice Turang and the NL-winning Milwaukee Brewers in the Fall Classic. Led by ex-Rays prospect and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, the Brewers swept the Dodgers en route to capturing their first pennant since 1982.
As if that weren't intriguing enough, we’re guaranteed to see baseball history, as neither the Rays nor the Brewers have won the World Series — and they’re not alone.
Which teams have never won the World Series?
As of October 2026, the Rays and Brewers are among five teams that have never won the World Series:
| Team | World Series appearances |
|---|---|
| Colorado Rockies | 2007 |
| Milwaukee Brewers | 1982, 2026 |
| San Diego Padres | 1984, 1998 |
| Seattle Mariners | N/A |
| Tampa Bay Rays | 2008, 2020, 2026 |
Unsurprisingly, all five franchises are expansion teams, with the Brewers (then the Seattle Pilots) and Padres debuting in 1969. The Mariners followed in 1977, and the Rockies (1993) and Rays (1998) joined in the two most recent expansions.
Who would have guessed the Rays, a franchise that didn’t have a winning record in its first 10 seasons of existence, would own three pennants since the start of 2008? Oh, and they’ve reached the World Series more times in that span than the Yankees, Blue Jays and Orioles. (That sound you hear is Yankees fans removing the chainsaws from their Halloween decorations and finding a new target to scare.)
As we discussed last week, the Brewers could become the second team to win the World Series after switching leagues. The Astros, who spent nearly five decades in the NL, achieved the feat in 2017 and 2022.
Milwaukee’s NLCS victory also means that all 15 National League teams have won a pennant while in the NL.
How did the Brewers and Rays do in their previous World Series appearances?
Well, they lost.
Jokes aside, we’ll head down Memory Lane and start with the 1982 Brewers. Led by Robin Yount and Pete Vuckovich, who respectively won the AL’s MVP and Cy Young Awards, the Brew Crew defeated the then-California Angels in the ALCS to capture their first pennant.
Milwaukee looked destined for a championship parade when the Brewers took a 3-2 World Series lead over the Cardinals. But the shift to St. Louis helped World Series MVP Darrell Porter and the Redbirds bring home their first title since 1967.
Yount was one of five future Hall of Famers on that Brewers team, joining Paul Molitor, Ted Simmons, Don Sutton and Rollie Fingers.
As for the Rays, there’s not much to say about their first World Series appearance. Chase Utley and the Phillies handled them with relative ease in 2008, and the greatest issue that October was the weather. If you’ve never experienced late-October rain in the Northeast, consider yourselves lucky.
The 2020 World Series was both forgettable and immensely more memorable, which is quite the contradiction. But the less said about 2020 as a whole, the better. Randy Arozarena’s postseason breakout is really the only thing that we personally remember.
Sorry, Rays fans. For your sake, we hope this year’s Fall Classic isn’t lost to time, too.
Evaluating the Rockies, Padres, and Mariners’ 2027 World Series chances
Forget whatever the way-too-early odds or prediction markets tell you … except as it relates to the Rockies’ World Series chances. You can effectively pencil them in for yet another losing record in 2027, regardless of how many games they play amid a potentially shortened season.
As we’ve discussed, speculation is growing that the Padres will make significant roster changes — including potentially trading likely future Hall of Fame third baseman Manny Machado — following an ownership change. Superstar outfielder/second baseman Fernando Tatis Jr. is likely safe, as is veteran shortstop Xander Bogaerts.
The Padres’ new ownership group recently emailed fans, saying the team is “all-in” ahead of the 2027 season. What that means, and whether it matters, depends on whether you’re an optimist or a pessimist.
We mentioned Arozarena earlier, and he’s a pending free agent who isn’t expected to re-sign with the Mariners. Seattle still hasn’t replaced Dan Wilson, and the organization overall reeks of dysfunction. If that sounds harsh, look no further than Cal Raleigh’s lack of leadership and the Mariners forcing Wilson to announce his own firing.
That said, the Padres have the best chance of these three to reach the 2027 World Series, though that’s not saying much.

item.title: [fansided.com] Rays and Brewers set for World Series showdown in updated MLB playoff bracket
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers
item.description: Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history. Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise histo
item.content:encoded:
Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history.
Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise history. Let's dive in.
Updated MLB playoff bracket after Rays advance to the World Series
And then there were two. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the World Series seemingly eons ago, dispatching of the Los Angeles Dodgers in a shocking sweep. Now that the Rays have knocked off the Guardians in the ALCS, our World Series matchup is set.
- World Series: Tampa Bay Rays (AL champs) vs. Milwaukee Brewers (NL champs)
It's not all that often that the top seed in each league meets in the Fall Classic; baseball's postseason is notoriously unpredictable. But these teams won 98 and 103 games in the regular season, respectively, and led the AL and NL more or less wire-to-wire. They were the best in baseball, and they proved as much in October. Now it's time to see which will make history and capture their franchise's first-ever World Series title.
Full World Series schedule: Milwaukee will be rocking for Game 1
We'll have a few days of waiting: Game 1 is set for Friday, Oct. 23, with first pitch from American Family Field in Milwaukee at 8 p.m. ET. The series will follow the traditional 2-3-2 format, with days off for travel after Games 2 and 5. Games 1, 2, 6 and 7 will be in Milwaukee, with Games 3-5 in Tampa.
| Game | Location | Date | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game 1 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 23 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 2 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 24 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 3 | Tropicana Field | Monday, Oct. 26 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 4 | Tropicana Field | Tuesday, Oct. 27 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 5 | Tropicana Field | Wednesday, Oct. 28 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 6 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 30 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 7 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 31 | 8 p.m. ET |
The Rays are grateful for the break, as it will allow them to reset their pitching staff and line ace Drew Rasmussen up to face off against Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1. Clinching on Monday also allows Freddy Peralta to potentially get the ball in Game 2 on Saturday on full rest, with Nick Martinez likely behind him in Game 3.
Of course, the last thing the Brewers need is more rest. They clinched the NLCS in Game 4 last Thursday, Oct. 15, meaning they've already been at home for four days. By the time Game 1 of the World Series rolls around, it'll have been over a week since they last played a competitive game. Rust is overblown this time of year, but it's still something to monitor.
How to watch the 2026 World Series
This year's World Series will be broadcast exclusively on FOX.
- Dates: Oct. 23-Oct. 31
- TV channel: FOX
- Streaming: FOX One, YouTube TV, Hulu + Live Sports
You can also stream all the action on FOX One, provided you have a Fox One subscription ($19.99/month) or a valid cable login. You can also stream FOX through a variety of platforms, from YouTube TV to Hulu to Sling TV — all of which have free trials for new customers.
Pitching and power will define Brewers-Rays matchup
Suffice to say that runs are going to be at a premium in this series. Milwaukee ranked second in baseball in team ERA during the regular season, while the Rays were seventh. With Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and the best bullpen in baseball on one side and Rasmussen, Peralta, Martinez and All-Star closer Bryan Baker on the other, these teams have arms for days.
As such, it's going to be awfully hard to string together rallies — which means the team that finds a way to access some power will be at a distinct advantage. Neither team played much long ball during the regular season; both ranked in the bottom third of the league in homers, and neither ranked in the top 10 in slugging percentage. But the Brewers actually outslugged the big, bad Dodgers in the NLCS, and the Rays pulled away from Cleveland when their big bats (Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda) finally found the power stroke.
There won't be a ton of homers in this series. But whichever team has the most will almost certainly be hoisting the Commissioner's Trophy when all is said and done. If you're trying to play small ball against Abner Uribe, good luck.

item.content:encoded:
Estados Unidos/Un viaje a la Serie Mundial está de por medio en el Juego 6 mientras los Rays trasladan la SCLA de vuelta al Tropicana Field.
Tras su victoria por 3-1 sobre los Guardianes en el Juego 5, los Rays lucen ahora como la mejor versión de sí mismos, jugando una defensa hermética detrás de un pitcheo élite y haciendo lo justo en el plato para que todo funcione.
Estos dos equipos son muy similares, comenzando desde la base de cómo adquieren y desarrollan talento, hasta cómo manejan los partidos jornada tras jornada, por eso no esperen palizas. Sin embargo, la estrella de los Rays, el cubano Yandy Díaz, tiene una predicción llena de confianza tras conectar cinco hits en los últimos dos encuentros en Cleveland.
Si los Guardianes pretenden robarse dos partidos ante los Rays en St. Petersburg y concretar otra sorpresa, tal como lo hicieron en la SDLA contra los Medias Blancas, necesitarán silenciar a Díaz, al mexicano Jonathan Aranda y al dominicano Junior Caminero, el 'Big Three' que encabeza la alineación del conjunto de Tampa Bay que están dando señales de vida. Sin embargo, todo comienza detrás de Díaz, el exjugador de los Guardianes que ha sido una de las caras de los Rays desde el 2019.
Te puede interesar: MLB resutado | Rays vencen a Guardianes y toman ventaja 3-2 en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana
Lanzadores abridores
Guardianes: Shawn Armstrong, LD
Datos clave: Ha lanzado cuatro entradas en blanco a lo largo de tres presentaciones en la SCLA, incluyendo un inning sin carreras concedidas como opener en el Juego 4.
Armstrong tendrá su segundo turno como opener en esta serie. A partir de ahí, Cleveland volverá a armar un juego del bullpen después de que la corta apertura de Parker Messick en el Juego 4 causara que Armstrong, Tim Herrin, Erik Sabrowski, Hunter Gaddis y Cade Smith cubrieran siete entradas. Debido a que Cleveland está en una situación de ganar o irse a casa, se contempla que gran parte de esos muchachos estén disponibles el lunes. Pero Slade Cecconi, Joey Cantillo y Tanner Bibee podrían tener que desempeñar un rol importante también, después de que ninguno lanzara en el Juego 5. Williams no es una alternativa para lanzar con corto descanso, según dijo Vogt tras el Juego 5.
Rays: Freddy Peralta, LD
Datos clave: Marca de 6-0 con efectividad de 0.79 en nueve presentaciones (ocho aperturas) desde el 26 de agosto.
Peralta está de vuelta lanzando a su mayor nivel, como lo indican los números anteriores. No estuvo del todo eficaz saliendo del bullpen para conseguir un par de outs en el Juego 4 el sábado, pero ha estado dominante en ocho aperturas desde finales de agosto. Y ha estado excelente en cinco aperturas en el parque de los Rays durante ese trecho, recetando 26 ponches contra ocho bases por bolas otorgadas, registrando efectividad de 0.99.
"Lo que ha hecho en casa, increíble. Pensé que volvió a ser un atleta con nosotros y no tan robótico", señaló el abridor Drew Rasmussen. "La verdad le dio la libertad de ser exactamente quien pensábamos que sería cuando lo conseguimos en la Fecha Límite de Cambios".
La presentación en relevo de Peralta ocurrió en lugar de su sesión del bullpen programada entre aperturas, por lo que eso no debería afectar ninguno de los planes de Tampa Bay en el futuro.
Te puede interesar: Selección de Panamá | Thomas Christiansen aparece como candidato para dirigir a Ghana
Posibles alineaciones
Guardianes: Vogt anotó a los mismos nueve jugadores en su tarjeta de alineación titular para los Juegos 3 al 5, y no parece probable que eso cambie ahora.
- Steven Kwan, LF
- José Ramírez, 3B
- Chase DeLauter, RF
- Jo Adell, BD
- Nathaniel Lowe, 1B
- Travis Bazzana, 2B
- Patrick Bailey, C
- Petey Halpin, CF
- Brayan Rocchio, SS
Rays: Con los Guardianes acudiendo a Armstrong en un juego del bullpen, nos mantendremos con una alineación proyectada relativamente normal.
- Yandy Díaz, BD
- Jonathan Aranda, 1B
- Junior Caminero, 3B,
- Liam Hicks, C
- Chandler Simpson, LF
- Víctor Mesa Jr., RF
- Jonny DeLuca, CF
- Richie Palacios, 2B
- Taylor Walls, SS

Datos adicionales
- El exjardinero central de los Rays, B.J. Upton, realizará el primer pitcheo ceremonial antes del Juego 6. Upton desempeñó un rol bastante importante en el camino de Tampa Bay al título de la Liga Americana en el 2008, sacudiendo siete jonrones en la postemporada, incluyendo cuatro en el triunfo de los Rays en siete juegos en la SCLA sobre Boston.
- La racha de Ramírez de 17 juegos embasándose en postemporada es la más larga en la historia de la franquicia de Cleveland.
- El pitcheo de Cleveland recetó seis ponches en el Juego 5, para llevar su total de postemporada a 120 a lo largo de sus 10 encuentros. Los 120 ponches son la tercera mayor cantidad para cualquier equipo de las Mayores en sus primeros 10 partidos de una postemporada, solo por debajo de los 123 de los Nacionales del 2019 y los 122 de los Astros del 2022.
- Fijándonos hacia adelante, la Serie Mundial del 2026 presentará un enfrentamiento inédito por séptima vez en las últimas ocho campañas (desde el 2019). En ese transcurso, la única Serie Mundial entre equipos que se habían enfrentado en un Clásico de Otoño previo fue en el 2024 (Dodgers vs. Yankees).
- Un choque de Serie Mundial entre Tampa Bay y Milwaukee sería el primero en un Clásico de Otoño entre equipos buscando su primer campeonato desde 1980 (Phillies vs. Reales).
Información de Tim Stebbins, Keegan Matheson y Adam Berry (MLB.com)

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – Hace un año, Alejandro Kirk llamó la atención como receptor de unos Azulejos que llegaron a estar a dos outs de un título de la Serie Mundial, antes de caer ante los Dodgers en un Juego 7 que se fue a entradas extras. En esa postemporada del 2025, el tijuanense tuvo OPS de .842 con cinco jonrones y 13 empujadas.
Durante ese recordado recorrido de Toronto hacia la Serie Mundial, el amigo de Kirk y también oriundo de Tijuana, Jonathan Aranda, estuvo presente como observador del Clásico de Otoño para presenciar lo hecho por el cátcher.
Ahora, es Aranda quien pretende competir por un anillo. Sus Rays se encuentran a una sola victoria de conquistar el banderín de la Liga Americana y medirse con los Cerveceros en la Serie Mundial, estando arriba 3-2 en la Serie de Campeonato sobre los Guardianes con el Juego 6 programado para este lunes en el Tropicana Field.
“En ese momento del año pasado, me imaginé en la misma situación”, dijo Aranda. “Entonces, ahora mismo, me sirve de motivación. Espero hacer realidad ese sueño que tenía el año pasado y ayudar a este equipo a llegar a la Serie Mundial”.
En el 2026, Aranda sí ha puesto de su parte. En la campaña regular, disparó 27 dobles y 22 cuadrangulares, además de empujar 92 carreras. De hecho, se convirtió en apenas el tercer mexicano, después de Vinicio Castilla e Isaac Paredes, en impulsar 90 vueltas o más en una temporada de Grandes Ligas.
“Él conoce la liga un poco más ahora”, dijo acerca de Aranda el manager de los Rays, Kevin Cash. “Creo que tiene una mayor comprensión de ciertos lanzadores con ciertas características también, y sus pitcheos”.
En los playoffs, Aranda brilló en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana frente a los Yankees. En el Juego 1, su bambinazo frente a Gerrit Cole fue la única carrera en un triunfo por 1-0 sobre Nueva York. Y en la serie, bateó de 12-4 (.333) con dos remolcadas.
En la ronda de campeonato frente a Cleveland, empezó de 11-0, pero desde entonces se ha visto bien afinado. En la victoria de los Rays sobre los Guardianes el sábado en el Juego 3, bateó de 4-3 con dos empujadas. Y en el cuarto choque del domingo, se fue de 5-2 con otra impulsada. Esa mejoría coincidió con la de los otros dos integrantes del “Big Three” latinoamericano de Tampa Bay, el dominicano Junior Caminero y el cubano Yandy Díaz.
“Yo creo que era simplemente relajar el juego, dejar que el juego viniera a nosotros”, comentó Aranda al tocar el tema. “Tal vez estábamos un poco ansiosos, queriendo forzar las cosas para que salieran. No somos ese tipo de jugadores. Tenemos que dejar simplemente que las cosas fluyan como sabemos y pueden pasar este tipo de resultados”.
Pase lo que pase en el terreno y, específicamente en la caja de bateo, afirma Aranda que reina la calma en el clubhouse de Tampa Bay.
“Todos estamos motivados. Nadie está con la cabeza para abajo”, expresó el bajacaliforniano de 28 años. “Es la postemporada y simplemente hay que estar divirtiéndonos con la cabeza en alto”.
Con eso en mente, la meta no sólo es igualar lo lejos que llegó su amigo Kirk en el 2025, sino también dar ese último paso y coronarse campeón de Grandes Ligas con los Rays.
“Hablamos todos los días”, afirmó Aranda acerca de su amistad con Kirk. “Su consejo fue que la pasara bien y que fuera yo mismo. Eso me ayudó a disfrutar el momento.
“Siempre va a ser un orgullo para mí ser mexicano. Va a ser de lo mejor que me ha pasado”, continuó Aranda sobre sus raíces. “Y estar a este nivel… obviamente, busco inspirar de la manera buena e impulsar a los que vienen detrás de mí. Ojalá que lo puedan lograr con mucha disciplina”.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are just hours away from their Game 5 ALCS clash against the Cleveland Guardians.
Before the game, the organization revealed its latest decision on Junior Caminero.
Rays Announce Caminero Decision Before Game 5
Per Underdog MLB, 23-year-old Caminero will be batting fourth in the order on Sunday.
During his 2026 regular season, Caminero appeared in 162 games and slashed .276/.360/.524 with a .884 OPS and 42 homers.
He smacked 25 doubles, one triple and 101 RBIs.
This marks his fourth season playing Major League Baseball after making his MLB debut in September 2023.

item.title: [MLB.com] LIVE on TBS/HBO Max: Rays-Guardians ALCS Game 5
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Keegan Matheson; Adam Berry
item.description: Sunday’s 5:08 p.m. ET game at Progressive Field will determine which side flies to St. Petersburg for Game 6 on the doorstep of the World Series and which team is fighting for their postseason lives. item.content:encoded:
Sunday’s 5:08 p.m. ET game at Progressive Field will determine which side flies to St. Petersburg for Game 6 on the doorstep of the World Series and which team is fighting for their postseason lives. The Brewers get to kick their feet up and wait on the National League side, but over here in the American League, the stakes couldn’t be higher.
The Rays are riding a high coming off their 7-3 win in Game 4, but as we’ve seen just about every day in this series, momentum can turn on a dime. The Guardians still feel like they’re playing their best baseball, going back to their incredible comeback to beat the White Sox in the ALDS, and they have a shot to take a commanding series lead in front of their home crowd Sunday.
“We're great. We're right in it. We're even,” said Guardians manager Stephen Vogt. “Again, now, it's a three-game series. I'll put our guys up against any team in the world in a three-game series. Of course, we would have loved to have taken a 3-to-1 lead tonight, but it's not in the cards. We can't control that now. We just show up, ready to play a good Game 5, and have a happy flight to Tampa.”
Drew Rasmussen will get the start for the Rays, and he’ll face Parker Messick, a premier pitching matchup on the biggest stage. These teams are starting to get aggressive, too, with the Rays using Freddy Peralta out of the bullpen in Game 4 while still keeping him available for later in the series.
The biggest threat to the Guardians now is the Rays’ Big Three of Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda, all of whom had big games in Game 4. Caminero’s was especially important, coming off four strikeouts in Game 3, and Aranda looks locked in. If that group can get back to Tropicana Field with a lead, look out.
“That was one of the main objectives that we had here coming into Cleveland, just to force the series back home,” Aranda said through interpreter Kevin Vera. “We're one of the best teams in the league when we're playing back on our home field, so we're going to use the fanbase and we're going to use that energy to push us forward. Drew is one of the best pitchers in the league, so it gives us a lot of confidence.”
After rain earlier this weekend, the forecast for Sunday is thankfully clear once again. It will still cool down as the evening stretches on, but the Guardians are used to these cold days, and the Rays, who play their home games under the dome at Tropicana Field, have already proven they can play in any environment.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 5 of the Guardians-Rays ALDS is underway at Progressive Field. The game is being broadcast on TBS and HBO Max.
Spanish-language game broadcasts will be available on UniMas for the ALCS, and Spanish-language radio broadcasts will be available on Univision’s TUDN Radio.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Guardians: Parker Messick, LHP
Key stats: 5 IP, 6 H, 3 R, 0 ER, 2 BB, 3 K, 1 HBP in Game 2 
Messick started Game 2 on Tuesday, which initially lined him up to take the ball in Game 6 on Monday. The postponement that moved Game 4 from Friday to Saturday also moved Game 5 to Sunday, which allowed Messick to start this game on normal rest. The rookie lefty will be making his fourth postseason start; he logged a 3.09 ERA with eight walks and 14 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings over his first three outings.
In a season where Messick emerged as an anchor in Cleveland’s rotation, this is among his biggest starts.
“To be able to take the ball in this game shows the confidence the team has in me,” Messick said. “Hopefully I'm able to go out there and do the job because I know how important it is going into opposing territory with a lead, one game away from heading to the World Series. I’m looking forward to the opportunity, and hopefully I do my best out there.”
Rays: Drew Rasmussen, RHP
Key stats: 14 IP, 2 R, 2 BB, 17 K in two postseason starts 
One benefit of the rainout? Rasmussen can start this game on five days’ rest, the way he made most of his starts during the regular season. The right-hander delivered a quality start in Tampa Bay’s Game 1 defeat, pitching into the seventh inning and ultimately allowing two runs while recording 18 outs. He was even better in Game 1 of the ALDS, when he struck out 10 while allowing just one hit over eight innings against the Yankees.
There’s nobody else the Rays would rather have on the mound with a chance to take the series lead before heading back home.
“It's still just baseball. I think that's led to a couple of successful outings up to this point,” Rasmussen said. “Just try and not make it anything bigger than what it actually is. It's you. It's preparation, and it's execution. Those are really the only things I'm concerned with.”
What are the starting lineups?
Guardians: Cleveland has kept a standard lineup this postseason, with the only change for Game 5 behind the plate. Though Austin Hedges had caught all but one of Messick’s starts this season and Patrick Bailey hadn’t caught him once, the Guardians wanted to get Bailey’s bat in the lineup as they attempt to take a 3-2 lead in the ALCS.
Rays: Tampa Bay slotted in Ryan Vilade in right field in place of Victor Mesa Jr. for a touch more right-handed punch against the left-handed Messick.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: Tampa Bay used five relievers behind starter Nick Martinez in Game 4, including presumptive Game 6 starter Freddy Peralta, but lefty Ian Seymour was the only one who threw more than 16 pitches. So expect the Rays to have everyone available between Rasmussen and closer Bryan Baker, who has finished each of Tampa Bay’s five postseason wins. Lefty Cam Booser has been the top left-handed option, right-hander Kevin Kelly gets most of the toughest right-handed matchups and setup man Tyler Wells asserted himself well with his two-inning appearance in Game 3. It’s possible that Griffin Jax, who started Game 3, could be called upon if needed. 
Guardians: Cleveland did not use closer Cade Smith and primary setup men Hunter Gaddis and Erik Sabrowski in the Game 4 loss. All three figure to factor into Game 5 as the Guardians look to take control of this series. In an ideal world, Messick will get Cleveland through five innings, if not six, and bridge the game to that trio.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: None.
Guardians: None.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Simpson has been a spark plug of late, contributing a key single during the three-run rally in the fourth inning of Game 2 and then accounting for all of the team’s offense with his two-run triple in the fourth inning of Game 3. And the Big Three atop the order finally joined the party in Game 4, going 6-for-14 with five RBIs after a combined 5-for-34 start to the series. Maybe Hicks (3-for-20 in the postseason) and Mesa (4-for-25 with 11 strikeouts) will be the next ones to get going.
Guardians: Bazzana went 3-for-4 with a home run in Game 4. DeLauter’s first-inning RBI single in Game 4 was his 10th hit of the playoffs. That's one shy of tying Rocchio (11 in 2024) for the most hits by a Cleveland rookie in a single postseason. Rocchio went 1-for-3 on Saturday and is 4-for-28 through nine postseason games.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• Bazzana recorded his first career postseason home run with a solo shot in the 7th inning on Saturday, becoming the first Australian-born player to homer in MLB postseason history.
• Ramírez walked in the sixth inning to extend his postseason on-base streak to 16 games, which ties Steven Kwan (Oct. 8, 2022-Oct. 19, 2024) for the longest in Cleveland postseason history.
• Mesa recorded his second outfield assist of the postseason in Game 4, throwing out DeLauter at second base in the 1st inning. He’s the fourth player in Rays postseason history with multiple outfield assists, joining B.J. Upton, Kevin Kiermaier and Hunter Renfroe (each had two outfield assists for the Rays).

item.content:encoded:
Game 5 of the ALCS between the Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians takes place on Sunday afternoon, and these teams are knotted at two games apiece after Tampa Bay won Game 4.
There are a ton of props to consider in Game 5 of the ALCS, including a home run prop or two as these teams look to deliver a key blow before the series shifts back to Tampa Bay on Monday.
Drew Rasmussen (14 home runs allowed in the regular season, two in the postseason) and Parker Messick (17 home runs allowed in the regular season, one in the postseason) are on the mound in this game.
The total (6.5) is pretty low in this matchup, so we may not see a ton of offense.
While betting on home runs is a fun way to get involved in the action, these props are extremely tough to hit with the pitching in the postseason. Still, there have been a few long balls in this series, and I’m targeting one player that has already gone deep over the course of the first four games to stay hot on Sunday.
Best MLB Home Run Prop Bet Picks for ALCS Game 5
Chase DeLauter to Hit a Home Run (+970)
Chase DeLauter homered 16 times during the regular season, and he took Drew Rasmussen deep in Game 1.
The Guardians youngster was 1-for-3 against the Rays ace in the series opener, and he’s 2-for-4 against him in the regular season in his career.
DeLauter is dangerous against right-handed pitching, homering 13 times while posting an .808 OPS during the regular season.
He’s also been hot in this series, picking up five hits, three RBIs and three runs scored in four games. Overall, he’s hitting .294 with two doubles in a homer in the 2026 postseason.
There are worse bets to make at nearly 10/1 odds in Game 5.
Junior Caminero to Hit a Home Run (+497)
During the regular season, Junior Caminero hit 42 home runs and was elite against left-handed pitching.
He had a .287 batting average, a .916 OPS and homered eight times against southpaws. He has not had a ton of success against Messick in his career (1-for-12), but the lefty did allow 17 home runs in the 2026 regular season.
At some point, Caminero is going to get a hold of a ball, as he’s yet to go deep in the playoffs. Still, Caminero is hitting, picking up at least one hit in three games in this series, including two doubles.
This prop has skyrocketed all the way to +497 with Messick on the mound, but the Guardians’ bullpen has been taxed over the last few days and could be vulnerable to a long ball.
With just one game to bet on, I’m going to take a shot on the best power hitter for either team to leave the yard on Sunday.

item.title: [puckettspond.com] This year's World Series shows where the Twins have failed
item.dc:creator: Chris Schad
item.description: The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful. Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a s
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful.
Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a sweep over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night and they will face either the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians in what will be a showdown between small-market teams.
While this year’s matchup could create a loophole for the Pohlad family to avoid dropping a large amount of money to improve the team, it also reflects poorly on their decisions that have kept them from competing over the past few years.
The Brewers, Rays and Guardians are showing the Twins how to build a winner
As you may have guessed, the Brewers, Guardians and Rays are not among MLB’s biggest spenders. According to Cot’s Baseball Contracts, the Brewers’ year-end salary ranked 23rd at $99.3 million and defeated the Dodgers’ No. 1 roster at $366.0 million. The American League finalists were also budget-conscious as the Rays ranked 20th with a year-end payroll of $103.1 million and the Guardians ranked 25th at $91.0 million.
All three of the remaining teams had a lower year-end payroll than the Twins, who ranked 17th with a figure of $123.9 million and while many, including owner and chairman Tom Pohlad, believe that adding to that number could lead to a championship, the other three teams show what they have done wrong.
The first is maximizing the value of players on the roster. The Rays, Guardians and Brewers have traded players before they get to free agency to add to their organization and it’s paid off in a big way. The Brewers most notably did this in a February 2024 trade featuring Corbin Burnes that brought back left-hander DL Hall and infielder Joey Ortiz.
The Rays also have done this with their trade of Triple-A right-hander Tobias Myers, who was traded to Cleveland as he was eligible for the Rule 5 Draft in 2021, and brought back star third baseman Junior Caminero in return. While the Guardians whiffed on Myers, they made other shrewd deals that netted them Craig Yoho, Patrick Bailey, Foster Griffin and Kyle Manzardo.
These trades are a double-edged sword as they usually involve popular players. But it brings back pieces that ensure a larger championship window. That leaves player development as the final phase of the three contenders and each team has a homegrown star to lean on such as Jose Ramirez, Jacob Misiorowski or Caminero.
The Twins’ biggest problems go beyond their payroll
Turning the attention back to the Twins, it’s easy to see where they have come up short. This year’s trade deadline was one opportunity to shift the narrative. But instead of trading players that could bring back a big return such as Ryan Jeffers and Joe Ryan, the Twins went the opposite direction, adding A.J. Minter, Jeff Hoffman and Dean Kremer.
Even when they tried to trade Trevor Larnach to the Houston Astros before owner Jim Crane vetoed it, they were seeking 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, a pitcher who posted his highest ERA (3.73) and lowest WAR (1.0) since his rookie season in 2021.
The other key issue is the Twins’ player development. While top prospects such as Royce Lewis and Matt Wallner thrive initially when reaching the major leagues, those players have hit a wall when pitchers adjust to them. The problem can be traced back to Miguel Sano’s downfall in the early 2020s and can still be seen in a group of post-hype hitters that haven’t lived up to their prospect status.
This leaves the Twins in a tricky spot this offseason. After failing to trade Jeffers at the deadline, there’s a good chance he’ll leave in free agency. Ryan has a year of team control remaining, but trading him now could get a pair of MLB-ready players in return. Several top prospects including Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodriguez and Kaelen Culpepper made their debuts this season, but the key will be to make sure they don’t regress entering their first full season in the bigs.
Of course, fans may cheer for a salary floor to hold the Pohlads accountable for what happens to the Twins next. But the Rays, Guardians and Brewers show that paying top dollar may not be necessary to build a contender and Minnesota would be wise to follow their blueprint.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Rays Need Junior Caminero to Wake Up Before It's Too Late
item.dc:creator: Christian Rauh
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays are now facing a difficult situation in the American League Championship Series after falling 3-2 to the Cleveland Guardians in Game 3 on Thursday. And while there are plenty of things to criticize about the performance, I think the biggest concern continues to be the lack of offensive production from Tampa Bay's biggest stars. Especially Junior Caminero. The Rays' star slugger had arguably his worst performance of the season against Cleveland, going 0-for-4 with four strikeou
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are now facing a difficult situation in the American League Championship Series after falling 3-2 to the Cleveland Guardians in Game 3 on Thursday.
And while there are plenty of things to criticize about the performance, I think the biggest concern continues to be the lack of offensive production from Tampa Bay's biggest stars.
Especially Junior Caminero.
The Rays' star slugger had arguably his worst performance of the season against Cleveland, going 0-for-4 with four strikeouts.
And it wasn't necessarily because Gavin Williams was throwing pitches that were impossible to hit. Caminero consistently took hittable pitches early in counts before chasing balls well outside the strike zone.
That's something we haven't seen much of throughout the regular season. A year where he has surely earned votes for American League MVP.
And I think it's fair to wonder whether Caminero is trying to do too much at the plate.
The 45-home-run slugger still hasn't hit a home run this postseason, and his batting average sits at .238 with a .666 OPS.
Those numbers certainly aren't what Tampa Bay needs from one of its biggest offensive weapons.
But Caminero isn't the only player struggling.
Yandy Díaz is hitting .240 with a .589 OPS, while Jonathan Aranda has managed just a .182 batting average and .568 OPS.
Victor Mesa Jr. is hitting .143, and Liam Hicks isn't doing much better at .167.
These are supposed to be the players carrying Tampa Bay's offense.
Instead, the Rays have relied on contributions from the bottom of their lineup.
Chandler Simpson delivered Tampa Bay's only two runs Thursday with an impressive two-RBI triple against Williams.
Richie Palacios has also provided some important hits, while Jonny DeLuca has been one of Tampa Bay's more productive hitters throughout the series.
But that can't continue being the expectation.
Tampa Bay won 98 games during the regular season because it had a lineup capable of consistently putting the baseball in play and creating scoring opportunities.
However, the Rays have yet to score more than four runs in a postseason game.
And Thursday might've been the most frustrating example.
Tampa Bay managed just three hits and struck out 13 times, including seven strikeouts from the top of the batting order.
The Rays also went down in order in seven of their nine offensive innings.
That's not going to get the job done in October.
Especially against a Cleveland team that has consistently taken advantage of its opportunities.
Now, I'm not suggesting Tampa Bay's season is over.
The Rays are only trailing 2-1 in a seven-game series, and there's still plenty of baseball left to play.
But if Tampa Bay wants to reach the World Series, its biggest offensive stars need to start playing like it.
And that starts with Junior Caminero.

item.title: [mlb.com] Who should Brewers want to face in the World Series?
item.dc:creator: Zach Sweet

item.content:encoded:
When the Brewers finished off the Dodgers on Thursday night, their World Series opponent was the last thing on anyone’s mind. An MLB official closed the postgame press conference by telling manager Pat Murphy and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, “We’ll see you in Milwaukee at the World Series.”
Murphy’s reply said everything: “When’s that start?”
Next Friday, Oct. 23, at American Family Field, where Milwaukee holds home-field advantage thanks to its franchise-record 103 wins. The Guardians took a 2-1 ALCS lead over the Rays into Friday night's scheduled Game 4 at Progressive Field. Milwaukee, meanwhile, will have a full week to rest, which leaves plenty of time to watch and wonder.
Here’s a guide to each potential matchup. You decide which one you’d rather see.
If the regular season is a guide ...
It doesn’t tell us much. The Brewers went 2-1 against both teams.
Milwaukee won the first two games against Cleveland on June 16-17 before rookie left-hander Parker Messick struck out nine over six innings in the finale. Cleveland was without José Ramírez, Angel Martínez and Chase DeLauter. All three are back.
When the Brewers hit
Milwaukee’s lineup is built on pressure. The Brewers ranked in the top five in doubles, runs, hits, walks, batting average and on-base percentage.
That approach might get more of a test against Tampa Bay. The Rays issued the fewest walks in the Majors (409) and ranked second in defensive runs saved (87). Drawing walks and finding holes gets tougher against that combination. And their top starters have carried it into October: Drew Rasmussen has a 1.29 ERA through two postseason starts, while Peralta has allowed one earned run in 10 2/3 innings, including six shutout innings in Game 2 of the ALCS.
Cleveland offers a different challenge. Gavin Williams has been a monster, striking out 33 over 16 2/3 innings this postseason. The Guardians have a 2.54 ERA this October, slightly better than Tampa Bay’s 2.72. But Cleveland issued 530 regular-season walks to the Rays’ 409, giving Milwaukee more reason to believe its patient approach can create traffic.
When the other side hits
The regular-season numbers favor facing Cleveland. The Guardians had the lowest OPS (.696) and fewest runs (678) of any postseason team. Tampa Bay offered a more complete attack, with Junior Caminero’s 42 homers anchoring a lineup that tied for fifth in on-base percentage (.326).
October has told a different story. Through Thursday, Cleveland was averaging 4.25 runs per game with a .685 OPS, compared with Tampa Bay’s 3.00 runs and .563 OPS. The Guardians haven’t suddenly become an offensive powerhouse, but they’ve been more productive than the Rays, whose lineup managed just three hits in Game 3 of the ALCS.
The larger sample still points toward Cleveland as the preferable opponent. The way these teams are hitting right now makes that a tougher call.
The bullpens
Neither ninth inning looks inviting. Tampa Bay’s Bryan Baker has saved all four Rays wins this postseason without allowing a hit in four innings. Ian Seymour has been a strong bridge, allowing one earned run in 6 1/3 innings.
Cleveland counters with Cade Smith, who has allowed two hits and one run while striking out 13 in nine innings this October. Hunter Gaddis has added six scoreless innings across seven appearances. Both teams have arms capable of shortening games.
The Brewers have made a habit of coming back this postseason, and their bats have shown they can pick at a bullpen late. Against either opponent, getting a lead before the closer enters would make life easier.
What about the intangibles?
The Guardians’ championship drought dates to 1948. The Rays, like the Brewers, have never won a World Series.
The Rays mirror Milwaukee in many ways. Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked in Tampa Bay’s front office alongside current Rays GM Erik Neander. Add Peralta facing his former team, and the storyline writes itself.
Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt played for Milwaukee and interviewed for the job that went to Murphy three years ago. And a Cleveland-Milwaukee World Series comes with a built-in movie reference: Major League, filmed in Milwaukee with Bob Uecker’s Harry Doyle calling Cleveland's improbable run.
The verdict
Give the Guardians a slight edge as Milwaukee’s preferred opponent, though their October bats have made that a tougher sell. The Rays were the more complete team over six months. Cleveland has spent the past two weeks making those six months feel a little less relevant.
The Brewers? They just sent the back-to-back champs home. They’ll let the AL sort this out. Somebody remind Murph what time Friday’s game starts.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Guardians ALCS Game 3 FAQ, lineups (1 ET, TBS/HBO Max)
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Keegan Matheson; Adam Berry
item.description: CLEVELAND -- It’s a new day in the ALCS, as the Rays and Guardians have shifted their matchup back to Cleveland tied up at 1-1. item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- It’s a new day in the ALCS, as the Rays and Guardians have shifted their matchup back to Cleveland tied up at 1-1.
The Rays' 3-1 win in Game 2 shifted this series back into focus after the Guardians pulled off a 7-3 come-from-behind win in the opener. We’ve seen each team’s best, and as these pitching staffs get stretched even thinner as the series wears on, they’ll need to lean on the identities they’ve built in 2026.
“It’s going to be a challenging place to play,” said Rays manager Kevin Cash. “We played there not too long ago in the postseason. That's as good an atmosphere as you're going to see. They've got a great fan base that's going to be behind their team. I'd like to think we can carry our momentum into there and just play good baseball for Game 3.”
Step back a few feet for a wider view, and this Guardians team has still won four of its past five games. The club ran into a Game 2 buzzsaw named Freddy Peralta, whose fastball was nearly unhittable, but Cleveland is still in an excellent spot after stealing Game 1.
“We feel great. Obviously we would have loved to have taken [Game 2],” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “That would have been really big. And we had our position and our opportunities to do that. But going home 1-1, to go have three games in front of our fans in Cleveland, we feel really good about that. And we're excited to get it going.”
The pitching matchup has the potential to lean in the Guardians’ favor, too, with Gavin Williams starting on regular rest, fresh off a dominant outing against the White Sox to clinch the ALDS. For the Rays, Griffin Jax has been officially named the starter, and while he spent the majority of the season working in a true starter’s role, he pitched two innings of relief against the Yankees in Game 3 of the ALDS, throwing just 32 pitches.
This series is still waiting for its first show-stopping moment, too, with all eyes on José Ramírez for the Guardians and Junior Caminero for the Rays. Ramírez's series has been up-and-down so far, from a solid Game 1 to a crucial error that opened the door in Game 2, while Caminero is still searching for his first career postseason home run.
There’s history on the line here, too, for whichever team advances to represent the American League in the World Series. The Rays haven’t won the World Series since entering the league in 1998 and have only reached the big stage twice (2008, 2020). The Guardians, on the other hand, still carry the weight of the longest World Series drought in the big leagues at 77 seasons, stretching all the way back to 1948.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Rays-Guardians American League Championship Series is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET on Thursday at Progressive Field. Due to inclement weather in the forecast, the original start time of 6 p.m. was moved up. The game will be broadcast on TBS and HBO Max. 
Spanish-language game broadcasts will be available on UniMas for the ALCS, and Spanish-language radio broadcasts will be available on Univision’s TUDN Radio.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Griffin Jax, RHP
Key Stats: 0.90 ERA over his past five appearances
Nick Martinez started ALDS Game 3 for the Rays, but they will turn to Jax this time after using him as a reliever against the Yankees, with Martinez likely in line to pitch Game 4 on Friday. Jax has been excellent since a rough return from the injured list on Sept. 2 after a bout of right elbow discomfort, permitting only two runs on 10 hits and four walks while striking out 19 in 20 innings over his last four regular-season starts and his Game 3 relief outing at Yankee Stadium. Jax is presumably prepared for Cleveland’s inclement weather, having pitched for Minnesota for most of his career, and he’s put up impressive numbers (including a 2.19 ERA, 0.89 WHIP and 20 strikeouts) in 13 relief appearances at Progressive Field.
Guardians: Gavin Williams, RHP
Key Stats: 1.54 ERA, 24 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings in ALDS
The Guardians officially named Williams their Game 3 starter on Wednesday afternoon, setting the 27-year-old up for a start on normal rest following his heroic performance in the ALDS, when he made two starts and an emergency relief appearance against the White Sox. After he recorded the final three outs of Game 4, Williams came back on one day’s rest in Game 5 and tied a franchise postseason record in strikeouts (12) to help Cleveland beat Chicago, 2-0, to advance. Williams starting Game 3 also positions him to start a potential Game 7 of this series on Tuesday, on normal rest.
What are the starting lineups?
Rays: With Williams on the mound, the Rays are going with their standard lineup against right-handers, with the “Big Three” followed by their other left-handed hitters. They're staying with Jonny DeLuca, who’s started every postseason game so far, over Cedric Mullins in center field.
Guardians: Patrick Bailey is back behind the plate in Game 3. He and Williams have been a customary battery this season, and Bailey is swinging a hot bat this postseason. The Guards are sticking with the standard lineup they’ve had in this series.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Guardians: Vogt will have a full bullpen at his disposal after the off-day, and will work getting the ball to closer Cade Smith. He and Hunter Gaddis did not appear in Game 2, after both pitched in each of the Guardians’ first six contests this postseason. Setup man Erik Sabrowski also did not pitch in Game 2 and will be working off two days’ rest.
Rays: The Rays should be in good shape after Wednesday’s off-day, although this will be the first time since the regular season that they’ve played three consecutive days in a row. Left-hander Ian Seymour has clearly established himself as a top setup option in front of closer Bryan Baker, and lefty Cam Booser has also been tasked with getting big outs against left-handed hitters. Right-hander Kevin Kelly and Tyler Wells are also setup options in front of Baker, who has recorded the save in each of Tampa Bay’s four wins this postseason.
Any injuries of note?
Guardians: None.
Rays: Caminero and DeLuca said they were fine after a nasty collision while chasing a foul ball in Game 1. Left-hander Shane McClanahan, who finished the regular season on the injured list due to left forearm tightness, was shut down for the rest of the postseason, Cash said on Sunday. Otherwise, nothing new.
Who is hot and who is not?
Guardians: Shawn Armstrong has allowed just one hit and struck out five batters in 5 1/3 scoreless innings over four postseason appearances. It’s been an impressive comeback after he missed two months with a left calf strain, before returning the final week of the regular season. DeLauter is hitting .346 (9-for-26) with just one strikeout in seven postseason games.
Rocchio is hitting .091 (2-for-22) in seven games.
Rays: Pretty much everyone who touched the mound for Tampa Bay in the ALDS and Game 2 of this series performed well, which is certainly promising for the team moving forward, even after some shaky bullpen work in Game 1. The Rays are starting to find some rhythm at the plate, too, with Caminero leading the way despite not yet having the big moment everyone’s expecting. Hicks drove in a couple runs in Game 2, and DeLuca had his second straight multihit game. Díaz is just 5-for-21 in the playoffs, and Mesa is only 3-for-18.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• Cleveland Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell will throw the ceremonial first pitch before Game 3.
• With his fifth-inning single in Game 2, Ramírez moved into second place in franchise history in postseason hits (49), breaking a tie with Kenny Lofton. Omar Vizquel (57) ranks first.
• Game 2 of the ALCS was Díaz’s 30th postseason game with the Rays, matching Evan Longoria for the most in franchise history. Game 3 should give Tampa Bay’s DH the club record.
• The Rays are 89-0 this year, including the regular season and postseason, when leading after eight innings. The last team to go a full year with a 1.000 winning percentage and at least 89 wins when leading after eight innings? The 2022 Mets, who went 90-0. The last team to do so in the AL was the 2002 Athletics (93-0).

item.title: [MLB.com] 11 on 11: Why José (NOT J-Ram!) is Cleveland's brightest star
item.dc:creator: Anthony Castrovince

item.content:encoded:
Well, OK, Guardians fans know it. And even casual fans know by now that Ramírez is a dynamic player. The "underrated" label has long since stopped applying to this seven-time All-Star.
With Ramírez’s Guardians in an ALCS that continues with Game 3 on Thursday night at Progressive Field, it’s a good time to share some fun and fascinating elements of his story that many fans might not be aware of. Though the prevailing narrative at this moment is his rare defensive miscue that opened the doors to the Rays’ win in Game 2, Ramírez is the primary reason the Guardians are in the ALCS in the first place, and his talent and personality are worth celebrating.
Here are -- appropriately, for the man who wears No. 11 for Cleveland -- 11 things every baseball fan should know about José Ramírez.
1) He hates being called 'J-Ram'
Let’s get this one out of the way right away. “J-Ram” is anathema to Ramírez, who is far too dynamic for such a dull nickname anyway.
If you must use a folksy nickname, “Hosey” works. But in Cleveland, Ramírez doesn’t need a nickname or a last name. He’s simply “José” (and it sounds best when sung to the stadium anthem “Ole! Ole! Ole!”).
2) He’s put the Guardians on his back
It’s funny to think that, a little more than a week ago, people were questioning Ramírez’s October clutchness. He had an injury-riddled regular season and struggled through Game 2 of the ALDS against the White Sox, with the Guardians down 0-2.
Be it the stakes or the crowd riding him, something snapped in Game 3. From that point on, he went 5-for-12 with five runs scored, seven RBIs, two homers, a double and a triple over three games. In the Game 5 clincher at home, he somehow golfed a curveball virtually in the dirt for a career-defining home run, then followed it up with a three-hit night in Cleveland’s Game 1 win in the ALCS.
As teammate Chase DeLauter put it: "He's the G.O.A.T. … When he comes out and has that kind of fire, it lights all of us up.”
3) He’s a likely future Hall of Famer
The postseason was the one element lacking from Ramírez’s resumé prior to this fall, but his Cooperstown case is already shaping up nicely. He sits at 60.3 bWAR, just 8.6 shy of the average of third basemen in the Hall of Fame, with a seven-year peak bWAR (44.7) just below Brooks Robinson’s (45.8).
At age 34, he is just three regular-season home runs shy of joining Alex Rodriguez as the only third basemen, shortstops, or second basemen with at least 300 homers, 400 doubles, 300 steals, and 1,000 RBIs. He’s finished as an AL MVP finalist four times. Last year, Sarah Langs made the definitive case for him as the best player never to win the award.
4) He’s a throwback
The stats are nice, but it’s the way this compact, 5-foot-8 player gets to them that makes him so fun to watch.
It’s pure hustle -- dirty uniforms, flying helmets and natural instincts. His steals stem from situational intelligence rather than elite speed, while his range, fluidity, and elite pitch-reading allow him to play an above-average hot corner and avoid strikeouts despite modest raw bat speed and arm strength.
5) His baseball smarts are off the charts
In the ninth inning of ALCS Game 1, Ramírez broke for third and came around to score when Jo Adell rolled a grounder through the left side of the infield. Cameras caught Ramírez laughing as he crossed home plate. 
Why? After the game, his agent relayed that Ramírez had planned the whole play out: He knew that Kevin Kelly was going to throw a changeup. He knew that Adell was going to roll over on it and hit a grounder to the left side. By stealing, he pulled Rays third baseman Junior Caminero to the bag -- and opened a hole exactly where the ball ended up going.
Ramírez will venture away from the on-deck circle just to get a better view of a pitcher's release point, playing the game through anticipation rather than mere reaction. One of his greatest joys is putting pressure on opponents by drawing throws, taking secondary leads and creating openings for his teammates.
Surrounded by younger players on a budget-conscious roster, he constantly tries to impart these nuances, noting, "When these guys really focus and pay attention to the game, we score a lot of runs."
6) He has humble roots
Hailing from Baní in the Dominican Republic, Ramírez grew up playing baseball on a rocky dirt square, crossing the Río Baní from a rural home that lacked running water.
Financial limitations meant playing with a glove that was too tight and using water jug caps as baseballs in games of "Vitilla.” A major childhood lifeline came when former AL MVP Miguel Tejada held a local clinic distributing equipment and food. Ramírez rushed to the front of the line.
“I never forgot it,” he said.
7) He was only scouted by accident
Undersized and often the youngest player in his league, a 13-year-old Ramírez played in rough adult leagues watched over by gamblers, with a machete dangling behind home plate as a warning for poor performance.
Scouts weren't watching him; he was usually just an extra man at showcases. But in 2009, Cleveland scouting director John Mirabelli and scout Ramon Peña happened to catch him filling in for another player and ripping hits in bunches. Peña pounded the table for him, and Ramírez was signed for $50,000.
“He’s not the guy that came in with a lot of acclaim,” Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti said. “He wasn’t afforded a ton of extra opportunities because of an investment.”
8) He’s incredibly loyal
That modest $50,000 investment bought an extraordinary level of allegiance.
Ramírez faced a crossroads in 2022, when the Guardians were contemplating a trade before his final two control years. Ramírez wanted no part of leaving. He implored his agent to secure a deal that would keep him in Cleveland, prioritizing happiness and stability over free-agent riches.
“I’m happier with $150 million in Cleveland,” he told his agent, according to an ESPN report, “than $200 million somewhere else.”
Now signed through his age-39 season, he explains it simply: "Cleveland is everything to me. When nobody wanted to give me a chance, they gave me a chance."
9) His community work is not just lip service
Crediting his late grandmother, Santa Ramírez, with teaching him the value of sharing his success, José insisted on partnering with the Guardians on community impact projects. He funded the $2.7 million José Ramírez Field alongside Cleveland Guardians Charities, serving the Lincoln-West High School team and Cleveland's Nike RBI program on a street the city proudly named José Ramírez Way.
He has also helped expand MLB's Fun At-Bat program locally and teamed up to completely refurbish the rough field in Baní where he first learned to play, making it a safe and usable space for the next generation of ballplayers.
“The reality,” he said, “is that those kids in the D.R. have no alternative. That’s why I feel it’s really important to help.”
10) He respects the game
While his famous 2023 altercation with Tim Anderson spawned popular Cleveland T-shirts celebrating the "Down Goes Anderson" moment, Ramírez was actually mortified by it. He never wants to show up an opponent or be viewed as a troublemaker, emphasizing that his goal is always to give 100 percent and set an example.
At its core, Ramírez has said what he loves most about baseball is that it is "a disciplined way of learning how to respect each other."
11) He’s hilarious
Cutthroat on the field, Ramírez loves to keep people loose off it.
He’s worn a chain with a picture of himself. Wearing a chain. He’s worn a belt adorned with his image, too.
He’s joked that he’s “more beautiful” than Shohei Ohtani. He’s yelled to Freddie Freeman, “You’re one of the best hitters … after me.”
He trash talks teammates during games of Mario Kart or playfully smacks them in the back of the head when it’s time to pay attention. Once, when a teammate was smashing an iPad after a bad at-bat, Ramírez calmly told him, “Bro, settle down, that iPad can’t hit.” He’ll field another player’s position during batting practice and josh about how easy it is.
Ultimately, he’s a connector of people, keeping things fresh with deadpan humor that keeps people guessing.
Now you know José Ramírez. He might not be your favorite player yet. But hopefully you understand why he’s a favorite to so many.

item.content:encoded:
Guardians vs. Rays: A qué hora y dónde ver a Jonathan Aranda en el Juego 2 de la Serie de Campeonato MLB 2026
Te decimos a qué hora y dónde ver en México el Juego 2 de Guardians vs Rays, con el tijuanense Jonathan Aranda buscando ayudar a Tampa Bay a empatar la Serie de Campeonato.
Los Guardianes de Cleveland y los Rays de Tampa Bay disputarán este martes 13 de octubre el Juego 2 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana 2026, nuevamente en el Tropicana Field, de St. Petersburg, Florida.
Cleveland llega con ventaja de 1-0 en la serie, después de remontar y llevarse el primer encuentro por 7-3, por lo que Tampa Bay está obligado a reaccionar antes de que la eliminatoria se traslade a Ohio.
El partido tendrá especial interés para los aficionados mexicanos por la participación del tijuanense Jonathan Aranda, quien intentará recuperar su producción ofensiva después de quedarse sin imparables en el primer encuentro.
Te decimos a qué hora comienza, dónde verlo EN VIVO y quiénes serán los pitchers abridores.
¿Cuándo y a qué hora juegan Guardians vs. Rays el Juego 2 de la Serie de Campeonato 2026?
El segundo encuentro de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana se disputará este martes 13 de octubre de 2026, con Tampa Bay como local.
Estos son los horarios para las cuatro zonas de México:
- Hora del centro de México: 6:00 PM.
- Hora del noroeste: 5:00 PM.
- Hora del Pacífico: 5:00 PM.
- Hora del sureste: 7:00 PM.
El encuentro se celebrará en el Tropicana Field, donde los Rays intentarán aprovechar su condición de locales para empatar la serie antes de viajar a Cleveland.
¿Dónde ver EN VIVO Guardians vs. Rays, Juego 2, en México?
Los aficionados mexicanos podrán seguir el enfrentamiento de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana mediante televisión de paga y servicios de streaming.
Las opciones de transmisión para México son:
- TV abierta: No disponible.
- TV de paga: ESPN.
- Streaming: Disney+ y MLB.TV, sujeto a las condiciones de suscripción y disponibilidad regional.
En Estados Unidos, las transmisiones oficiales están programadas por TBS, truTV, HBO Max y UniMás.
¿Cómo quedó el Juego 1 entre Guardians y Rays en la Serie de Campeonato?
Los Guardianes de Cleveland sorprendieron a Tampa Bay en el primer compromiso, disputado el lunes 12 de octubre, al conseguir una remontada que terminó con marcador de 7-3.
Los Rays comenzaron con ventaja de 2-0 en la primera entrada, gracias a sencillos productores de Junior Caminero y Jonny DeLuca. Durante las primeras cinco entradas, el abridor Drew Rasmussen mantuvo controlada a la ofensiva de Cleveland.
Sin embargo, los Guardianes comenzaron su reacción en la sexta entrada con un cuadrangular solitario de Chase DeLauter, mientras que Patrick Bailey conectó otro jonrón en el séptimo episodio para empatar el marcador.
El batazo decisivo llegó en la octava entrada, cuando Nathaniel Lowe conectó un sencillo productor de dos carreras que puso a Cleveland adelante por 4-2.
Aunque Cedric Mullins acercó a los Rays con un cuadrangular solitario, Cleveland agregó tres anotaciones en la novena entrada para asegurar el triunfo.
Con esta victoria, los Guardianes llegaron a cuatro triunfos consecutivos en la postemporada, contando los últimos tres encuentros que ganaron frente a los Medias Blancas de Chicago.
¿Cómo llega Jonathan Aranda al Juego 2 con los Rays de Tampa Bay?
El mexicano Jonathan Aranda, originario de Tijuana, Baja California, buscará recuperar el protagonismo que tuvo durante la Serie Divisional contra los Yankees de Nueva York.
En el primer partido frente a Cleveland, Aranda apareció como segundo bate y primera base de los Rays, pero terminó sin hits en tres turnos oficiales, con un ponche.
No obstante, el mexicano contribuyó a la primera carrera de Tampa Bay mediante un toque de sacrificio que permitió a Yandy Díaz avanzar hasta la tercera base en el primer episodio.
Aranda llegó a la Serie de Campeonato después de registrar una destacada actuación contra los Yankees, a quienes los Rays eliminaron por barrida de 3-0.
Durante aquella eliminatoria, el tijuanense conectó cuatro imparables en 12 turnos, con promedio de .333, un cuadrangular y dos carreras impulsadas.
Su batazo más importante fue un jonrón solitario contra Gerrit Cole, que representó la única anotación en la victoria de Tampa Bay por 1-0 en el primer encuentro de la Serie Divisional.
Además, Aranda terminó la temporada regular de MLB 2026 con 22 cuadrangulares y 92 carreras impulsadas, consolidándose como una de las piezas más importantes de la ofensiva dirigida por Kevin Cash.
Para el Juego 2, el mexicano tendrá enfrente a un lanzador zurdo, por lo que su participación será importante en los ajustes ofensivos que busquen los Rays.
¿Quiénes serán los pitchers abridores del Juego 2 entre Guardians y Rays?
Los equipos tienen definidos a los lanzadores encargados de iniciar el segundo encuentro de la Serie de Campeonato.
Parker Messick (Guardians de Cleveland)
El lanzador zurdo será el encargado de abrir por Cleveland, con la misión de contener a una ofensiva que cuenta con bateadores como Jonathan Aranda, Junior Caminero y Yandy Díaz.
Messick tiene marca de 0-1, efectividad de 5.40 y 11 ponches durante la postemporada de 2026.
Su actuación será importante para unos Guardianes que buscan regresar a casa con ventaja de dos victorias en la eliminatoria.
Freddy Peralta (Rays de Tampa Bay)
Tampa Bay enviará a la lomita al derecho Freddy Peralta, quien intentará igualar la Serie de Campeonato.
Peralta llega con récord de 0-0, efectividad de 1.93 y tres ponches en esta postemporada.
El abridor tendrá la responsabilidad de frenar a una ofensiva de Cleveland que conectó 14 imparables durante el primer encuentro, encabezada por José Ramírez, Chase DeLauter y Nathaniel Lowe.
¿Qué necesitan los Rays para empatar la Serie de Campeonato contra Cleveland?
Tampa Bay necesita ganar el encuentro de este martes para colocar la Serie de Campeonato 1-1, antes de disputar los siguientes partidos como visitante.
Los Rays finalizaron la temporada regular con 98 victorias y 64 derrotas, el mejor récord de la Liga Americana, además de eliminar por barrida a los Yankees en la Serie Divisional.
Sin embargo, en el primer enfrentamiento contra Cleveland dejaron escapar una ventaja de dos carreras y su cuerpo de relevistas no logró contener a los bateadores rivales durante las últimas entradas.
Por su parte, los Guardianes llegan con la motivación de haber remontado una desventaja de 0-2 contra los White Sox para ganar tres encuentros consecutivos y avanzar a esta instancia.
Si Cleveland consigue otra victoria, regresará al Progressive Field con ventaja de 2-0 y la posibilidad de conquistar el campeonato de la Liga Americana ante sus propios aficionados.
En cambio, una victoria de Tampa Bay garantizaría que la serie viaje a Ohio empatada, dejando abierta la lucha por el boleto a la Serie Mundial 2026.
¿Cuál es el calendario completo de Guardians vs. Rays en la Serie de Campeonato 2026?
La Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana se disputa al mejor de siete encuentros, por lo que el primer equipo que consiga cuatro victorias avanzará a la Serie Mundial.
Este es el calendario programado, con horarios del centro de México:
| Juego | Fecha | Hora (CDMX) | Sede |
|---|---|---|---|
| Juego 1 | Lunes 12 de octubre | Cleveland 7-3 Tampa Bay | Tropicana Field |
| Juego 2 | Martes 13 de octubre | 6:00 PM | Tropicana Field |
| Juego 3 | Jueves 15 de octubre | 4:00 PM | Progressive Field |
| Juego 4 | Viernes 16 de octubre | 4:00 PM | Progressive Field |
| Juego 5* | Sábado 17 de octubre | 6:00 PM | Progressive Field |
| Juego 6* | Lunes 19 de octubre | 3:00 PM | Tropicana Field |
| Juego 7* | Martes 20 de octubre | 6:00 PM | Tropicana Field |
Los Juegos 5, 6 y 7 solamente se disputarán en caso de ser necesarios. La MLB también contempla posibles modificaciones de horario dependiendo del desarrollo de las Series de Campeonato.
El ganador de esta eliminatoria enfrentará al campeón de la Liga Nacional, que saldrá de la serie entre Dodgers de Los Ángeles y Cerveceros de Milwaukee, por el título de la Serie Mundial 2026.
