item.title: [WSLS] Chase DeLauter and José Ramírez lead the Guardians to a 7-3 win over the Rays in Game 1 of the ALCS
item.dc:creator: Rob Maaddi; Associated Press
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – The Cleveland Guardians used small ball, the longball and played solid all-around baseball to keep winning in the postseason. Nathaniel Lowe snapped an eighth-inning tie with a two-run single after Chase DeLauter and Patrick Bailey homered off Drew Rasmussen, and the Guardians rallied past the Tampa Bay Rays 7-3 in Game 1 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night. Recommended Videos After losing the first two games at home to the Chicago White Sox in their
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – The Cleveland Guardians used small ball, the longball and played solid all-around baseball to keep winning in the postseason.
Nathaniel Lowe snapped an eighth-inning tie with a two-run single after Chase DeLauter and Patrick Bailey homered off Drew Rasmussen, and the Guardians rallied past the Tampa Bay Rays 7-3 in Game 1 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night.
Recommended Videos
After losing the first two games at home to the Chicago White Sox in their AL Division Series, Cleveland has won four straight in the postseason for the first time since winning their first six playoff games in 2016 on the way to a World Series berth.
“It feels good to see some balls fall, to see some guys get on the barrel, to see some guys have some great at-bats, because the first two games of the White Sox series, we got beat. We did,” Lowe said. “We had to go get our backs against the wall and do something crazy, and this group did. It’s nice to feel some momentum coming here and to take Game 1.”
Jose Ramírez had three hits and DeLauter was a triple shy of the cycle as the Guardians banged out 14 hits against a Tampa Bay staff that allowed just 12 in its entire Division Series against the New York Yankees.
Junior Caminero and Jonny DeLuca had RBI singles in the first and Cedric Mullins hit a solo homer for the Rays, who never trailed in their three-game sweep of the Yankees.
“It’s been a while since we lost, so I think that’s a good thing, and I know the guys will come back and respond tomorrow,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said.
Game 2 is Tuesday night at Tropicana Field. Rookie left-hander Parker Messick starts for Cleveland, and right-hander Freddy Peralta takes the mound for the Rays.
Five relievers combined for five innings of one-run, two-hit ball for the Guardians, who became only the 11th team to overcome an 0-2 deficit in a best-of-five playoff series with a victory over the White Sox on Saturday night.
Hunter Gaddis worked a scoreless seventh for the win. Cade Smith, who pitched in all five games against Chicago, tossed a perfect ninth.
“Obviously we came off an emotional series, had a quick turnaround. But these guys come ready to play every day. Couldn’t be more proud of them,” Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. “We got punched early. And our pitching staff, credit to them, for stopping it and keeping us in the game as long as they did. And the offense came alive.”
Rasmussen took a 2-0 lead into the sixth before DeLauter led off with an opposite-field homer to left-center. Bailey started the seventh with a towering shot to center that went a projected 436 feet, ending Rasmussen’s night.
Rasmussen carried a no-hitter into the eighth in Game 1 of the ALDS against the Yankees.
Ramírez opened the eighth with an infield single off losing pitcher Tyler Wells, and DeLauter ripped a double to right. After Wells retired Jo Adell on a grounder to second, Ian Seymour entered. Lowe lined an 0-2 pitch up the middle to drive in two, giving Cleveland a 4-2 lead.
Lowe made his major league debut with Tampa Bay in 2019 and won a World Series with Texas in 2023.
“I love coming back here, I really do,” Lowe said. “It’s nice to see some familiar faces on the other side.”
Mullins connected off Erik Sabrowski for a solo shot in the bottom half.
Ramírez, whose two-run homer lifted Cleveland to a 2-0 win in Game 5 against Chicago, provided an insurance run with an RBI single in the ninth off Cole Sulser.
Ramírez then helped the Guardians get two more by breaking for third with two outs and two strikes on Adell. Caminero ran to cover the bag and was out of position when Adell hit a sharp grounder toward third. The ball rolled into left field for a two-run double.
A crowd of 35,361 fans waved yellow rally towels and rang cowbells at the Trop as Tampa Bay made its third ALCS appearance in the franchise's 29-season history.
They were fired up when the 98-win Rays jumped ahead 2-0 in the first and Rasmussen battled to keep it there until the sixth.
Coming off that dominant performance against the Yankees, Rasmussen went six-plus tough innings. The two-time All-Star right-hander, who was four outs from a no-hitter in a 1-0 victory against New York, allowed a hit to the second batter he faced and eight total, striking out seven.
Guardians starter Foster Griffin gave up two runs and five hits in four innings.
Glove work
The Rays helped Rasmussen with outstanding defense.
Nick Fortes threw out Ramírez trying to steal second in the first. Caminero made an excellent play to retire Adell on a hard bouncer to third. Caminero short-hopped the ball with his backhand and fired a strong throw to first.
The Guardians had a runner on first with one out in the third when second baseman Ben Williamson robbed DeLauter of a hit that prevented a first-and-third jam. Williamson, who wasn’t on the ALDS roster, made a diving grab on DeLauter’s sharp grounder, got up and threw him out.
Stranded runners
Rays slick-fielding shortstop Taylor Walls was 0 for 3 and left six runners on base. He struck out with the bases loaded to end the first, lined out with a runner on in the fourth and grounded out with runners on first and second to end the sixth.
Up next
Messick took the loss in Game 1 of the AL Division Series, allowing two runs over 4 1/3 innings. He threw 2 1/3 innings in relief during a Game 4 victory, giving up two runs. Messick had 11 strikeouts in the two appearances. He was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA in the regular season.
Peralta allowed one run and three hits over 4 2/3 innings in Game 2 of the Division Series vs. the Yankees. He was 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts after joining Tampa Bay at the trade deadline. Peralta was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA for the Mets this season.
___

item.title: [Sporting News] Junior Caminero trade, revisited: How Rays took advantage of 'bad' Guardians move for budding superstar | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Daniel Chavkin
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays have made it a habit of taking undervalued players and turning them into stars. No one exemplifies that more than star third baseman Junior Caminero. item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays have made it a habit of taking undervalued players and turning them into stars. No one exemplifies that more than star third baseman Junior Caminero.
The Rays acquired Caminero from the Cleveland Guardians in a minor deal after the 2021 season, which turned out to be one of the biggest trade heists in recent memory. Caminero is now one of the premier sluggers in the entire league, making the Guardians miss their former prospect.
Caminero was confused at the time, wondering why Cleveland gave up on his so quickly.
"That happened really quick. In that moment, as a young player, I was surprised," he told MLB.com. "'Why did Cleveland trade me? We played just one year in the Dominican, and they traded me?' I said, 'Am I a bad guy? Why would they trade me?' But in that moment, I didn't understand baseball. Like, hey, if you get traded, it's good for you. It was an unbelievable trade. Thank God."
Now, Caminero has made the Guardians regret their trade, potentially even forcing them to change the way they approach certain deals. Here's a recap of that trade from 2021.
MORE: Comparing the payrolls for the ALCS, NLCS teams
Revisiting Junior Caminero trade
Rays receive:
- 3B Junior Caminero
Guardians receive:
- RHP Tobais Myers
In November of 2021, the Rays and Guardians connected for what at the time was a very minor deal involving two minor leagues. The Rays, needing to clear space on its 40-man roster, sent Tobias Myers to Cleveland, who was interested in adding the young pitcher. In return, the Rays got young infielder Junior Caminero, who had been in the Cleveland system for two years.
According to MLB.com, Caminero became the Rays' 30th-best prospect before the 2022 season, while Myers was ranked No. 22 for the Guardians' system. Neither had made their MLB debut up to that point, but both were considered intriguing young players.
Of course, the Rays went on to win the trade easily. The Guardians traded Myers to the San Francisco Giants in June of 2022 for cash considerations, and Myers would go on to play in the Chicago White Sox system before making his MLB debut with the Milwaukee Brewers. He currently plays for the New York Mets.
Caminero, meanwhile, has blossomed into being one of the best hitters in baseball, and is someone who Cleveland would love to have in their lineup.
MORE: Yankees playoff history with Aaron Judge
Why did Guardians trade Junior Caminero?
The Guardians seemingly just didn't value Caminero's talent as much as they should've, and they paid the price as a result. Just two years after the deal, when Caminero vaulted to become a top-five prospect in he league, Guardians president Chris Antonetti acknowledged how much the team lost the deal.
"That's a bad trade," he said.
In reality, the Rays did their due diligence and targeted Caminero when it became clear the Guardians were interested in trading for Myers. However, the Rays immediately realized they got a hidden gem in Caminero.
"The immediate reaction upon acquiring him was wondering how in the world we were able to make that acquisition," former Rays director of Minor League operations Jeff McLerran said. "Really from the get-go, the guys felt like we had something special with Junior. Just his ability to impact the baseball and what he could do at the plate was not something that they had seen much from a guy that age."
Caminero made his MLB debut in September of 2023, almost two years after the deal went through, at just the age of 20 years-old. Since Caminero was just 18 years-old at the time of the deal, the Guardians probably didn't see his potential success as more than a lottery ticket.
Junior Caminero stats
| Year | Games | Hits | Runs | HR | RBIs | BA | OBP | OPS |
| 2023 | 7 | 8 | 4 | 1 | 7 | .235 | .278 | .631 |
| 2024 | 43 | 41 | 15 | 6 | 18 | .248 | .299 | .724 |
| 2025 | 154 | 159 | 93 | 45 | 110 | .264 | .311 | .846 |
| 2026 | 162 | 170 | 100 | 42 | 101 | .276 | .360 | .885 |
After getting his feet wet in the majors in 2023 and 2024, Caminero broke out in 2025 with the first of two-straight seasons with 40 home runs. Since the start of 2025, Caminero has the most home runs in the American League and second-most in the majors, just short of Kyle Schwarber.

item.description: If Boston Red Sox fans are still watching the Major League Baseball postseason, they're probably picking up on some reasons their team didn't make it this far. item.content:encoded:
If Boston Red Sox fans are still watching the Major League Baseball postseason, they're probably picking up on some reasons their team didn't make it this far.
Though the Red Sox had one magical stretch of 32-5 baseball this season, it was painfully obvious by the time they finished their Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium that they were never built for a deep playoff run. And the way their offense functioned in that series was a microcosm of the season.
When the chips were on the table, the Red Sox couldn't put anyone next to Willson Contreras in the lineup that was capable of inflicting damage. Even with a bum hand, Contreras hit well enough in that series to help the team move on — it was just that all of his teammates failed to rise to the task.
Red Sox fall short of other lineup cores
The teams still playing all have some sort of dynamic duo, trio, or better in their lineup. The Milwaukee Brewers have Jackson Chourio, Brice Turang, and William Contreras. The Los Angeles Dodgers have the most star-studded lineup we've ever seen, with $60 million man Kyle Tucker batting eighth.
The Tampa Bay Rays have Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda providing thump in front of Junior Caminero. Even the Cleveland Guardians have a strong supporting cast around José Ramírez, with Steven Kwan getting on base, Jo Adell driving balls in the gap, and Chase DeLauter lurking.
But in the Wild Card Series, as soon as it was clear that Roman Anthony's hand was toast, the Red Sox had no other threats in front of or behind Contreras. Adley Rutschman's at-bats got worse as the series went along, while Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela looked absolutely lost in the batter's box.
There's a lesson to be learned here. Even if the Red Sox feel good about the steps forward some of their hitters can take from this season into next, it seems imperative at this point to add another star-caliber bat. And that's not going to be easy, given the impending lockout and soft free agency class.
Whether it's buying high on Randy Arozarena or further depleting the farm system for Hunter Goodman, the Red Sox are going to have to do something uncomfortable to give themselves a real shot at contention.
Jackson Roberts is a former Division III All-Region DH who now writes and talks about sports for a living. A Bay Area native and a graduate of Swarthmore College and the Newhouse School at Syracuse University, Jackson makes his home in North Jersey. He grew up rooting for the Red Sox, Patriots, and Warriors, and he recently added the Devils to his sports fandom mosaic. item.content:encoded:
My expectation going into this exercise was that third base would be terrible, clearly the worst position for Fantasy in 2027. Now, I'm not sure.
It's bad, yes, offering only six players that I'd feel great about drafting, but having just ranked second base a few days ago ... I don't know. Third base might be better.
- Early rankings: | | | 3B | SS | OF | SP | RP
Just look at the crossover players. Bryson Stott ranked 11th for me at second base. He's 16th here. Javier Sanoja, Willi Castro and Ezequiel Duran all placed in my top 20 at second base. None of them do here.
Second base may have safer options, by and large, but there's more upside to be found at third base. And while second base is losing a whole host of players due to eligibility restrictions, only one of real significance, Jazz Chisholm, is dropping out at third.
Note that the focus here is standard 5x5 scoring (such as Rotisserie leagues), but scroll a little further, and you'll see my rankings for points leagues as well.
| 1 | |
| Whatever doubts existed for Caminero heading into 2026 were thoroughly expunged by a second consecutive 40-homer campaign in which he nearly doubled his walk rate -- a telltale sign that he's now among the most feared hitters in the game. At 23, he's poised for a lengthy reign atop this position. | |
| 2 | |
| Between the massive increase in average bat speed and the pull-air rate verging on 30 percent, there's little reason to doubt Vargas' power contributions, and he's fast enough to continue impacting the stolen base category as well. Some will be inclined toward skepticism given the enormity of his breakthrough, but third base unfortunately doesn't allow for such nitpicking. | |
| 3 | |
| Stewart's totals were more impressive than his percentages in 2026, which could make him a polarizing player heading into the new season, but based on his minor league numbers, I think he has more ground to gain in strikeouts and pull-air rate. The 15 steals are the most iffy part of his 2026 stat line, judging by his 27th percentile sprint speed. | |
| 4 | |
| Ramirez's power completely vanished in the second half, when he hit just two home runs, which is concerning enough to dethrone him at the position he has long dominated. He does have a valid excuse for it, seeing as he was coming off a broken hamate bone during that time, and I'll note that his contact skills and base-stealing remained perfectly intact. Still, he doesn't get the full benefit of the doubt at age 34. | |
| 5 | |
| After a sluggish opening act in Chicago that positioned him to be a free agent bust, Bregman made some mechanical changes midseason that led to the sort of power production we hadn't seen from him since his 41-homer 2019. While the .317 batting average, 17 homers and 1.103 OPS that he delivered over his final 43 games isn't projectable over a full season, it makes him out to be a trustworthy choice at this thin position. | |
| 6 | |
| McGonigle had a historic rookie season in many ways, but not necessarily the most Fantasy-friendly ways, owing much to his superlative defense and on-base skills. How much power he can pack onto his 5-foot-9 frame, particularly at a restrictive venue, will go a long way toward determining his ceiling. Still, he has ground to gain in batting average and stolen bases. | |
| 7 | |
| The decline for Machado in 2026, while marked, was mostly restricted to batting average, which normally isn't the first indicator of a player aging out. But he is 34 and had only one month (July) with an OPS of .800 or better. I suspect that his issues were mostly mechanical, but it's hard to take a glass-half-full approach with him when he still commands a premium at the position. | |
| 8 | |
| Gelof faked us out once before with a splashy rookie showing in 2023, but his success in 2026 went beyond just the surface level. He added more than 2 mph in average bat speed and shaved more than 10 points off his strikeout rate from the previous two years. Of course, he missed some time with injuries, but if you project his 22 homers and 16 steals over 162 games, they come out to 32 homers and 23 steals. | |
| 9 | |
| If Okamoto simply repeats his 2026 stat line, he'll be well worth drafting here, but that's a big if. The league learned to force-feed him breaking balls, diminishing his power over the course of the year, and his poor batting average and uninspired defense already give him a thin margin for error. His success depends on him piling up counting stats, so any threat to his playing time could be a deal-breaker. | |
| 10 | |
| An early injury to Carlos Correa conferred everyday duty upon Paredes, and it went about as swimmingly as it always does for him, which hopefully means the playing time question won't be raised again. He has little raw power but excels at lofting the ball to the shallowest part of left field, which is generally good for 25-plus home runs, particularly with the Crawford Boxes at his disposal in Houston. His plate discipline elevates him all the more in points leagues. | |
| 11 | |
| Muncy played in a career-high 149 games in 2026 and performed equally against righties and lefties, which may be enough to quiet the talk of decline. Seeing as he's 36, though, it's still going to be on the tip of everyone's tongue, and just because he performed adequately versus lefties doesn't mean the Dodgers were eager to use him against them. The profile is similar to Isaac Paredes, but I think with more playing time risk. | |
| 12 | |
| Improved pull-air and strikeout rates put Mead on the breakout path with a .253/.353/.498 slash line. It also compelled the Red Sox to give up an intriguing young hurler ( Connelly Early ) for him at the trade deadline. They have yet to see any benefit since he got hurt right away. However, Mead is in line to start for them at second base, which would only expand his already favorable eligibility. His swing should theoretically play well at Fenway Park, but he remains largely unproven. | |
| 13 | |
| Like Curtis Mead Schmitt's breakout was interrupted by a midseason injury (torn meniscus), and in some ways, it was the more compelling of the two. He picked up 1 mph in average bat speed and had an xBA (.288) and xSLG (.512) that were 95th percentile or better. He has a tendency to swing at everything, though, which leaves him vulnerable to the right game plan. Also, while Mead's home venue is likely to help, Schmitt's is likely to hurt. | |
| 14 | |
| It's hard to keep giving Bichette the benefit of the doubt when he fails us twice in three years, and by ranking him this low at a weak position, I would say that I'm not. But I'm also not burying him for three reasons: He hit .284 with a .772 OPS over the final four months, was reportedly still feeling the effects of a PCL sprain early in the year, and will only be 29 next year. It's a batting average-dependent profile, and those can be volatile. | |
| 15 | |
| It's even harder to give Riley the benefit of the doubt now that his numbers have declined five straight years, with the biggest drop coming in 2026, but by golly, he still hits the ball hard. The jump in chase rate this year suggests that his issues are more related to mechanics or approach than diminished tools, which leaves the door open for a fix. It's a long shot, of course, but it's glimmer enough for a budget corner infield pick, particularly with his kind of upside. | |
| 16 | |
| Stott ranks 11th for me at second base, which makes a compelling case that it's actually the weaker position, despite third base's reputation. His upside is more limited than the four ahead of him here. Still, I could see him leapfrogging them on Draft Day, depending on how the scarcities shake out (not just positionally but also statistically, with him being a superior base-stealer). | |
| 17 | |
| The jump from seven home runs to 16 made Garcia a premier third baseman in 2025, so when he regressed to only three (albeit in 82 games) the following year, it's probably reason enough to dismiss him as a one-hit wonder. Trouble is that all three came before he suffered a hand injury in mid-May, and I'm not sure he was ever quite right thereafter, needing separate IL stints for the injury. That he stopped stealing bases is another concern, though. | |
| 18 | |
| Arenado seemed to be on his way out as a power hitter, his dwindling exit velocities reaching a tipping point as he failed to deliver 20 homers in consecutive seasons, and this made it all the more shocking to see him bounce back with 30 this year, 16 of which came in the final two months. I'm skeptical of a repeat, both because he's in his mid-30s and because his average exit velocity actually diminished further to the 3rd percentile. If the Diamondbacks are at all to credit for the turnaround, he'll surely enjoy having another season with them. | |
| 19 | |
| Availability can sometimes trump ability, and simply by virtue of starting 151 games for the Twins (and coming off the bench in five others), Lee compiled some pretty good totals in 2026. The only area where you might consider him a plus, though, is home runs, and those came more from an optimal pull-air rate than a natural ability to impact a baseball. Any slippage in health or production would reduce him to mediocrity again.  | |
| 20 | |
| Westburg spent all of 2026 recovering from a UCL tear, submitting to full-blown Tommy John surgery in May, but since he's a hitter and not a pitcher, he should be in pretty good shape come spring training. The 27-year-old was a burgeoning power threat prior to the procedure, showing the capacity for 30-plus homers in a healthy season, and isn't near the batting average liability that, say, Colson Montgomery is. | |
What changes in points leagues?
1. Junior Caminero, TB
2. Miguel Vargas, CHW
3. Jose Ramirez, CLE
4. Sal Stewart, CIN
5. Alex Bregman, CHC
6. Kevin McGonigle, DET
7. Manny Machado, SD
8. Isaac Paredes, HOU
9. Max Muncy, LAD
10. Curtis Mead, BOS
11. Zack Gelof, ATH
12. Casey Schmitt, SF
13. Bo Bichette, NYM
14. Nolan Arenado, ARI
15. Bryson Stott, PHI
16. Maikel Garcia, KC
17. Kazuma Okamoto, TOR
18. Brooks Lee, MIN
19. Austin Riley, ATL
20. Jordan Westburg, BAL

item.title: [Bettors Insider] Shohei Ohtani, Jonathan Aranda, Junior Caminero Props: 3 MLB Batter Bets to Back Today | Bettors Insider

Monday’s slate gives us two of those players squarely in the spotlight: Shohei Ohtani trying to find his timing again in Milwaukee, and a pair of Tampa Bay bats that have already authored the signature moments of their ALDS sweep heading into Game 1 of the ALCS against Cleveland. None of these three lines are “free mone
item.content:encoded:
October baseball is a different animal for prop bettors — smaller sample, bigger stakes, and lineups built around whoever’s been carrying their team through the first two rounds. Monday’s slate gives us two of those players squarely in the spotlight: Shohei Ohtani trying to find his timing again in Milwaukee, and a pair of Tampa Bay bats that have already authored the signature moments of their ALDS sweep heading into Game 1 of the ALCS against Cleveland.
None of these three lines are “free money,” and we’re not pretending otherwise. But each one is backed by a real statistical case, and one of them is a legitimate longshot worth a small piece of your bankroll. Here’s the breakdown.
Shohei Ohtani Hits Over 0.5 (-115) vs. Logan Henderson
Ohtani’s .275/.377/.512 slash line with 30 home runs, 144 hits, and 268 total bases over 135 games this season is the baseline case for betting him to reach base in literally any game he plays. A .377 on-base percentage means Ohtani is getting on base better than one out of every three plate appearances even before you isolate hits specifically, and his contact skills remain elite even in a year where he split time managing a knee issue.
The matchup context matters here too. Henderson is a rookie-caliber arm who hasn’t faced a lineup with this level of postseason pressure attached to it, and the Dodgers as a group have shown they can grind out at-bats against less experienced starters. At just 0.5 hits, this line is asking Ohtani for a single knock in what will likely be 4-5 plate appearances. Even accounting for recent cold stretches, betting against Shohei Ohtani recording one hit in a full game remains one of the tougher outs in the sport to actually complete.
Jonathan Aranda Hits Over 0.5 vs. Franco Griffin
If you watched any of the Rays-Yankees ALDS, you already know the Aranda story. His third-inning solo shot off Gerrit Cole in Game 1 — a 417-foot blast to right-center — was the only run of a 1-0 series-opening win, and it set the tone for a clean three-game sweep. Across that series, Aranda hit .333/.385/.583 for a .968 OPS, numbers that dwarf his already-solid .274/.358/.434 season line.
That’s the core of the case: Aranda is seeing the ball well right now, has shown he can do damage against a well above-average Yankees pitching staff, and now draws a left-handed starter in Griffin to open the ALCS. First baseman with sticky contact skills facing a lefty he hasn’t built extensive familiarity with is a profile that tends to produce base hits, not shutouts. At 0.5 hits, the number is simply asking for one knock from a hitter who’s been getting multiple most nights since the calendar flipped to October.
Junior Caminero Home Run Over 0.5 (+525 BetRivers)
This is the one we’re framing honestly: a value shot, not a lock. Caminero is coming off a 42-homer season — his second straight 40-bomb campaign — and projection models still put him around a 0.24 expected home run probability for any single game, which sits below what the plus-money price implies you need for a coin-flip bet. In other words, this isn’t the kind of prop where the math says “take the over all day.” It’s a power bet on a player who has legitimate 40-plus-homer pop and a juicy price if he connects.
Where it gets more interesting is the matchup and the moment. Caminero is drawing another lefty in Griffin tonight, and left-on-right power threats like Caminero have shown they can turn a mistake into a souvenir in a hurry — he’s also shown an .817 OPS against the Yankees in this postseason run specifically, proof the bat is playing up on the biggest stage, not shrinking from it. At +525, you’re not betting that Caminero goes deep most nights. You’re betting that on a night where ESPN’s own expert panel has him tabbed as a leading ALCS MVP pick, the long ball is live enough to make the number worth a small stake.
Today’s Edge
Two contact-driven hits bets and one true power longshot — that’s the balance we’re carrying into Monday’s games. Always confirm the latest line movement with your sportsbook before locking anything in, since postseason numbers can shift quickly as lineups are finalized.
- Shohei Ohtani OVER 0.5 Hits (-115)
- Jonathan Aranda OVER 0.5 Hits
- Junior Caminero OVER 0.5 Home Runs (+525 BetRivers)
The hits props lean on two hitters who have been nearly impossible to keep off base in October, while the Caminero shot gives this card real upside if the Rays’ slugger connects early in the ALCS. If you’re shopping for better plus-money odds on power props like that one, it’s worth comparing a few books before locking in your DraftKings Promo Code or another book’s current offer.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – As he waited in the on-deck circle before an at-bat last Saturday in Game 1 of the American League Division Series, with more than 40,000 vociferous Rays and Yankees fans in attendance at Tropicana Field, Tampa Bay third baseman Junior Caminero remarked to manager Kevin Cash that he hadn't seen an atmosphere like that since the World Baseball Classic in March at Miami’s loanDepot park.
In that tournament, Caminero tied for the overall lead in home runs with three and slashed .350/.409/.850 for the Dominican Republic in six games. This month, after coming into this postseason with just two playoff at-bats under his belt as a rookie in the 2023 AL Wild Card Series against the Rangers, Caminero is 3-for-10 with a double and two runs scored, helping the Rays sweep the Yankees in the ALDS.
Another member of the Rays who stood out in the World Baseball Classic has also had a solid start to this year’s postseason for Tampa Bay. That would be Jonathan Aranda, who had had just one postseason at-bat in his career before this season – also in '23 against Texas.
After slashing .357/.438/.643 with a home run for Team Mexico in four games at Houston’s Daikin Park in March, the Rays' first baseman came up big in the ALDS, producing the only run in Game 1 with a 417-foot round-tripper off Gerrit Cole and posting a .333/.385/.583 for the series, including an RBI single in Wednesday’s clinching victory.
Seeing Caminero and Aranda have that type of success in their first prolonged Major League postseason, Cash sees a correlation between their exposure to the atmosphere of the WBC and what they’re experiencing now in the postseason.
“I go back to the WBC,” Cash said. “If you ask those two individuals you’re talking about, I think they would say that that environment in the WBC is as intense as any environment that they’ve witnessed in their careers.
“We know that both of those guys really took off for their countries; whether it was the Dominican Republic or Team Mexico, they were huge parts of their success. The big at-bats, the big hits, I think it really helped them. And more than anything, they were excited to get the opportunity to do this now in Major League playoff baseball.”
In Miami’s Pool D, the atmosphere was electric, with the Dominican Republic and eventual tournament champion Venezuela among the countries playing in front of passionate sellout crowds cheering on their nations’ teams. And in Houston’s Pool B, Mexico also had large partisan crowds rooting for the bordering nation, an environment crescendoed with the matchup against the United States in pool play.
“I don’t think you can say the moment’s been too big for either of them,” Cash said, once again crediting their experiences in the Classic as part of their overall preparedness for the MLB postseason. “I think they had really good, strong series in the DS. I think those two guys have had tremendous at-bats for us.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Junior Caminero did a lot of elite trolling after Rays swept Yankees
item.dc:creator: Kyle Koster
item.description: To the victors go the spoils and the Tampa Bay Rays have earned every right to crow. The plucky upstarts, who happened to win the American League East with the junior circuit's best record this year, completed a three-game sweep over the mighty New York Yankees on Wednesday night to secure a spot in the ALCS. MORE: Jazz Chisholm 'confused' by Yankees' fans reaction Everything this team does well was on full display as unheralded players continuously rose to the occasion. Junior Caminero, the Ray
item.content:encoded:
To the victors go the spoils and the Tampa Bay Rays have earned every right to crow.
The plucky upstarts, who happened to win the American League East with the junior circuit's best record this year, completed a three-game sweep over the mighty New York Yankees on Wednesday night to secure a spot in the ALCS.
MORE: Jazz Chisholm 'confused' by Yankees' fans reaction
Everything this team does well was on full display as unheralded players continuously rose to the occasion. Junior Caminero, the Rays' sole superstar, went 3-for-10 in the series and worked two walks. Though he did not contribute much in the realm of power, the third baseman had plenty of energy to take up the mantle as chief trash-talker after the final out was recorded.
Caminero threw out a bit of everything in his defiant celebration. First there was the exaggerated sweeping motion to let a dejected Yankees Stadium crowd know just how thoroughly their beloved team had been beaten.
He continued the revelry by channeling David Ortiz and bellowing about the Yankees' loss.
Once in the clubhouse, his fire only burned brighter and by the time those suds-soaked interviews began, he was under the impression he was the best in the world.
There are a lot of not very fun people out there who shame baseball teams for celebrating like they've just won the World Series on every step to winning the World Series. By the time the Fall Classic wraps a squad can have four or five of these out-of-control parties under their belt.
And to be clear, most of them don't age well because only one franchise can win the whole dang thing.
But here's a rebuttal. Baseball is an insane marathon and there are thousands upon thousands of boring hours against the actual game action. Teams are together for seven or eight months and need every excuse they can to blow off some steam and celebrate what they've accomplished together.
Just think of how much Yankees fans are going to hate Caminero for his entire career now based on just a few clips. That is, if they don't use their considerable funds to take him away from small-market Tampa in a couple years. None of that would be possible without carte blanche to party it up and take every available opportunity to twist the knife.

What It Means
Caminero is hitting for a .276 BA, .360 OBP and .524 SLG with an 18.4% strikeout rate and an 11.3% walk rate. His OPS is .885, which ranks 7th in MLB, and he has scored 100 runs. item.title: [MLB.com] Caminero y Díaz reconocidos por sus hazañas al bate en la boleta del Hank Aaron
item.dc:creator: David Venn
item.description: Hay 10 candidatos en cada circuito, pero sólo dos equipos cuentan con más de un candidato: Los Rays (Junior Caminero y Yandy Díaz) en la Liga Americana y los Rojos (Sal Stewart y Elly de la Cruz) en la Nacional. Tampa Bay terminó en el lugar 22 de MLB en cuadrangulares durante la campaña regular con 169, pero estuvo en el lugar 12 en carreras anotadas. ¿Qué significa para los Rays la presencia de Caminero y Díaz en la boleta en el 2026? “Dice que han tenido grandes temporadas”, comentó el lunes
item.content:encoded:
Hay 10 candidatos en cada circuito, pero sólo dos equipos cuentan con más de un candidato: Los Rays (Junior Caminero y Yandy Díaz) en la Liga Americana y los Rojos (Sal Stewart y Elly de la Cruz) en la Nacional.
Tampa Bay terminó en el lugar 22 de MLB en cuadrangulares durante la campaña regular con 169, pero estuvo en el lugar 12 en carreras anotadas.
¿Qué significa para los Rays la presencia de Caminero y Díaz en la boleta en el 2026?
“Dice que han tenido grandes temporadas”, comentó el lunes el manager de Tampa Bay, Kevin Cash, en el marco de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana entre sus Rays en los Yankees. “Ése es un gran premio para el cual ser nominado. También habla de la supuesta falta de jonrones de nosotros. Sí contamos con algunos muchachos que saben sacar la bola”.
En el caso del dominicano Caminero y del cubano Díaz, es cierto. El primero disparó 42 bombazos en la temporada regular, luego de dar 45 en el 2025. Y el segundo conectó 22.
Además, Caminero impulsó 101 carreras este año, a la vez que Díaz remolcó 85 y fue líder de la Liga Americana en hits con 180.
“Si estás recibiendo un premio o siendo nominado para estar en la misma conversación con Hank Aaron, tienes bastante poder”.
El Premio Hank Aaron, por supuesto, le hace honor al fallecido toletero del mismo nombre, quien disparó 755 cuadrangulares en una carrera de 23 años en Grandes Ligas. De 1974 al 2007, tenía el récord de todos los tiempos en las Mayores en vuelacercas, hasta que Barry Bonds lo rompió en aquel 2007 y terminó su carrera con 762. Además, Aaron es el líder de por vida de MLB en empujadas con 2,297 y bases alcanzadas con 6,856, entre muchos otros logros de mayores proporciones en las Mayores.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays are back at it Monday night for Game 2 of the ALDS at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida, after an off day Sunday. The Yankees dominated Boston in their AL Wild Card Series to advance to the ALDS to face fellow AL East rivals the Rays, but Game 1 on Saturday was far from how New York performed in the previous round.
The Yankees’ lineup ran into Rays All-Star right-hander Drew Rasmussen in Game 1, who carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning before allowing a double to Austin Wells, who ended up getting thrown out at third base to end the inning while trying to stretch it into a triple. Rasmussen finished his outing with eight scoreless innings and 10 strikeouts, with Bryan Baker recording the save and Jonathan Aranda accounting for the only run of the game with his third-inning solo home run in the Rays’ 1-0 shutout victory.
Veteran right-hander Freddy Peralta will look to shut down New York’s lineup Monday night just as Rasmussen did in Game 1. Peralta had a down year overall, but he ended the regular season strong, posting a 4-0 record with a 0.96 ERA and 0.89 WHIP across five starts in September.
Peralta will be going toe-to-toe with likely 2026 American League Cy Young Award winner Cam Schlittler of the Yankees, who’s set to make his second start of this year’s MLB playoffs. The young right-hander owned a 1.95 ERA and 0.92 WHIP and recorded 239 strikeouts during the regular season. He also pitched 6.1 scoreless innings with 10 strikeouts in a win over Boston in the AL Wild Card Series.
See our Yankees vs. Rays MLB playoff predictions, picks, and more below for Monday night’s ALDS Game 2 at Tropicana Field.

The Stats Hub notes that there has been no run scored during the first inning in each of the Yankees’ last six games. That trend could continue Monday night.
There wasn’t much offense at all in Game 1 between the Yankees and Rays on Saturday. The Yankees were shut out and nearly no-hit, and even though the Rays scored a run in the win, Tampa Bay’s offense totaled only five hits and went 0-for-5 with runners in scoring position.
Now Cam Schlittler is taking the mound for the Yankees in Game 2, and we already mentioned how dominant he was during the regular season, in his first start this postseason, and through his first three career playoff outings. We also mentioned that Freddy Peralta didn’t quite have his best season on the mound, but he ended the regular season on a high note and has allowed only three runs over his last six starts.
Both lineups feature plenty of offensive firepower, but it’s hard to ignore how well these two starting pitchers have been throwing the ball.

item.content:encoded:
The Athletic has live coverage of the MLB Playoffs, including the ALDS Game 2s of White Sox vs Guardians and Yankees vs Rays.
After three days of Wild Card Series action, the dust has settled and four teams (Houston Astros, Boston Red Sox, Philadelphia Phillies and Chicago Cubs) have found themselves on an early vacation. Major League Baseball’s 12-team postseason field has been whittled to eight.
Now, the race for the World Series shifts to the next round: the Division Series. Four teams (Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Dodgers, Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers) that had first-round byes will now be in action. Additionally, while the Wild Card Series featured a best-of-three format, the Division Series will be best-of-five.
Here’s how MLB’s bracket looks right now:
You can watch the MLB playoffs on Fubo (Stream Free Now).
What is Saturday’s MLB Playoff schedule and starters?
White Sox at Guardians (AL Division Series Game 1): Hagen Smith vs. Parker Messick
First pitch: 1 p.m. ET (TBS)
After the 23-year-old Smith pitched three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series against the Astros, the White Sox turn to him for an encore performance in Game 1 of the ALDS. While the club was able to pile on six runs against the Astros in a win, it won’t be as easy against the Guardians and Messick.
An All-Star this season, Messick finished his rookie campaign with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts over 32 starts. Against the White Sox, Messick carded a 2.81 ERA in four starts (25 2/3 innings).
Braves at Dodgers (NL Division Series Game 1): TBD vs. Tarik Skubal
First pitch: 4 p.m. ET (Fox)
Having burned Chris Sale to take Thursday’s winner-take-all game against the Phillies, and with Tyler Mahle also unavailable, the Braves appear to be looking at another bullpen game.
“They’ve pitched in big situations during the season, and no matter who we really see right now in that bullpen in any situation, no matter what inning it is, we’re feeling pretty confident about them,” catcher Drake Baldwin told reporters.
The Dodgers, coming off a first-round bye, will counter with Tarik Skubal, the crown jewel acquisition of this year’s trade deadline. The AL’s reigning Cy Young Award winner has a 2.61 ERA with his new team, his final starts before reaching a highly anticipated free agency.
Yankees at Rays (AL Division Series Game 1): Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen
First pitch: 6:30 p.m. ET (TBS)
Faced with an embarrassment of riches on the pitching side, the Yankees will deploy 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner Gerrit Cole against the AL East champs. After Cole in Game 1, the Yankees will have Cam Schlittler in Game 2 and some variation of Max Fried or Carlos Rodón in Games 3 and 4, the last matchup only if necessary.
On the Tampa Bay side, Drew Rasmussen, arguably one of the most underrated aces in the sport, will get the ball at Tropicana Field. For his career, Rasmussen has a 1.81 ERA in 11 games (10 starts) against the Yankees.
Padres at Brewers (NL Division Series Game 1): Robbie Ray vs. Jacob Misiorowski
First pitch: 8:30 p.m. ET (FS1)
Saturday’s final matchup will feature two pitchers at opposite ends of their careers. On the San Diego side, Robbie Ray, the 2021 AL Cy Young Award winner, has been largely unable to replicate the success he had that season. After a deadline trade from the San Francisco Giants to the Padres, Ray has carded a 5.02 ERA over nine starts.
For the Brewers, Jacob Misiorowski is just getting started. An All-Star in his rookie year, Misiorowski finished his sophomore campaign as the favorite to win the NL Cy Young Award, leading MLB with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. He’s wowed the sport with his ability to repeatedly fire fastballs in excess of 100 mph, and there’s reason to believe that, at 24 years old, his best is yet to come.
What to know about each Division Series matchup
White Sox at Guardians: The two AL Central clubs played each other 13 times during the regular season, with the White Sox winning the season series 7-6. That, however, was not enough to overcome a late surge by the Guardians and a collapse by Chicago that led to the White Sox losing control of the division and having to play their way out of the wild card.
Now, the two clubs will meet again for at least three games, a spot in the Championship Series on the line. By winning the division and finishing with a better record than the AL West winner, the Guardians were granted a first-round bye. No mind, the White Sox dispatched the Astros in two games and have been off since Thursday. That extra rest has allowed the club to realign its depleted pitching staff.
One thing to watch: How Chicago’s thin, matchup-dependent pitching staff is deployed against Cleveland’s newfound offense — the club led the AL in wRC+ (108) from Aug. 1 onward. The urgency, or lack thereof, by White Sox manager Will Venable could swing the series either direction.
Braves at Dodgers: The Braves’ pitching staff will enter Game 1 with very little margin for error, as it will likely be a group effort without a starter available. That alone could be the difference, as teams that take Game 1 in any best-of-five series have historically won the series 72 percent of the time. That said, these Dodgers have not played their best against the Braves, losing the season series 5-1, including a late-August sweep when Tyler Glasnow and Yoshinobu Yamamoto both pitched.
One thing to watch: Shohei Ohtani’s ability to contribute. The four-time MVP has spent much of the second half of the season compromised, leading to an abbreviated September, with some of it on the injured list.
“I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth, and just a little tweaks here and there, and I’ll be ready for tomorrow,” Ohtani said through interpreter Will Ireton.
Yankees at Rays: Only one team had a better record over its final 30 games than the Rays, who went 20-10 to fend off a late Yankees push to claim the AL East. That, plus a 55-26 home record that tied the Brewers for the best in MLB, has Tampa Bay inching toward its first World Series appearance since 2020. To get there, the Rays will need to beat the Yankees, who made quick work of the Red Sox in the wild-card round. That they did so without Aaron Judge on the roster or needing to call on Giancarlo Stanton in a pinch hit capacity is all the more impressive.
One thing to watch: Junior Caminero was 20 years old the last time the Rays made the postseason, going hitless in two at-bats. Since then, Caminero, now 23, has morphed into a perennial All-Star, hitting 40 home runs in consecutive seasons, the latter of which should earn him major MVP consideration. Few players love the big stage as much as Caminero. One of those players just so happens to be Cam Schlittler, the presumptive AL Cy Young Award winner, who will take the ball at least once this series. How these two match up will be one of the best subplots of this postseason.
Padres at Brewers: In a battle between arguably MLB’s hottest team (the Padres) and the league’s best team all season (the Brewers), there will be a lot of firsts. This is San Diego’s first Division Series under new owners José E. Feliciano and his wife and business partner Kwanza Jones. It will be the first extended runway for Padres rookie catcher Ethan Salas. It will be the first postseason series for Christian Yelich as the Brewers’ captain. And it will be the first time Misiorowski faces these Padres since May.
Should Milwaukee win, it will be the first time in franchise history that the club has made it to back-to-back league championship series. If San Diego upsets MLB’s No. 1 team, it will be the club’s first trip since 2022 and just its fourth overall.
One thing to watch: The bullpens. Behind multiple high-leverage arms, San Diego has made the late innings nearly impossible for opposing teams. If there’s one club that can match the Padres in that regard, it’s the Brewers. The late innings will likely be the deciding factor in who advances.

item.description: The Detroit Tigers made one of their best draft choices in the 2019 MLB Draft, taking outfielder Riley Greene with the fifth overall pick. item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Tigers made one of their best draft choices in the 2019 MLB Draft, taking outfielder Riley Greene with the fifth overall pick. Since Greene debuted for the Tigers, he's become known as the face of the offense, collecting multiple achievements along the way.
A three-time All-Star from 2024 to 2026, a Silver Slugger Award winner in 2025, and a reliable defender, Greene leads the Detroit offense into the future. It was proof enough when Greene went down with an injury in August that this offense needs him, but that's a good thing to have within the organization.
With the offseason in full swing for the Tigers, nominations for the prestigious Hank Aaron Award have been released as the playoffs continue.
The Hank Aaron Award is awarded annually to the best overall offensive performer in each league. The award was introduced in 1999 to mark the 25th anniversary of Hank Aaron breaking Babe Ruth's all-time home run record. A panel of Hall of Famers combines with a fan vote to determine the winners.
Of the 10 American League players representing 10 American League teams, Greene takes center stage for the Tigers organization.
How to Vote for Riley Greene
Greene finished his 2026 campaign with 21 home runs, 75 RBIs and an OPS of .844. While his home run and RBI totals were down from his 2025 campaign, the All-Star outfielder set a new career-high in OPS and doubles with 32.
Voting is open through Oct. 12, and Greene needs all the votes he can get from Tigers fans. Some of his biggest competitors for the award this season are Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros, Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays, and Ben Rice of the New York Yankees.
Of all the American League nominees, Greene ranked ninth in home runs, ninth in RBIs, and seventh in OPS. If Greene brings home the hardware, he will become the first Tigers player to do so since Miguel Cabrera won the award in back-to-back MVP seasons in 2012 and 2013.
If Greene doesn't win, it doesn't take away from how much improvement he had in 2026. A big flaw in Greene's game was strikeouts, punching out the most in Major League Baseball in 2025 with 201. He lowered that total to 157 in 2026 and improved his overall offense.
Greene is easily the top candidate to get a contract extension to ensure Detroit has a well-rounded athlete on their roster for years to come.
Dominic Minchella is a 2024 Eastern Michigan University graduate with a BA in Communications, Media, and Theatre Arts and a Journalism minor. He covers Major League Baseball for On SI and spends his free time watching games and sharing his insights.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline

item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
October has officially arrived, just in time for the MLB postseason to ramp up.
With all four Wild Card series now over — three of which ended in two-game sweeps — just eight teams remain alive in the pursuit of a World Series title, with the Guardians, Rays, Dodgers and Brewers entering the picture after watching the first round from home.
Some of baseball's biggest stars, from Shohei Ohtani and Jacob Misiorowski to Junior Caminero and Cam Schlittler, will be on full display for the division series. On both sides of the bracket, the question will be whether the teams carrying their Wild Card momentum can now take down a well-rested heavyweight.
With a chance to reset between rounds, the best-of-five ALDS and NLDS matchups begin Saturday. Who will advance to the championship series?
With Wild Card matchups in the rearview mirror, The Sporting News predicts the 2026 MLB division series matchups.
MORE: Complete MLB playoff schedule for 2026 postseason
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 2 Cleveland Guardians
You can certainly debate whether the Guardians (85 regular-season wins) or White Sox (84 regular-season wins) really belong on the postseason stage this season, with neither AL Central squad owning a ton of big-name star power. Regardless, the fact is that Cleveland and Chicago both find themselves with an opportunity to make a serious postseason run in a weaker AL bracket — and the White Sox have already taken advantage.
Chicago enters the ALDS the momentum of its first postseason series win since the 2005 World Series, proving in the Wild Card round that it has the power and pitching depth to challenge opponents. Cleveland, though, has better top-end starting pitching in Parker Messick, Gavin Williams and Tanner Bibee.
These two teams are well familiar with each other; the White Sox won the season series, 7-6. Cleveland's offense isn't very threatening, ranking last among all postseason teams in team OPS (.696) — this matchup will likely come down to how early the White Sox's bats can get to Guardians starters.
Saturday will mark the first time in MLB history that the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland have met in the postseason.
The White Sox began playing baseball in 1894 as the Sioux City Cornhuskers.
The Guardians began playing baseball in 1896 as the Columbus Buckeyes/Senators.
The fact that this is a divisional matchup means it will likely be close, but Chicago's momentum is hard to ignore, and there was only a one-win discrepancy between the sides in the regular season. The White Sox are finally building something serious, seemingly with a new hero every night. The power in Will Venable's lineup is dangerous enough to reach the ALCS.
Prediction: White Sox in 4
No. 4 New York Yankees vs. No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays
It's been clear since the start of the postseason that whichever AL East team emerged from the lower half of the bracket would be favored to reach the World Series. This is the heavyweight matchup of the two ALDS series, featuring elite starting pitching on both sides and some of MLB's premiere sluggers.
Of course, the massive question lingering over this matchup is how much, if at all, Aaron Judge will play for the Yankees. Even as the lower seed, if he's near 100 percent, it's hard not to view New York as the favorite to reach the ALCS; a healthy Judge, alongside Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. and Ben Rice, takes Aaron Boone's lineup to a new level, capable of matching the all-around offensive excellence of Tampa Bay's quartet: Caminero, Yandy Siaz, Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson.
The Rays won this season series 7-6, but it may be the most evenly matched division series. Both sides can roll out a trio talented starters — New York with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole, and Tampa Bay with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and Shane McClanahan — to pair with deep offenses.
Yankees can line up their pitching as follows against the Rays:
Game 1: Gerrit Cole
Game 2: Cam Schlittler
Game 3: Max Fried
Game 4: Gerrit Cole
Game 5: Cam Schlittler
For two reasons, the Yankees are the pick here. For one, between Schlittler and arguably the best bullpen in baseball, New York is loaded with leverage arms. And the Yankees are also riding high off a dominant Wild Card series, biding time for Judge and Giancarlo Stanton to heal. Assuming those two sluggers can at least be used in some key at-bats, the Yankees' lineup is capable of changing games in an instant.
Prediction: Yankees in 5
No. 3 Atlanta Braves vs. No. 2 Los Angeles Dodgers
The Dodgers' path to becoming the first National League team to win three-straight World Series will begin with a matchup against a 94-win Braves squad fresh off a Wild Card win over the Phillies.
Los Angeles' rest advantage could be significant. Even if he's not pitching, Ohtani has been dealing with lingering injury concerns over the last few months. A week off between his last regular season game should only benefit him, not to mention the Dodgers' ability to line up their loaded starting rotation however they choose. With the Braves using Chris Sale in two games against Philadelphia, he may not be available early in the NLDS.
The Dodgers and Braves have built quite the postseason history. 👀🔥
2013 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2018 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2020 NLCS — LAD def. ATL
2021 NLCS — ATL def. LAD
2026 NLDS — ??? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/mHhbDO9gDX
The top of Atlanta's lineup is potent enough to make this an interesting series, and the team did beat the Dodgers five times in the regular season, but Ronald Acuna Jr., Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies will have to meet the moment in the NLDS. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has pitched well against Atlanta in his career, as have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow.
Even if the Braves' bats can keep things close, it's hard to imagine Atlanta's pitching staff beyond Sale being able to contain Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Kyle Tucker and Mookie Betts over a five-game series. The Braves are a good team, but the Dodgers are far too talented to fall this early in the bracket.
Prediction: Dodgers in 4
No. 4 San Diego Padres vs. No. 1 Milwaukee Brewers
This matchup pins baseball's best team all season, Milwaukee, against one of its hottest over the past month, San Diego. While the Brewers are the clear favorites here, between the best starting pitcher in the game this season and a deep lineup that plays to contact, the Padres do pose some interesting challenges, going 4-2 against Milwaukee in the regular season.
On one hand, San Diego has stars made for October. As shown in the Wild Card round, when the top of the Padres' lineup is on, they're a hard team to beat — Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado, Xander Boegarts, Ty France and Jackson Merrill can look like one of the best 1-through-5 groups in baseball at times. Add in an elite starter (Michael King) and a strong bullpen led by Mason Miller, and there's a path for the Padres to pull off a stunner here.
Most data has shown that the more of a threat a team is to hit the ball out of the yard, the better they'll fare in the postseason. If this is finally going to be the year the Brewers reach a World Series — putting an end to their cycle of regular season success with playoff shortcomings — they'll need to slug more. This is an offense that's outstanding at making contact and getting on base, but has also continually come up short in October and finished second-to-last in team home runs (154) in the 2026 regular season.
Chances are, Milwaukee won't only be able to rely on its strong pitching staff to reach the World Series. The Brewers' bats will need some extra-base hits. But with the Padres' lackluster starting pitching depth, this is still a series the Brewers can claim even if they're not pristine.
San Diego may have some top-end talent and momentum, but the Padres can't match Milwaukee's all-around depth.
Prediction: Brewers in 4

item.title: [si.com] MLB Postseason Power Rankings: Strength and Weaknesses for Every Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Karl Rasmussen
item.description: The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series. The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.
Follow Karlras920
