item.title: [si.com] The Potentially Fatal Flaw For Each MLB Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early. With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team. Brewers: Lack of Power The Brewers were baseball’s best team
item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.
Follow rumorsandrants

item.title: [sfexaminer.com] No matter who wins, MLB will push salary cap
item.dc:creator: Ken Rosenthal; The Athletic
item.description: (Commentary) Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners. Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken. Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite a
item.content:encoded:
(Commentary)
Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners.
Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken.
Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite argument. Its public-relations department, in news releases before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, described competitive balance as a hallmark of MLB.
Let's be clear: Revenue disparity between large- and small-market clubs is a legitimate concern. The league and players union need to adopt significant measures to make the playing field more level. But the league's argument for greater competitive balance, if not a red herring, is at least an argument of convenience. And not a particularly strong one, if you watched the regular season.
The Brewers finished with the best record in the National League. The Rays produced the best record in the American League. And the Guardians became the third small-market team to earn one of four first-round byes. Perhaps the Guardians were undeserving, considering their record was only the 11th best in the majors. But by finishing with the second-best mark among AL division winners, they clinched the bye under the postseason format the league and union created.
So is the sport really that far gone?
The league's own news release in 2022 noted that MLB produced 15 different World Series champions in the prior 21 seasons. The Texas Rangers in 2023 made it 16. And before the 2024 World Series, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred told The Athletic, "Our record on competitive balance is darn good."
Just two years later, to hear Manfred & Co. tell it, the sport is having an existential crisis. All because the league's highest-revenue team, the Dodgers, won back-to-back World Series. All because the team owners want to build their case for a cap.
The league cites a need for greater competitive balance as justification to drastically overhaul the game's economic system. And it is trumpeting a new set of facts -- specifically, the absence of a small-market champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals -- to make its case.
There is no denying that in that time, large-market teams have accounted for 90% of World Series winners, 85% of World Series participants and 77.5% of league championship series participants. And sure, the same pattern might continue this year.
Never mind that the Dodgers performed below expectations in the regular season for the second consecutive year. According to FanGraphs, they still stand the best chance of winning the World Series -- 36.7%, with the Brewers next at 11.6%. As if on cue, and in some cases by design, the Dodgers' best players are getting healthy and rounding into form.
If Los Angeles becomes the first team since the 1998 to 2000 New York Yankees to win three consecutive World Series titles, the league will surely use that data point in its pitch that only a salary cap can save the sport.
And if the Brewers or Rays win their first Series, or if the Guardians win their first since 1948? The league will consider it an aberration, a single-season outcome that means little when compared with the larger sample size of the previous 10 seasons. An exception that proves the rule.
But let's broaden the discussion.
By emphasizing postseason results, the league is devaluing the most accurate measure of a club, the six-month grind of the regular season. Not to mention devaluing the 162 games of inventory all 30 clubs must sell.
Since 2015 -- the line of demarcation the league has set with the Royals' World Series triumph -- the Guardians rank fourth in regular-season wins, the Brewers fifth and the Rays seventh. They are models for other small-market teams, proof that those clubs do not have to operate without hope.
It's true none of those teams won a World Series in the past 10 years. But the Rays got there in the shortened 2020 season. The Guardians reached the American League Championship Series in 2024, the Brewers in 2025. Inferior depth, resulting in part from lower payrolls, might be part of the reason none went further. Adjustments to the collective bargaining agreement could help address that.
No reasonable person would start a league from scratch and adopt baseball's current economic system, in which the league says that the top four spenders -- the Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies -- outspent the bottom 22 in free agency over the course of the current labor agreement.
Reasonable people can disagree, however, whether a cap is the only possible solution when the players' historic opposition to the concept might lead to the cancellation of part or all of the 2027 season.
The league keeps referencing polls saying fans want a cap. Fans, though, evidently are not too upset with the current state of affairs: The league's attendance increased again this year, reaching its highest level since 2016.
Even in cap sports, not every team begins every season with the expectation of competing for a title. The most successful franchises are the shrewdest. Part of baseball's problem is that innovative small-market clubs no longer hold the competitive advantage they once did over less forward-thinking opponents.
Ex // Top Stories
Some of the large-market teams plucked top small-market executives. Very few clubs, if any, continue to lag behind in the intellectual arms race. Even the Colorado Rockies and Washington Nationals, two of the slowest clubs to adapt to baseball's information age, have gotten smarter.
If everyone is essentially working off the same data, payrolls become more of a separator. But even then, the edge money provides is not an absolute guarantee of success in October.
Before winning in the shortened 2020 season, the Dodgers had not won a World Series since 1988. The Mets have not won since 1986. The Phillies and Yankees are experiencing championship droughts that began in 2008 and 2009.
Many baseball executives consider the postseason a crapshoot, fearing the random outcomes that occur in small samples.
The Dodgers, without question, have inordinate financial advantages, including the right to withhold a healthy portion of their massive local TV deal from revenue sharing, a benefit that arose from a settlement the league reached in bankruptcy court with the team's former owner Frank McCourt.
Still, the Dodgers in 2022 and 2023 were eliminated in the division series by rivals from smaller markets, the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks. In 2024, the Dodgers' first year with Shohei Ohtani, they nearly lost to the Padres again in division series play. And if not for a series of fortuitous events, they would have lost the 2025 World Series to the Toronto Blue Jays.
Another thing lost in the discussion about the Dodgers' dominance is that villains are good for business. This is the third consecutive season the Dodgers led the majors in road attendance. Their spending forces other NL clubs to try to keep pace. The small-market Padres, in particular, are better for it.
Yet the ability to spend is sometimes a double-edged sword. Long-term contracts sometimes backfire. Seemingly capable of papering over any mistake by simply printing more money, the Dodgers roll merrily along even when free-agent additions such as Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott slump. But several of the Dodgers' biggest and most expensive stars are facing age-related decline. A number of other top-10 payroll clubs, including the Padres, are locked into the same kinds of players.
None of that means that the league and union should proceed as if all is well, assuming the game's cyclical nature will balance things out. The concerns of the small-market clubs must be addressed, and the union acknowledged as much in May with its initial proposals, some of which addressed revenue disparity.
The union proposed enhanced revenue sharing that included protections "to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering"; financial rewards for successful revenue-sharing recipients and draft-pick incentives for them to sign free agents and retain their own players on the verge of hitting the open market.
The league scoffed at the union proposals, as one might expect with the collective bargaining agreement months away from expiration and the parties holding completely different worldviews. Finding a middle ground will be tricky. At least to this point, large-market clubs are willing to share more revenue -- and yield their inherent financial advantages -- but only under a cap system that fixes their costs.
Teams like the Brewers, Rays and Guardians clearly do not require more money to win regular-season games. But the way they operate, frequently trading stars as they get closer to free agency, is far from fan-friendly. Brewers fans buying a Jacob Misiorowski jersey and Rays fans buying a Junior Caminero jersey know not to get too attached to those players. As one small-market executive says: "Championships are won with talent, continuity and experience. We can get talent. The other two are tough to come by."
Tough, but not impossible. Countless examples exist of revenue-sharing recipients signing homegrown players for the long term. The Brewers did it with Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara, the Guardians with José Ramírez and Tanner Bibee. The Pittsburgh Pirates might not keep Paul Skenes, but they locked up Konnor Griffin. The Royals secured extensions with Bobby Witt Jr. and Maikel Garcia, the Seattle Mariners with Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez, the Arizona Diamondbacks with Corbin Carroll and Geraldo Perdomo.
Based on its proposals, the union thinks giving small-market teams an even better opportunity to retain players would benefit the sport. A salary cap is not necessary to make those adjustments and others to the collective bargaining agreement. Much as the league would like fans to believe otherwise, this is not an all-or-nothing situation.
In June, a reporter asked Manfred why he portrays a league he described in 2024 as having a "darn good" record on competitive balance to be out of whack just two years later.
"In the context, particularly of the postseason, where you're trying to generate interest and maximize viewership, I think it's important to emphasize competitiveness," Manfred said. "And there are aspects of competitiveness."
He added: "When we think about it from a labor perspective, we're focused on an entirely different part of the calendar. And that's the offseason, when you're trying to sell season tickets, and the perception among our fans that's really strong that we have a lack of competitiveness."
Maximizing viewership in the postseason? Viewership in the United States last year was the sport's highest since 2017. Selling season tickets? Sure, it's a problem in markets where team owners do not adequately invest in their franchises. It should be less of a problem in places like Milwaukee, Tampa Bay and Cleveland, if we're just talking about the product.
Make the current system fairer, and those clubs will stand even better chances of reaching a postseason that the league expanded to 12 teams from 10 in 2022. Give those clubs enough cracks at the postseason, and eventually one or more will break through.
It could happen this year, if the Brewers, Rays or Guardians win the World Series. The system needs improvement, no doubt. But if competitive balance is the object, it's a lot closer than it appears.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Rays Most Important Hitter for Playoffs Not Named Junior Caminero
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Teape; Unknown
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays were the first team in the MLB to clinch a playoff spot and earned the No. 1 seed in the American League, taking home the AL East title for the fifth time in franchise history. item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays were the first team in the MLB to clinch a playoff spot and earned the No. 1 seed in the American League, taking home the AL East title for the fifth time in franchise history.
It was a complete team effort to achieve all of that success, with third baseman Junior Caminero leading the charge. An AL MVP candidate, he is one of the most feared power hitters in the sport, launching 42 home runs this season after bursting onto the scene with 45 in his first full season in 2025.
Heading into the postseason, he is as important as any player to the team’s success. However, there is one player who is going to be relied upon just as much to make the most of some advantageous positions: catcher Liam Hicks.
Acquired from the Miami Marlins ahead of the trade deadline in August, Hicks was brought on to upgrade the offense and lengthen the lineup beyond Caminero, first baseman Jonathan Aranda and designated hitter Yandy Diaz.
Liam Hicks provides excellent protection for Junior Caminero
He certainly succeeded in that regard, continuing the breakout power campaign that he started with the Marlins. Inserted into the lineup as protection for Caminero, he is the most important hitter on the team after the team’s superstar slugger.
That is because teams are going to be very careful pitching to Caminero. He has shown a willingness to take a walk and not swing at pitches outside of the zone, making major improvements from the 2025 season.
Willing to pass the baton to his teammates, a lot of that responsibility is going to fall upon Hicks to make opposing pitches pay. During his time with the Rays thus far, he has shown he is capable of doing just that with a .288/.379/.440 slash line, hitting four home runs and seven doubles with 20 RBI.
His strike zone recognition and contact skills remain elite, drawing the same number of walks as times he has struck out with Tampa Bay: 16. If the Rays were going to make the perfect player who fits what they are looking for in a laboratory, the product would come out looking a lot like Hicks’s profile.
He has a skill set that translates really well to October baseball, providing some pop with elite contact ability. That is the perfect combination to succeed against some of the best pitching in baseball in high-pressure situations.
Caminero is certainly going to have his moments to lead the team offensively, but he will need help. Hicks is in a prominent position to earn himself some hardware if he can keep up this level of production as protection in the lineup for his superstar teammate.
Kenneth Teape is an alumnus of SUNY Old Westbury and graduated in 2013 with an Honors Degree in Media Communications with a focus on print journalism. During his time at Old Westbury, he worked for the school newspaper and several online publications, such as Knicks Now, the official website of the New York Knicks, and a self-made website with fellow students, Gotham City Sports News. Kenneth has also been a site expert at Empire Writes Back, Musket Fire, and Lake Show Life within the FanSided Network. He was a contributor to HoopsHabit, with work featured on Bleacher Report and Yardbarker. Previously, he is a reporter for both NBA Analysis Network and NFL Analysis Network, as well as a writer and editor for Packers Coverage. You can follow him on X, formerly Twitter, @teapester725, or reach him via email at teapester725@gmail.com.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Why Ben Rice's MVP case deserves more love in a lost Aaron Judge season
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: Without Aaron Judge for most of the season, the AL MVP race is wide open. The favorite for much of the year has been Houston Astros slugger Yordan Álvarez, but he's far from a sure thing. The New York Yankees have seen Cam Schlittler's candidacy get more recognition in recent weeks, but there's another Yankee who's being grossly overlooked. Ben Rice was obviously a breakout star for New York last season, but this year he has reached a new gear. Aaron Boone predicted that Rice would clock 39 ding
item.content:encoded:
Without Aaron Judge for most of the season, the AL MVP race is wide open. The favorite for much of the year has been Houston Astros slugger Yordan Álvarez, but he's far from a sure thing. The New York Yankees have seen Cam Schlittler's candidacy get more recognition in recent weeks, but there's another Yankee who's being grossly overlooked.
Ben Rice was obviously a breakout star for New York last season, but this year he has reached a new gear. Aaron Boone predicted that Rice would clock 39 dingers this season, which was the total the Dartmouth product was sitting on when the Yankees took on the Tampa Bay Rays on September 23, with five games left to play. Neither team had anything left to play for with playoff positions solidified, so it seemed like a good chance that Rice would finish at that number.
But just like that, the 27-year-old bested his manager when he led off the bottom of the first with a solo shot. That wasn't all, though, as Rice came back up to the plate to lead off the bottom of the fourth and smacked his second tater of the game. He now sits at 41 homers and enters the Yankees' record book as a result.
His 40th blast of the year put him in some elite company in franchise history. Rice became just the eighth Yankee to hit 40 or more homers in a season at age 27 or younger. The rest of the list includes four inner-circle Hall of Famers: Babe Ruth (twice), Lou Gehrig (twice), Mickey Mantle (twice), and Joe DiMaggio. In addition to those four, the other three are former single-season home run king Roger Maris, Juan Soto, and, of course, Judge.
Ben Rice's 40th homer underscores how incredibly valuable he's been to the Yankees in Aaron Judge's absence
MLB.com's latest awards poll has Rice as a distant fifth in the voting, behind Álvarez, Junior Caminero, Bobby Witt Jr., and Schlittler, in that order. There are a few things that don't make much sense here.
Álvarez has been great this year, but there's a narrative among some that he's been Judge-like that just isn't true. Air Yordan has posted a 181 wRC+ through September 23, which is still over 20 points lower than Judge's 203 mark last season, which also happened to be the lowest wRC+ he has put up in any of his three MVP campaigns. That's relevant because he is seeking to become the first full-time DH to take home the honor other than Shohei Ohtani.
As for Caminero, he began generating a lot of MVP buzz with his two walk-off homers in mid-September, as if those wins somehow count more than victories at any other point during the season. More importantly, Rice has caught up to him, as both now have 41 homers. Rice has also surpassed him in on-base percentage (.362 versus .360) and slugging percentage (.537 versus .523).
The DH argument also works against Rice, but only to an extent. He's played 55 games at first base and has mostly ceded playing time in the field to accommodate trade deadline acquisition Luis Garcia Jr. It should also be noted that Caminero isn't a great defensive third baseman and is last among qualifiers at the position with -11 outs above average.
More importantly, there's the Judge factor in all of this. The Astros are on the brink of either missing the playoffs for the second year in a row or winning the most pathetic division in MLB history, dipping under .500 late in the campaign. The Rays have had their big boppers like Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda healthy for most of the year.
Losing a player as singular as Judge is a huge blow to a team, but the Yankees are playoff-bound yet again. Throw in a lengthy absence from Cody Bellinger and the fact that they're starting to print milk cartons with Giancarlo Stanton's face on them, and it's been Rice who has kept the offense afloat all year.
If the point of this exercise is to recognize the player who has been the most valuable, then the loss of Judge looms large. We've had our frustrations, but the Yankees really haven't skipped a beat without Judge and his enormous value. Rice is a big reason why, and while it might not be enough to win him the award, he should be a much larger part of the conversation.

item.title: [thestar.com] Yordan Alvarez goes deep as Astros hit 5 homers in 13-2 rout of A’s to close in on AL West title
item.dc:creator: Adam Camarena The Associated Press
item.description: WEST SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Yordan Alvarez launched a three-run homer and the Houston Astros went deep five times Saturday night as they moved closer to a division title with a 13-2 victory over the Athletics. Houston (80-81) can clinch the AL West crown and the No. 3 seed in the American League playoffs with another win Sunday over the A’s in their regular-season finale or a Texas Rangers loss at Minnesota. item.content:encoded:
WEST SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Yordan Alvarez launched a three-run homer and the Houston Astros went deep five times Saturday night as they moved closer to a division title with a 13-2 victory over the Athletics.
Houston (80-81) can clinch the AL West crown and the No. 3 seed in the American League playoffs with another win Sunday over the A’s in their regular-season finale or a Texas Rangers loss at Minnesota. Either team will become the first to win a division with a .500 record or worse, excluding shortened seasons.
Alvarez homered in the fifth inning to put the Astros up 6-1. His 42nd homer of the season tied him with Tampa Bay slugger Junior Caminero for second in the AL.
Houston finished with 16 hits as Jeremy Peña, Isaac Paredes and Jose Altuve combined for nine of them and seven RBIs.
Peña hit a pair of two-run homers, one in the third and the other in the eighth. He finished 4 for 6 with four RBIs. Parades homered in the first to open the scoring and went 3 for 5.
Hayden Wesneski (6-2) threw seven innings and struck out five while allowing six hits and two runs.
The Astros scored six runs, including Lucas Spence’s solo homer, between the seventh and ninth to expand their lead to 13-2.
Jack Perkins (3-13) pitched five innings for the Athletics. He struck out nine but gave up six runs and three homers.
Up next
Neither team had announced a starting pitcher for Sunday’s regular-season finale.
___

item.title: [Field Level Media] Orioles' Pete Alonso looks to play all 162 games again in finale vs. Yankees
item.description: A majority of the focus for the New York Yankees is planning their roster and preparing to host the Boston Red Sox in next week’s wild-card series. Another area of focus will be finishing out the regular season with their 94th win when the Yankees host the Baltimore Orioles on Sunday, weather permitting. The start time has been moved up to 1:05 p.m. The Yankees (93-68) were off on Saturday because a nor’easter resulted in a single-admission doubleheader on Friday. Since New York was eliminated f
item.content:encoded:
A majority of the focus for the New York Yankees is planning their roster and preparing to host the Boston Red Sox in next week’s wild-card series.
Another area of focus will be finishing out the regular season with their 94th win when the Yankees host the Baltimore Orioles on Sunday, weather permitting.
The start time has been moved up to 1:05 p.m.
The Yankees (93-68) were off on Saturday because a nor’easter resulted in a single-admission doubleheader on Friday. Since New York was eliminated from the American League East race on Tuesday night, its past four games have seen the team give regulars time off and rest some of its prominent relievers while seeing other defensive alignments.
On Friday, the Yankees took a 10-2 loss in the opener and earned their fifth doubleheader split of the season with a 6-3 victory before the tarp was put on the field immediately after the final pitch.
Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. were among those who rested in the opener before starting in the second game. Anthony Volpe played third base in the first game and shortstop in the second game after playing only at second base following his return from the minor leagues on Sept. 10.
Volpe had three hits in the doubleheader, including a two-run double in the sixth inning Friday night. Volpe’s newfound versatility may be something for the Yankees to consider for their postseason roster as he’s hitting .265 (11 for 49) with nine RBIs in 14 games since returning.
“This is the most important part of the season,” Volpe said. “This is the best part of why you do it; this is why you play. It’s Yankees/Red Sox — that’s what October baseball is.”
Ben Rice had three hits in the doubleheader and enters the regular-season finale with 41 homers and 97 RBIs in a year when Aaron Judge has played 66 games and may miss the wild-card series because of a moderately strained right calf.
The Orioles (79-82) are concluding their second straight losing season after winning 275 games from 2022-2024.
Pete Alonso enters Sunday with 43 homers and 113 RBIs in his first season with the Orioles. He will win the AL RBI title and is one ahead of Yordan Alvarez and Junior Caminero for the AL home run crown.
Alonso is looking to play in his 162nd game of the season for the third consecutive year.
Eight of Alonso’s past 10 hits are homers and he has the most homers by an Oriole since Mark Trumbo mashed 47 in 2016.
“It’s impressive,” manager Craig Albernaz said. “It’s not only the at-bat quality and the pitches he’s getting, he’s not missing them. He’s squaring them up pretty good.”
If the game gets played, the Yankees will get another look at Elmer Rodriguez (0-3, 5.40 ERA). Rodriguez has made six starts this season and has 21 strikeouts and 16 walks in 26 2/3 innings.
Rodriguez last pitched in the major leagues when he struggled through 3 2/3 innings during a 10-1 road loss to the Angels on Aug. 31. He also showed increased velocity Aug. 26 in a no-decision in New York’s 9-3 win over Houston when he allowed three runs on three hits in six innings.
Shane Baz (6-15, 4.11) starts for Baltimore and likely will pitch an abbreviated outing similar to Trevor Rogers, who threw 55 pitches in four innings Friday. Baz is 2-6 with a 4.37 ERA in his past 10 starts and took a no-decision Monday against Toronto when Baltimore rallied in the eighth inning.
Baz is 0-3 with a 6.48 ERA in eight career starts against the Yankees.
–Field Level Media

What It Means
Caminero is hitting for a .275 BA, .360 OBP and .522 SLG with an 18.2% strikeout rate and an 11.3% walk rate. His OPS is .882, which ranks 9th in MLB, and he has scored 96 runs. In 692 plate appearances, he has hit 41 home runs (3rd in MLB) and driven in 99 runs (8th in MLB). He had two hits (going 2 for 5 with two RBIs) in his last game against the Yankees.
Cristopher Sanchez gets the start for the Phillies, his 33rd of the season. He is 18-6 with a 2.93 ERA and 221 strikeouts through 200 2/3 innings pitched.

item.title: [tsn.ca] MLB 2026 playoff intel: Bold predictions, dangerous teams, more
item.dc:creator: Jorge Castillo; Alden Gonzalez; Buster Olney; Jeff Passan; Jesse Rogers
item.description: With less than a week until the 2026 MLB playoffs begin, our baseball insiders have been cultivating their sources and are ready to break down the questions, teams and themes that will shape October -- even before the final 12-team postseason field is set. What is the boldest take we’ve heard from an MLB exec? Is a Los Angeles Dodgers three-peat coming? Can the New York Yankees make a deep run -- with or without Aaron Judge? And who are the sleeper teams and under-the-radar players to watch? Her
item.content:encoded:
With less than a week until the 2026 MLB playoffs begin, our baseball insiders have been cultivating their sources and are ready to break down the questions, teams and themes that will shape October -- even before the final 12-team postseason field is set.
What is the boldest take we’ve heard from an MLB exec? Is a Los Angeles Dodgers three-peat coming? Can the New York Yankees make a deep run -- with or without Aaron Judge? And who are the sleeper teams and under-the-radar players to watch?
Here’s the latest intel our MLB experts are hearing as Jeff Passan, Buster Olney, Jesse Rogers, Jorge Castillo and Alden Gonzalez empty their notebooks heading into the playoffs.
What is the boldest prediction you’ve heard from an MLB exec or scout?
Olney: The Padres are going to win the World Series for the first time in their history, with just about everything trending in the right direction. “Once you get into the postseason with all of the built-in off days, that’s going to help their bullpen -- which is the best,” he noted. The Padres’ starting pitching is the team’s biggest concern, but as the Dodgers demonstrated in 2024, you can win with three or four functional starters who are backed by a deep bullpen.
Passan: The Red Sox might be the No. 5 seed, but they’re going to win the American League pennant. Since the All-Star break, one evaluator pointed out, the Red Sox have the best offense in the AL. They’re also an MLB best in Fielding Independent Pitching, a predictive metric that suggests they will continue to throw well. It’s a deep bullpen. It’s a solid-enough rotation. It’s a productive lineup. And, perhaps most helpful of all, it’s the AL, where the path to the World Series is a sandy beach compared to the jungle of the National League.
Do MLB insiders think the Dodgers will turn it on in October again like they did the past two postseasons?
Gonzalez: The general sentiment about the Dodgers seems to be this: They’ll be the favorites until proven otherwise. That’s what they’ve elevated to. They’re too talented, too deep, and they’ve become too adept at navigating seasons to have many detractors, regardless of whatever adversity they might face.
These past couple of weeks have offered a perfect snapshot. The Dodgers’ offense was a serious concern, but now -- with Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez and Kyle Tucker on a heater, and Shohei Ohtani back -- not so much. Their bullpen was, too, but Edwin Diaz has looked sharp since coming back, Roki Sasaki could once again become a weapon and Emmet Sheehan might be too. Regardless, their rotation is widely expected to be an equalizer.
Passan: They’re still the favorites, which is saying something when considering the fatigue that often attaches itself to dynastic teams. But the Dodgers have shown enough vulnerabilities that a number of evaluators believe another team will represent the NL in the World Series. One GM’s sentiment -- “I’d take every NL playoff team over every AL playoff team,” he said -- speaks to the sort of competition the Dodgers will face.
And with so many question marks about how Ohtani and Andy Pages and Blake Snell will fare after returning on the eve of the postseason with no rehab assignments, the Dodgers are not nearly the sure thing they’ve been in recent postseasons. At the same time, they remain, top to bottom, the most talented team in the game, and nobody would be surprised if they win their third consecutive World Series.
How much faith does the industry have in the Rays and Brewers turning the best regular-season records into World Series appearances?
Olney: There is more faith in the Brewers than I’ve ever heard, because the general perception is that they are just a better, deeper team than the group that was bulldozed by the Dodgers in last year’s postseason -- and they’ve got the best starting pitcher, in Jacob Misiorowski. “I think he might hit 107 [mph] in the playoffs,” speculated one evaluator, assessing the impact of the adrenaline, expectations and Misiorowski’s heightened competitiveness. And generally, there is a lot of respect for the Rays, particularly when measured against the low bar of the American League.
Rogers: As much as ever. The Brewers have more believers this year than last simply based on the top of their rotation led by Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. Their depth there is better as well. Robert Gasser has come on strong while rubber-armed Aaron Ashby is a key bullpen guy to go along with Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill.
On the Rays side, their draw for the postseason isn’t perfect -- according to one insider -- but if the Yankees and Red Sox play three games in the wild-card round, it’ll set things up nicely for them in the division series. After that, they’ll be heavy favorites to get to the Fall Classic.
Given Aaron Judge’s health questions, do those in the game think the Yankees will make another deep October run?
Castillo: Opinions vary around the majors. One front office executive said the Yankees have “no chance” of making a World Series run without Judge. Another said he believes it’s possible behind the pitching staff, though the executive added that the bullpen is seemingly running on fumes down the stretch.
Anything can happen in a three-game series. The Red Sox nearly bounced New York last year, falling short in Game 3 thanks to Cam Schlittler’s sterling performance.
After that, the Rays are reminiscent of the Blue Jays club that gave the Yankees trouble last year -- from the regular season through eliminating them in four games in the ALDS. Not having Judge undoubtedly hurts the Yankees’ chances of surviving the gauntlet.
Olney: It wouldn’t be a surprise if they emerge in the American League -- and nor would it be a surprise if they got knocked out in the first round. Without Judge, they are vulnerable against left-handed pitching, and Boston is loaded with lefties.
If they do survive the Red Sox, then they’ll open the division series on the road in the Trop, where they don’t match up well; the Rays’ style of play on their home surface caused all kinds of problems for the Yankees this year.
That all said, the Yankees have the best pitching of the AL teams; they have a good lineup (albeit not great); and their defense has improved.
Who else do MLB insiders feel could be this October’s most dangerous teams?
Rogers: As easy as it would be to pick an AL team to make a surprising run simply because the draw there is softer, experts like the Padres as a dangerous lower-seeded team. They have a good playoff formula now that the rotation has some help and the lineup is hitting for power. In fact, San Diego leads MLB in home runs in September. And of course, they have that vaunted bullpen.
With Aaron Judge on the shelf, the Red Sox are becoming a favorite pick among experts in the AL. Others point to Yankees pitching as their key to advancing. It’s really good behind Cy Young fave Cam Schlittler.
Gonzalez: The Phillies are often a popular pick for this question, and this year it’s no different. They have obvious flaws, from the makeup of their bullpen to their overall defense to, mostly, the status of Jesus Luzardo. But they have a bevy of top-shelf stars, the type that tend to make a major impact on October. They have the experience of having navigated these stakes as a group many times. They have a raucous home environment, one that arguably trumps any in the sport. And, lately, they have Aaron Nola looking like his vintage self.
Still: it’s hard to dismiss the Luzardo factor in all this. He changes everything. “If he’s healthy,” a rival front office executive said, “they’re my answer.” If not, he added, the Brewers are the better, more well-rounded team. Luzardo is that important.
Who are some under-the-radar players with industry buzz as potential postseason stars?
Castillo: Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr., Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers and Padres first baseman Ty France. Mesa, dumped in a trade by the Marlins in February, surfaced from Triple-A in late May to join Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda as dangerous bats. Bauers and France are veterans who lead their respective teams in wRC+ this season -- indicating, at least by that measure, that they’ve been the best hitters on their clubs -- and have been overshadowed.
Passan: In an era when the average fastball is 94.6 mph and pitchers throw it around 30% of the time, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick and Milwaukee right-hander Logan Henderson are anomalies.
Messick, 25, is a favorite of scouts. He throws a four-seamer that averages 94 mph more than 40% of the time, and despite the relative lack of velocity, it’s been a banger of a pitch, the third-most-valuable heater in MLB behind Jacob Misiorowski’s and Cam Schlittler’s.
Henderson leans even more heavily on his fastball (45.7%) even though it’s slower (93.1 mph) and it has the sixth-highest run value.
Why do they work so well? Messick and Henderson both have exceptional control, and as much as velo rules the modern game, there is still room for pitching artistry, and they personify it.

item.description: We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives. Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

item.content:encoded:
Mariners rally past Astros 6-5 in 10 innings to keep faint playoff hopes alive
Posted/updated on: September 24, 2026 at 6:59 am
SEATTLE (AP) — Josh Naylor singled home Randy Arozarena with the winning run in the 10th inning and the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive by rallying past the Houston Astros 6-5 on Wednesday night.
Houston (78-80) remained tied atop the AL West with Texas, which has lost three straight games. The Astros hold the head-to-head tiebreaker if the teams finish with the same record.
The Mariners (74-84) are four games back with four to play.
Seattle was down 5-4 after automatic runner Yordan Alvarez scored on a triple to right field by Isaac Paredes in the top of the 10th.
With one out and the bases loaded in the bottom half, Julio Rodríguez worked a full-count walk from Astros closer Josh Hader, forcing in J.P. Crawford with the tying run. Naylor sent Hader’s next pitch to right-center, and Arozarena scored his third run of the night.
Alvarez went 2 for 4 without an RBI in his pursuit of the AL Triple Crown. That raised his league-leading batting average to .316. Tampa Bay’s Chandler Simpson, second at .309, did not play Wednesday against the New York Yankees.
Alvarez is part of a four-way tie for the home run lead at 41 with the Rays’ Junior Caminero, Baltimore’s Pete Alonso and the Yankees’ Ben Rice. The Houston slugger is second in RBIs with 102, eight behind Alonso.
Before his tying walk, Rodríguez had three hits for the Mariners.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz and Nick Allen each had two hits for Houston. One of Diaz’s hits was his 14th homer, a two-run shot to cap a four-run third.
Cooper Criswell (4-2) pitched the 10th inning to earn the win for Seattle. Hader (4-2), who also pitched the ninth, took the loss.
Seattle scored three times in the third to pull to 4-3. The first two runs came on Dominic Canzone’s double as he extended his hitting streak to a career-best 12 games. Canzone’s single in the fifth scored Arozarena to tie it at 4.
Up next
The Mariners will send right-hander Bryan Woo (12-9, 3.92 ERA) to the mound Thursday in the opener of a season-ending four-game series against the Angels.
Right-hander Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.70) will pitch for the Astros in the first game of a four-game set at the Athletics.
