| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Sean Barber • Weather: 63°, Wind 13 mph • O/U: 7 Runs • Line: TB +112 / NYY -135. | | | | |
Boone’s Platoon Explains Goldschmidt Sit
Aaron Boone’s lineup card for Tuesday’s series opener against Tampa Bay leaves Goldschmidt out again, extending a run that traces back to Saturday. He started Friday against left-hander Eduardo Rodriguez in Arizona and went 1-for-4 with a walk and two runs, then sat both weekend games against right-handers Brandon Pfaadt and Corbin Burnes. That’s three benchings in the last three games against right-handed starters.
Why? Goldschmidt has produced an elite 1.006 OPS against lefties this season but an anemic .572 mark versus right-handers, a gap wide enough that Boone starts Ben Rice at DH and Luis García Jr. at first whenever a right-hander pitches. An The Athletic report on the lineup moves after Aaron Judge’s calf strain named Goldschmidt and Heliot Ramos as the bats Boone leans on against lefties, with García handling the right-handed side.
Nick Martinez, Tuesday’s Tampa Bay starter, has largely dominated Goldschmidt in his career. The former National League MVP is 2-for-10 with four walks and two strikeouts against Martinez, and he is 0-for-13 with four strikeouts in his last three meetings with the right-hander since 2024. Martinez enters at 15-4 with a 2.94 ERA this year, and beat the Yankees in the Bronx in May, giving Boone both the season splits and the head-to-head history pointing toward a Goldschmidt benching.
Tuesday’s day-night doubleheader against two more right-handed Rays starters gives Boone an easy excuse to sit the 39-year-old.
| TAMPA BAY RAYS STARTING LINEUP (GAME 1) | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SP: Nick Martinez (RHP) • 15-4, 2.94 ERA | | | | |
| September 22, 2026 • Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY • 1:05 PM ET • Rays at Yankees | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Yandy Díaz | DH | .292 | .807 |
| 2 | Jonathan Aranda | 1B | .277 | .800 |
| 3 | Junior Caminero | 3B | .277 | .892 |
| 4 | Liam Hicks | C | .288 | .811 |
| 5 | Chandler Simpson | LF | .309 | .697 |
| 6 | Jonny DeLuca | CF | .259 | .700 |
| 7 | Víctor Mesa Jr. | RF | .251 | .825 |
| 8 | Jorge Mateo | SS | .207 | .573 |
| 9 | Richie Palacios | 2B | .234 | .707 |
| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / OPS). Umpire: Sean Barber • Weather: 63°, Wind 13 mph • O/U: 7 Runs • Line: TB +112 / NYY -135. | | | | |
Goldschmidt’s Future in New York
Goldschmidt becomes a free agent again this winter, and the Yankees have made no public commitment either way. A cheap return as a lefty-masher and clubhouse mentor remains plausible given Rice’s grip on first base, and his credentials, a 2022 NL MVP award, seven All-Star selections, four Gold Gloves and five Silver Sluggers still make him a name teams will inquire about this winter.
First base belongs to Rice, who has grown into an everyday role with 39 home runs and 95 RBI this season, pushing Goldschmidt into a complementary, short-side platoon job. That role fits the final stretch of a one-year, $4 million contract that can grow by $500,000 at each of four plate-appearance thresholds, according to Spotrac, a modest deal compared with the $12.5 million he earned in his first Yankees season a year earlier.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Toughest players to rank at third base for 2027: Jose Ramirez's decline creates a major Fantasy dilemma
item.dc:creator: Chris Towers
item.description: Third base wasn't viewed as a strong position entering 2026, and it doesn't look much stronger. Sure, we had players like Sal Stewart, Miguel Vargas, and Kevin McGonigle breaking out and establishing themselves as the next generation of the position, perhaps, and that ain't nothing. But we also had deeply disappointing seasons from Jose Ramirez, Jazz Chisholm, Manny Machado, Austin Riley, Maikel Garcia, Bo Bichette, Eugenio Suarez, and Noelvi Marte, all of whom were drafted in the top 10 at the
item.content:encoded:
Third base wasn't viewed as a strong position entering 2026, and it doesn't look much stronger. Sure, we had players like Sal Stewart, Miguel Vargas, and Kevin McGonigle breaking out and establishing themselves as the next generation of the position, perhaps, and that ain't nothing.
But we also had deeply disappointing seasons from Jose Ramirez, Jazz Chisholm, Manny Machado, Austin Riley, Maikel Garcia, Bo Bichette, Eugenio Suarez, and Noelvi Marte, all of whom were drafted in the top 10 at the position. It would not be an overstatement to say that eight of the top 10 at the position busted, and you can throw Matt Chapman (3B12 in ADP) and Addison Barger (3B14) in there, too, to round it out.
So, yeah, we needed the breakouts. Because a lot of the old standbys let us down and it's not like the breakouts are without their flaws or concerns – any player who has only done it once is going to enter the next season with at least some question marks. Looking ahead to 2027, Junior Caminero might be the only sure thing at the position. He's going to be a first-rounder no matter what, but if you're the type to play position scarcity games, you might need to make sure you reach for him no matter where you're picking. Because if not, you're going to be left with a big question mark at an important position.
The toughest players to rank at third base
Jose Ramirez, Guardians
There are those who will argue Ramirez is very easy to rank. Some will say you should take his decline at face value; when a 34-year-old starts to fall off, they don't generally get it back. Ramirez enters the final week of the season hitting .237, his worst mark since 2015, while his 12 homers are his fewest since 2016. Sure, there was a mid-season hand surgery to blame it on, but to reiterate an earlier point: You probably shouldn't expect a 34-year-old to be healthier than he was in the past. Just take the numbers and the decline at face value.
That's one approach you can take. But I don't think it'll be mine. Because, despite the mediocre production, it doesn't actually look like Ramirez's skill set has declined much at all. His strikeout rate is up, but at 12.9%, it's still within a percentage point of his career mark, while his walk rate is actually his highest since 2021. His .306 wOBA is his worst mark since 2015, but his .329 expected wOBA is basically right in line with what he did in 2024, when he hit 39 homers and had arguably his best season ever. It's down from 2025, but not so much that it looks like a total collapse of the skill set. Ramirez still makes a ton of contact and he still hits the ball in the air to the pull side as often as anyone, the primary way he has overcome middling quality of contact metrics throughout his career.
Now, I'll grant that it's possible that the small, almost imperceptible changes in Ramirez's underlying skills have more impact than you might expect. Ramirez has been an outlier in how he outruns his underlying metrics, but that can be a delicate dance to keep up; Marcus Semien was an elite Fantasy player with a very similar skill set right up until the point he lost it. The margin for error with this kind of skill set might just be narrower than for guys who can crush the ball consistently, so maybe Ramirez's decline won't be stopped by a healthy offseason.
I'm open to that. He won't be a top-five player in my overall rankings for 2027. But he'll definitely still be a top-five third baseman, and might still be the second option off the board for me.
Miguel Vargas, White Sox
I don't think it's tough to figure out where Vargas ranks among third basemen. He belongs no lower than fourth, and I think you can make an extremely compelling case that only Junior Caminero should be ahead of him. So this might be more about just making sure everyone is prepared for the possibility that Vargas will be a second-round pick in 2027. The level he has reached in 2026 is completely unprecedented for Vargas, who has been playing pretty regularly since the second half of 2024 and had never really shown this kind of difference-making upside. But his .366 wOBA is actually a mild underperformance relative to his .381 expected wOBA, which is actually tied for the fifth-best mark of any hitter in the league.
I don't think Vargas is actually a top-five hitter in baseball. But if you wanted to argue he was a top-10 Fantasy option after this season, I wouldn't have a strong argument against it; the best argument I could muster is just, "Well, he's only done it once." But in addition to the underlying numbers, here's the other thing I love about what we're seeing from Vargas: He just refuses to slow down. July was the worst month of his season, but he responded with a .948 OPS in August, and then he went out and won AL Player of the Week last week. He's hitting .260/.373/.467 in the second half with strong plate discipline and plenty of speed and power.
Those gaudy underlying numbers are a little worse than they were early in the season, which might portend some regression in 2027. But, again, it probably wouldn't be reasonable to expect him to be a top-10 hitter again. But that doesn't mean the breakout isn't real, and where you rank him among Ramirez and Sal Stewart will mostly come down to personal preference. I imagine all three will be at least top-30 picks for me.
Manny Machado, Padres
There was a period in 2026 where Machado looked like himself again, and I was ready to write his slow start off as just that. He started hitting for real power again in June, and then in July he hit .292/.369/.552, putting the miserable start to the season behind him. But despite hitting three homers in his first five games back from the All-Star break, Machado enters the final week with just nine homers in 59 games since the break, while hitting .242/.331/.388 in the second half overall. If he deserved some benefit of the doubt for the slow start, it's hard to keep extending that when he came crashing back to earth over the final two months.
Machado's .330 xwOBA is definitely better than his actual .311 mark. However, it's still his worst since Statcast tracking began, and unlike Ramirez, he doesn't have a consistent track record of overcoming his underlying stats. There's still room for some improvement in 2027, most notably with his batting average, as a .234 BABIP isn't likely to sustain. But if he hits to his .244 xBA instead, that's still a drag on your average. Think about it this way: How excited have you been to have Nolan Arenado in your lineup this season? He hasn't been awful, but he hasn't been worth near the kind of price we've gotten used to paying for Machado. Neither is Machado at this point.
Kazuma Okamoto, Blue Jays
It's been an extremely successful first major-league season for Okamoto, though not necessarily in the way anyone expected. Okamoto was supposed to bring a contact-forward skill set, with just enough power to be a potential all-around impact hitter. Instead, he's been a pretty all-or-nothing power bat, hitting .235/.310/.459 with 33 homers and 89 RBI heading into the second half of the season. A longtime elite contact hitter in Japan, Okamoto has struck out 29% of the time and posted a 14% swinging-strike rate, both bottom-15 marks among qualifiers.
The strikeout issues got a little better in the second half, though he was a sub-.700 OPS bat in July and August before getting really hot in September, so it's hard to argue there's too much momentum building here. It's not unreasonable to expect a bit better from Okamoto with a full season under his belt, but the swing and miss issues on display were worrisome enough that he might just never get past it. Draft him for what he did in 2026, and if you get a .260 average from him instead, that'll be a huge win. But there are enough red flags in this profile that there's a real risk he'll end up being exposed before long.
Curtis Mead, Red Sox
Mead comes with all the typical questions of a one-season breakout, except he didn't even get the chance to do it for a full season. He platooned for part of the early part of the season and then suffered a fractured wrist in his very first game after being traded to the Red Sox in July. When he played, he was terrific, putting up a .253/.353/.498 line and more than holding his own against righties, so the case is pretty similar to that of Vargas as a former top prospect who finally made good. Only he did it for about half as many plate appearances, which makes it inherently more difficult to trust. I mean, just look at Michael Busch, who fully broke out in 2025 and had the underlying data to back it up, but then regressed badly in 2026. That doesn't mean the same thing will happen to Mead (or to Vargas, for that matter), but there's real regression risk that should keep his price down. I still think Mead deserves to be ranked as a top-10 third baseman, but I don't think he'll be worth drafting until at least the double-digit rounds.
Zack Gelof, Athletics
This feels like we're all Charlie Brown and we're gonna run up and try to kick that football again. Gelof has had a pretty awesome season, hitting 19 homers and stealing 14 bases in 105 games, while putting up a very solid .252/.314/.456 line. He has cut his strikeout rate to 25%, the best mark of his career, and while his underlying numbers don't quite back it up, his home park in Sacramento could help explain why it might not be unsustainable.
But we did this with Gelof after his rookie season. We overlooked scary plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues because he was a young, exciting hitter with a power-speed combo, and that was worth betting on. And I'm just not sure I want to make that mistake again. He's a pretty good athlete, but that doesn't really translate into much more than above-average raw power, and I just don't have much faith that's enough to overcome what are still some pretty scary issues under the hood. Gelof has, to his credit, become a more patient hitter, though not necessarily a more discerning one; his chase rate has dropped about as much as his in-zone swing rate has. He still has big swing-and-miss issues, and it just always feels like Gelof is going to be dancing on a knife's edge. If he's still there after the first 150 picks or so, I might be willing to take a chance on him. I just don't think I can bring myself to rank Gelof as a starting-caliber player in most leagues.

item.title: [MLB.com] Claros favoritos en la última encuesta del JMV, pero ¿podrá esta semana cambiar algo?
item.dc:creator: Brian Murphy
item.description: Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026. El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempo
item.content:encoded:
Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026.
El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempos recientes.
Treinta y ocho expertos de MLB.com emitieron sus votos sobre quiénes creen que se llevarán los honores de JMV tras esta temporada, con 32 jugadores recibiendo al menos un voto. Como recordatorio, los votos se basaron no solo en el desempeño hasta ahora, sino también en cómo se espera que evolucionen las cosas durante el resto de la campaña.
Los votantes clasificaron a sus cinco principales candidatos de cada liga con un sistema de 5-4-3-2-1: cinco puntos por un voto al primer lugar, cuatro por el segundo, y así sucesivamente. Estos son los resultados.
Todas las estadísticas son hasta la jornada del domingo, a menos que se indique lo contrario.
LIGA AMERICANA
Álvarez ha tenido un desempeño tan bueno este año que lo que califica como un bache para él sería un gran trecho para la mayoría de los demás bateadores. En sus últimos 41 encuentros, batea .264 con OPS de .840. Reiteramos, nada mal para la mayoría, pero muy por debajo del nivel del líder de la Americana en promedio (.313) y OPS (1.027). Álvarez lleva tres cuadrangulares y cinco impulsadas a lo largo de 16 partidos este mes, dejándolo a un jonrón del dominicano Junior Caminero de los Rays por el liderato en el Joven Circuito y a seis empujadas de Pete Alonso por la cima en dicho departamento. Aunque sus posibilidades de la Triple Corona se están desvaneciendo un poco, Álvarez todavía ha armado un 2026 asombroso en el plato. Su wRC+ de 179 es al menos 27 puntos mejor que el de cualquier otro bateador calificado.
Sabemos que el quisqueyano es uno de los grandes cañoneros del juego. Está cerrando su segunda temporada consecutiva de 40 vuelacercas y está dando swings más fuerte que nadie. Pero lo que ha sido más impresionante de su temporada es su mejorado criterio en la zona de strike. Aumentó su tasa de boletos desde un 6.3% por debajo del promedio a un 11.5%, lo que se ubica en el 80mo percentil de MLB. También ha mantenido una tasa de ponches muy sólida (18.5%). Ya no persigue tantos pitcheos fuera de la zona, ha reducido su tasa de swings en blanco y está haciendo más contacto en general. Esa mezcla de paciencia, trueno y control del bate es una combinación especial, sobre todo en un jugador de 23 años. Luciendo un porcentaje de embasarse de .363 (52 puntos mejor que la campaña pasada), el OPS de .892 de Caminero se ubica tercero en la Americana.
Witt ha tenido mejores campañas a la ofensiva, aunque 18 bambinazos, 43 estafadas y wRC+ de 119 en 137 partidos no está nada mal. Pero cuando se consideran todas sus capacidades, Witt sigue siendo extremadamente valioso. Su valor de carreras defensivas de +16 está empatado en el tercer lugar de las Grandes Ligas, y sus 22 outs por encima del promedio encabezan la Liga Americana. También cuenta con un valor de carreras en el corrido de bases de +8, a uno de Corbin Carroll de los Diamondbacks por el liderato de MLB. Por eso, aunque no ha sido tan indiscutible en la caja de bateo como lo fue en el 2024 (wRC+ de 169), la grandeza integral de Witt lo tiene en la cima de la tabla de posiciones de WAR de FanGraphs en el Joven Circuito (6.6) y posiblemente perfilándolo entre los primeros cinco en la votación para JMV por tercera vez en tres años.
Ha habido bastante conversación de JMV entorno a Schlittler en las últimas semanas. ¿Y por qué no? Está marcando el paso en la Americana en efectividad (1.94), WHIP (0.91) y WAR de pitcheo de FanGraphs (6.1). Se ubica segundo en el Joven Circuito en promedio de bateo en contra (.182) y en tasa de ponches menos boletos (25.0%). Ha permitido una carrera o ninguna en 21 aperturas. Ese es un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees y algo que apenas otros dos lanzadores de 25 años o menos han logrado en la Era de la Pelota Viva (desde 1920): Blake Snell (2018) y Dean Chance (1964). Seguramente será reconocido con el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana a estas alturas, pero Schlittler recibirá su merecida cuota de consideración para el JMV.
Schlittler no ha sido el único miembro de los Bombarderos que ha sido indispensable este año. Mientras Nueva York ha estado sin Aaron Judge durante una gran parte de la campaña y ha echado de menos a otros bates estelares debido a lesiones, Rice ha sido demostrado consistencia. Se ubica tercero en el Joven Circuito en jonrones (39) y anotadas (100). Es cuarto en la liga en impulsadas (95) y OPS (.888), y está empatado en el cuarto lugar en valor de carreras al bate (+34). Con dos vuelacercas durante la última semana, Rice se convertiría en apenas el segundo miembro del equipo del Bronx diferente a Judge en la última década en conectar al menos 41 jonrones en una temporada, acompañando al dominicano Juan Soto (2024).
Otros que recibieron votos: El venezolano Willson Contreras, Medias Rojas; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigres; el cubano Miguel Vargas, Medias Blancas; el cubano Randy Arozarena, Marineros; Munetaka Murakami, Medias Blancas; Dylan Cease, Azulejos.
LIGA NACIONAL
El mes pasado, PCA dio el salto por encima de Ohtani hacia el puesto Nro. 1 de nuestra encuesta. Este mes, se ha apartado por completo del resto del grupo. Crow-Armstrong, quien recibió cada voto de primer lugar emitido por nuestro panel, está empatado con Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de bambinazos de MLB (45). Nadie tiene más anotadas (118), extrabases (83) o total de bases anotadas (351) esta campaña. Con 38 estafadas, el dinámico jardinero central del equipo del Norte de Chicago podría convertirse en el séptimo miembro del club 40-40 más adelante esta semana. Y no pase por alto el hecho de que es posiblemente el mejor jugador a la defensa en cualquier posición en estos momentos. Ya no es una cuestión de si Crow-Armstrong es el JMV de la Nacional. El premio es prácticamente suyo ahora mismo. Pero ¿lo ganará de manera unánime?
Ohtani se mantiene como el claro escolta en el Viejo Circuito a pesar de haber jugado en apenas tres partidos este mes debido a sus persistentes lesiones en la rodilla izquierda y el bíceps derecho. La buena noticia es que el dirigente de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, dijo que "hay una buena posibilidad" de que Ohtani sea activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días el miércoles tras cumplir la estadía mínima. No lanzará por el resto de la temporada, dejándolo con efectividad de 1.79 y 95 ponches en 85.2 entradas. Pero Ohtani tendrá unos cuantos partidos para sumar a sus totales ofensivos (30 jonrones, wRC+ de 142).
Mencionamos antes cómo Schlittler luce como el gran favorito para el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Misiorowski tendría su premio más asegurado en la Nacional. A lo largo de 169.1 episodios, Miz encabeza la Gran Carpa en casi cada categoría, incluyendo efectividad (1.86), WHIP (0.80), tasa de ponches menos boletos (31.7%) y fWAR (6.5), por nombrar solo algunas. Sus oponentes tienen un diminuto OPS de .474 contra Misiorowski, la segunda menor cifra para cualquier abridor calificado en la Era Divisional (desde 1969). Los oponentes del quisqueyano Pedro Martínez, en una de las mejores campañas para un lanzador, registraron OPS de .473 en el 2000.
El dominicano, quien no recibió un solo voto en nuestra anterior encuesta de JMV, ha estado encendido con Cincinnati durante el último mes. En sus últimos 27 encuentros, batea .404 con ocho vuelacercas, seis bases robadas y OPS de 1.205. Dio múltiples hits en 14 de esos partidos, y su fWAR de 2.5 durante este transcurso es el mejor de las Mayores. Esta prolongada racha encendida le ha dado a De la Cruz un wRC+ de 139 -- el mejor de su carrera -- y lo deja a dos jonrones más dos estafadas de convertirse en el cuarto jugador de los Rojos en el club 30-30 y el primero desde Brandon Phillips en el 2007.
Schwarber ha caído en un pequeño bache, bateando de 34-4 con un cuadrangular en sus últimos 10 encuentros. También está a ocho ponches de establecer un récord de ponches en una misma campaña. De todas maneras, hay que admirar la consistencia de Schwarber. Terminará con más de 40 vuelacercas y 150 juegos disputados en cuatro de las últimas cinco temporadas. Ha superado los 100 boletos negociados por cuarto año consecutivo, y un tercer título de bambinazos del Viejo Circuito está a su alcance.
Otros que recibieron votos: El dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Cerveceros; Matt Olson, Bravos; James Wood, Nacionales; Jordan Walker, Cardenales; Alex Bregman, Cachorros; Bryce Harper, Filis; Jake Bauers, Cerveceros; el dominicano Otto López, Marlins; el venezolano Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Rafael Devers, Gigantes; Alec Burleson, Cardenales; CJ Abrams, Nacionales; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez, Filis.

item.title: [MLB.com] Our final MVP poll has clear frontrunners, but can this week change anything?
item.dc:creator: Brian Murphy
item.description: As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll. Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory. Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they
item.content:encoded:
As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies

item.title: [tsn.ca] The latest on MLB postseason clinches, Ohtani and Judge health updates, awards races and more
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: Major League Baseball’s postseason is rapidly approaching, with the Los Angeles Dodgers seeking a third-straight World Series title. The Dodgers are once again among the best teams in the big leagues, and they’ll have several challengers in October, including the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. All three teams could finish the regular season with 100 wins or more. Los Angeles i
item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball’s postseason is rapidly approaching, with the Los Angeles Dodgers seeking a third-straight World Series title. It remains to be seen how much some of the game’s biggest stars will be able to participate come October, though.
The Dodgers are once again among the best teams in the big leagues, and they’ll have several challengers in October, including the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. All three teams could finish the regular season with 100 wins or more. Los Angeles is there even though four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani’s health is a concern.
The New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox and Atlanta Braves have also clinched spots in the postseason. The Yankees’ three-time MVP Aaron Judge is dealing with a right calf strain that will keep him on the injured list until at least the final day of the regular season.
The regular season ends this Sunday, and while the 12-team playoff field appears mostly set, there are a few long-shot contenders for the postseason, and specific matchups are in flux.
Here’s some of what to watch as the season comes to a close.
Here’s who can clinch a playoff spot Monday
No team can clinch a playoff spot on Monday with most of the league getting a day off.
There is one important game in the American League, where the Toronto Blue Jays travel to face the Baltimore Orioles. The Blue Jays are hanging on the fringe of the AL race, starting the day three games back of the final wild-card spot.
AL race is murky while NL is more defined
There’s quite a bit of mediocrity in the AL Central and West divisions this season, which has led to some fascinating pennant races and could lead to a sub-.500 team making the postseason.
The Cleveland Guardians (81-75) have a narrow advantage over the Chicago White Sox (80-76) in the AL Central while the Texas Rangers (78-78) are just ahead of the Houston Astros (77-79) in the AL West.
Over in the National League, the playoff bracket is close to set.
The Chicago Cubs (87-69), San Diego Padres (87-69) and Philadelphia Phillies (86-70) are jockeying for position in the wild-card race but will almost certainly make the postseason. The only team within shouting distance is the Arizona Diamondbacks (82-74), who are four games back.
MVP races, stats to watch
MLB’s major awards probably won’t have much drama this season.
Both MVP races have strong favorites with Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong running away with the NL honor while Houston’s Yordan Alvarez is the probable choice in the AL, though Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero has also had a fantastic season. Alvarez still has a shot at a rare Triple Crown. He leads the AL in batting average at .313 but his 40 homers are one behind Caminero and his 99 RBIs are six back of Baltimore’s Pete Alonso.
For the Cy Young Award, Milwaukee flame thrower Jacob Misiorowski and New York ace Cam Schlittler are the favorites in the NL and AL, respectively.
The Rookie of the Year races also look set with Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart and his 110-RBI season the leader in the NL and Detroit’s Kevin McGonigle the favorite in the AL.
What is the MLB playoff format?
There are 12 teams that qualify for MLB’s postseason, including six teams from both the AL and NL. The three division winners in each league get seeds No. 1 through No. 3, ranked by win-loss record. Then the three wild-card teams get seeds No. 4 through No. 6, also ranked by win-loss record.
The top two teams with the best record in both the AL and NL automatically advance to the Division Series. The other eight teams play in the Wild Card Series, which is a best-of-three format beginning on Tuesday, Sept. 30. In both the AL and NL, the No. 6 seed will travel to face the No. 3 seed while the No. 5 seed goes to No. 4. The higher seed hosts all three games.
The winners then advance to the best-of-five Division Series, followed by the best-of-seven League Championship Series and a best-of-seven World Series between the winners of the AL and NL.
What is the MLB postseason schedule?
Wild Card Round: Sept. 29-Oct. 1 (NBC/Peacock)
Division Series: Oct. 3-10 (AL on TBS, NL on FOX/FS1)
Championship Series: Oct. 11-20 (AL on TBS, NL on FOX/FS1)
World Series: Oct. 23-31 (FOX)
Who are the favorites to win the World Series?
The Dodgers (+220) are the favorites to capture a third straight World Series title while the Brewers (+600), Yankees (+800) and Rays (+800) are viewed as the top contenders.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
David Brandt, The Associated Press

item.title: [mlb.com] Who sits atop final Power Rankings of the regular season?
item.dc:creator: Will Leitch
item.description: These are the last MLB.com Power Rankings of the 2026 regular season. In exactly one week, 18 of these teams will go home, and 12 will be left. We have made it all the way through. item.content:encoded:
These are the last MLB.com Power Rankings of the 2026 regular season. In exactly one week, 18 of these teams will go home, and 12 will be left. We have made it all the way through. Since these will be the final rankings, let’s take a look at each team, even the ones who did not make the playoffs, and find something positive its fanbase can feel about the 2026 season … now that it’s almost in the rearview mirror.
These rankings, as always, are compiled from MLB.com contributors whose names you can find at the bottom of this (and every) piece, but the words are mine. If you dislike the rankings, yell at all of us. But if you dislike the words, feel free to yell at me.
Also, as we close the season, we note for each team the highest they were ranked in our Power Rankings all season -- when they hit the peak.
1. Brewers (previously: 1)
Season High Water Mark: 1, this week
It’s the best season in Brewers history. It sure looks like they’re going to win 100 games for the first time ever. They’ve got a Cy Young frontrunner in Jacob Misiorowski, they’ve got all the momentum, and they’ve got a team that wins by doing all the little things right. Last year was a huge postseason bummer. Now is the time to right that wrong.
2. Dodgers (previously: 2)
Season High Water Mark: 1, Aug. 17
The Dodgers have had a lot of drama this year, much of it revolving around a hugely disappointing first season at Chavez Ravine for Kyle Tucker and injury concerns for Shohei Ohtani. And yet here they are, one of the best teams in baseball, as always, and the team everyone knows is looming in October.
3. Rays (previously: 4)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 25
Don’t forget, almost no one picked the Rays to win the tough AL East this year. But it looks like it’s going to be theirs, with a deep, versatile roster led by Junior Caminero, who looks like he’s going to be a signature star in this league for the next decade-plus.
4. Braves (previously: 3)
Season High Water Mark: 1, June 15
Every year since their World Series title in 2021 has felt a little bit like a disappointment in its own way, even the 104-win season in '23. But this one sure hasn’t, with the Braves overcoming a '25 losing season by winning the division again. And check out Ronald Acuña Jr., who looks like a superstar again.
5. Yankees (previously: 5)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 4
For a long time, it was assumed that if Aaron Judge was hurt for an extended period of time, the Yankees were cooked. But thanks to a fantastic pitching staff -- including Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler -- the Yankees look as strong as ever. But it still may all ride on Judge regardless.
6. Cubs (previously: 6)
Season High Water Mark: 1, May 11
What more can you say about Pete Crow-Armstrong at this point? He’s about to end the Shohei Ohtani MVP reign, and he’s doing so while becoming one of the most popular players in the sport and having one of the best seasons in Cubs history. And it sure feels like October is going to fit him like a glove.
7. Red Sox (previously: 8)
Season High Water Mark: 6, Aug. 5
This season looked absolutely lost in June, and Red Sox fans were tearing their hair out. Then, suddenly, the Sox were playing the best of any team in baseball, and they rode that run all the way to a playoff spot. And it's sure looking like we'll get another installment of The Rivalry in the Wild Card.
8. Padres (previously: 9)
Season High Water Mark: 3, April 20
The Padres have justified all the investments A.J. Preller and company have made in the offseason with this late-season run, but they still have won just one game past the Division Series round this century. The top of the NL is tough this year, but no one’s hotter than the Padres.
9. Phillies (previously: 7)
Season High Water Mark: 5, July 16
It has been a rocky road, with Don Mattingly taking over early in the season, the team righting itself, and then struggling down the stretch. But in this ear, all that matters for the Phillies is the postseason. All of their questions are about to be answered, one way or the other.
10. Guardians (previously: 12)
Season High Water Mark: 5, June 8
The Guardians’ fight back to the top of the AL Central wasn’t as dramatic as last year’s, but if they can end up atop the division when it’s all said and done, it won’t matter. And if they do … they might just get a first-round bye out of it.
11. White Sox (previously: 11)
Season High Water Mark: 6, June 15
If the White Sox aren’t able to get into the playoffs after the fun season they’ve had, it will feel like a heartbreaker, but it probably shouldn’t be. This is a team that has lost 100-plus games for three consecutive seasons! Look at where they are now! The playoffs would be wonderful. But what a major step forward they’ve made. With more to come.
12. Rangers (previously: 16)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 3
The Rangers have never gotten higher than three games over .500 this year … but that has not kept them out of the middle of the AL West, and even atop the division. They’ve only made the playoffs once in the last decade -- the year they won the World Series. That may well change this season.
13. Diamondbacks (previously: 10)
Season High Water Mark: 9, Aug. 17
The Padres’ torrid run down the stretch may end up keeping Arizona out of the playoffs, though the season’s final series between the two teams could have something to say about that. But a year of uncertainty ended up being a positive one, despite some off-field drama … and there’s still time left in this one.
14. Astros (previously: 13)
Season High Water Mark: 7, April 6
Yordan Alvarez had a fully healthy season and responded with an all-timer of an offensive performance. The only question now is whether they can catch the intrastate-rival Rangers for the AL West crown -- and it looks like they're going to have to, if they want to make the playoffs at all.
15. Blue Jays (previously: 14)
Season High Water Mark: 2, March 23
It looked for a while like the Jays, after the brutal way they lost the World Series last year, would make up for a disappointing season by sneaking into the final Wild Card spot. How fans feel about this season may depend on whether or not they can crawl their way back in. It’s going to be an uphill climb.
16. Pirates (previously: 15)
Season High Water Mark: 5, April 20
Pirates fans had big hopes for this year, and while they weren’t the playoff team that some had expected, they nevertheless have won 79 games and could notch their first winning season since 2018. It’s progress.
17. Orioles (previously: 19)
Season High Water Mark: 10, March 23
It may have hurt to do it, but the O’s did maximize their return for Adley Rutschman with even more young players to add to the ones they already have. It’s understandable if O’s fans are skeptical, but you can’t argue that Pete Alonso was a great investment, and really a North Star for the whole franchise at this point.
18. Marlins (previously: 18)
Season High Water Mark: 8, July 16
Take away that 12-game losing streak, and the Marlins are a playoff team this year. You obviously can’t do that, but the different way the Marlins have been doing things started to pay off this year. And they may well have a star in Otto Lopez.
19. Tigers (previously: 21)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 27
This turned out to be their first losing season since 2023, which is frustrating because hopes were so high heading into the year, but there is still a ton of young talent here, led by Riley Greene, who is quietly putting together a stellar start to his career. And with the Tarik Skubal trade, there’s even more young talent on the way.
20. Cardinals (previously: 17)
Season High Water Mark: 8, May 18
The bullpen fell apart down the stretch, making the record look worse than the season felt, but the Cardinals made many steps forward this year, particularly with the lineup: Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt, Joshua Báez, Alec Burleson and Leo Bernal all look like lineup mainstays … with even more talent coming down the pipe.
21. Nationals (previously: 24)
Season High Water Mark: 12, June 22
James Wood is a star, but he was hardly the only National to emerge in 2026, with CJ Abrams and the recently extended Cade Cavalli setting themselves up as players the Nationals can build around. The offense was terrific this year: That’s the first time you’ve been able to say that in a long time.
22. Mariners (previously: 20)
Season High Water Mark: 3, March 23
So, yeah, it was a bit of a disaster season for the Mariners, in just about every possible way. But this was not a now-or-never season for the M’s: They have a very exciting rotation for 2027, and note that Cal Raleigh started to warm up as the season came to a close as well.
23. Mets (previously: 23)
Season High Water Mark: 5, March 23
That most of the offseason moves blew up in their faces is the reason they’re not in the playoffs, but they certainly played well enough in the second half to look like a playoff team, thanks largely to rookies Carson Benge, A.J. Ewing and Nolan McLean. The Mets will look different next year, but that’s a good thing.
24. Twins (previously: 22)
Season High Water Mark: 15, Aug. 5
The next generation of Twins stars has arrived: Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez all made their debut this year (and still have Rookie of the Year eligibility for next season). This was a transition year for the Twins. There’s plenty of reason to think they can turn the corner in 2027.
25. Reds (previously: 25)
Season High Water Mark: 6, April 27
This was the superstar step forward the Reds have been waiting for from Elly De La Cruz. They no longer have to wonder if he’s ever going to make the leap: He now has. And remember, he is still only 24 years old.
26. Royals (previously: 26)
Season High Water Mark: 14, May 11
Not much went the way it was supposed to this year, but there’s still a lot of young talent here. And there is Bobby Witt Jr., who, even in a down power year (for him), leads the American League in WAR, per FanGraphs.
27. Giants (previously: 27)
Season High Water Mark: 18, March 23
The terrible start, and the occasional discord and chaos, made this season feel like it was over with before it even began. But don’t overlook the fact that Rafael Devers, for most of this season, looked like the superstar the Giants traded for.
28. Angels (previously: 29)
Season High Water Mark: 19, April 20
A potential sale of the team is something that fans have wondered could change the trajectory of this franchise, and they’re going to get the opportunity to find out. There’s some young talent starting to percolate here, perhaps most notably Walbert Ureña, a 22-year-old who looks like he might already be an ace.
29. A’s (previously: 28)
Season High Water Mark: 10, May 11
The onslaught of injuries to their position players made people forget how good this lineup was at some point, and how late in the year they were in contention. As they move closer to their move to Las Vegas, there’s still plenty to build on here … and plenty of reason to have optimism for the future.
30. Rockies (previously: 30)
Season High Water Mark: 27, May 4
It does not look like the Rockies are going to avoid 100 losses this year, alas, marking four straight years with 100-plus losses. But they’ll still be double-digit games better than they were last year, and they’ll do so with a front office that seems, at last, to have a clear plan moving forward.
Voters: Jason Catania, Dan Cichalski, Theo DeRosa, Rick Gold Jr., Jared Greenspan, Will Leitch, Brent Maguire, Travis Miller, Brian Murphy, Arturo Pardavila, Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, Andrew Simon, David Venn, Andy Werle.

item.title: [FanGraphs] Bobby Witt Jr. and the Off-Peak MVP Season
item.dc:creator: Davy Andrews
item.description: Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr
item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

item.title: [MLB.com] Top 9 things at stake in the final week
item.dc:creator: Brent Maguire
item.description: The final week of the 2026 regular season has arrived and there is still much to be determined. While six teams have clinched playoff spots and a few others are close, multiple playoff positions are still up for grabs. item.content:encoded:
The final week of the 2026 regular season has arrived and there is still much to be determined.
While six teams have clinched playoff spots and a few others are close, multiple playoff positions are still up for grabs. And from an individual perspective, there are awards that could be determined in the coming days.
Here’s what is at stake in the final week of the season.
Who will win the AL West and Central?
There’s no telling who will win these two divisions in the American League. The Rays have just about wrapped up the AL East, but the White Sox and Guardians are still battling for the AL Central, while the Rangers and Astros are battling for the West.
This is where things stand. The Rangers lead the Astros by one game in the AL West but Houston won the pivotal tiebreaker against Texas. That means if the two clubs end the season with the same record, the division would go to the Astros.
In the AL Central, the Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox, but Chicago holds the tiebreaker advantage. Any tie between the two clubs means the White Sox would win the division.
Who gets the last AL Wild Card spot?
The AL West and Central battles are directly linked to what’s happening for the final Wild Card spot. It’s very likely that one of those four aforementioned teams will grab the last AL Wild Card spot, unless the Blue Jays have something to say about it. Right now, the White Sox have a fairly comfortable three-game lead over the Blue Jays and Astros.
Could Yordan still win the Triple Crown?
For a while, Yordan Alvarez looked like he might win the MLB Triple Crown, leading the Majors in average, home runs and RBIs. Now, the lefty slugger and presumptive AL MVP winner might merely finish first or second in average, home runs and RBIs. Heading into the final week, Alvarez has a slight edge in average (.313) over Chandler Simpson (.309) and is second in home runs (40) behind Junior Caminero (41) and second in RBIs (99) behind Pete Alonso (105). Alvarez could still snag the AL Triple Crown, but it’ll take a monstrous final week.
Simpson’s unique season and quest for an unusual batting title
Back to Simpson for a second, though. The Rays outfielder is having an excellent season, hitting for average, swiping bases and playing solid outfield defense. What he hasn’t done, though, is hit a single home run. The last hitter to win a batting title without hitting a home run was Rod Carew in 1972. Even if he doesn’t win, he could be the first qualified hitter to bat .300 without a home run since Luis Castillo in 1999.
Will Misiorowski win the ERA title?
It's been a remarkable season for Jacob Misiorowski, who has a 1.86 ERA and 247 strikeouts after Sunday's outing against the Orioles. Assuming he's in line for one more start next weekend -- even if it's abbreviated like his three-inning outing on Sunday -- Misiorowski is in line to join some impressive company. If he can hold his ERA edge over Cam Schlittler's 1.94 mark, he'd join 2021 Corbin Burnes (2.43 ERA in 2021) as the only Brewers to win an ERA title.
If Misiorowski keeps his ERA under two and gets to 250 strikeouts, there's some other fun company he'll join. He'd be just the 13th pitcher (15th instance) since earned runs became official in 1913 to finish a season with a sub-2 ERA and 250-plus strikeouts. The last to do so was Jacob deGrom in 2018.
Will Schwarber or PCA lead the Majors in home runs?
Kyle Schwarber led the National League with 56 home runs last year. As hard as it is to believe, though, Schwarber has never led the Majors in home runs. That could change this year, as the Phillies’ slugger is tied for the MLB lead with 45 homers. The last Phillie to pull that off was Ryan Howard in 2008, when he hit 48 homers and helped lead Philly to a World Series title.
Schwarber, though, has Pete Crow-Armstrong tied with him at the top. The surefire NL MVP has completely taken off this season with 45 homers, 38 stolen bases (more on this shortly), a .949 OPS and his usual excellent center field defense, which has led to an MLB-best 10.5 WAR, per FanGraphs. If PCA surpasses Schwarber, he’d be the first Cub to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa’s 49 homers in 2002 and the first to lead the Majors in long balls since Sosa hit 50 in 2000.
Does PCA get to 40-40?
Crow-Armstrong is making all sorts of history this season. Reaching 10 WAR puts PCA in rarified territory and it seems very likely that the Cubs’ superstar center fielder will be a unanimous MVP winner, something no Cub has ever achieved. Crow-Armstrong is also a mere two stolen bases away from a 40-40 season, something no Cub has done and only six other MLB players have achieved.
Burleson vying to join impressive Cardinals history
Alec Burleson leads the Majors with 111 RBIs, putting him in line for some impressive Cardinals history. He’s looking to become the first Cardinal to lead the National League since Albert Pujols in 2010 and the first to lead the Majors in the category since Joe Torre drove in 137 runs in 1971. His stiffest competition is Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart, who sits at 110 RBIs entering the final week.
How does Verlander's final start go?
Justin Verlander returned to the Tigers for the 2026 season, which will be his final before retiring. Unfortunately, he only made one start in April and hasn't pitched since that point. The good news is he's lined up to pitch on Saturday at Detroit's Comerica Park, which will surely be a feel good moment and send off for the likely future Hall of Famer. Verlander can also add a few more strikeouts to his career total of 3,554.

item.dc:creator: Nathanael P; Eacute; Rez Ner; Oacute
item.description: Yordan Álvarez edificó con los porcentajes un muro que parece impenetrable para merecerse el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana. item.content:encoded:
Yordan Álvarez edificó con los porcentajes un muro que parece impenetrable para merecerse el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana. En la semana final de la fase regular saca 34 puntos sobre Junior Caminero en promedio de bateo (.313-.277), uno de los renglones que encabeza detrás de la Triple Corona.
Pero donde se separa del resto por cuerpo entero es en la principal referencia ofensiva de hoy, el OPS. Es el único en toda la MLB que supera los 1.000 (1.027), 135 puntos sobre el .892 del de los Rays. La superioridad es apreciable en la frecuencia de embasarse (.430-.363) y de extrabases (.597-.515).
Ante esa respetable ventaja porcentual, que hace que en Las Vegas den como un hecho su MVP, clasifique Houston o no, los partidarios de Caminero argumentan el aporte defensivo que hace el dominicano al salir a diario al terreno.
En la ecuación que arroja el WAR de FanGraphs y Baseball-Reference, el ajuste posicional le da a Caminero +2.5 carreras como antesalista y Álvarez -17.5 como un bateador designado que no aporta con el guante.
Antes de salir al terreno, el quisqueyano sale delante, pero el de Las Tunas remonta con el madero hasta liderar en esa casilla.
Lo que dice la Sabermetría
Hay métricas que dejan bien parado a "La Máxima" como 3B, otras no. Baseball Info Solutions dice que ha salvado 4 carreras defensivas, un salto impresionante con relación a las -5 de 2025.
Sin embargo, Savant "opina" todo lo contrario. En OAA saca -12 out por encima del promedio, es decir, la cantidad de outs que hace con relación al antesalista average.
El cálculo se apoya en cámaras e inteligencia artificial que miden desde la velocidad de salida del batazo, el ángulo del roletazo, la distancia recorrida hacia la bola y la fuerza/precisión del disparo a la base.
En carreras prevenidas, medido por Statscat, queda con -9. Es líder en errores entre los defensores de la esquina caliente (19) en la Americana.
A pesar de que Álvarez, quien ha jugado 24 partidos en el prado izquierdo (con -5 DRS) y 129 como designado, queda con -1.7 WAR defensivos al sumar las 6.7 ofensivas totaliza 6.3, líder de todo el béisbol. Caminero, con 0.7 defensivas, tiene 5.7 en total.
De las 25.6 WAR de los jugadores de posición de los Rays, Caminero lidera el aporte con 5.7 (22.2 %). En cambio, Álvarez es responsable de 6.3 de las 19 de los Astros o el 33.1 %.
Dicho esto, el cubano ha sido más determinante para Houston que Caminero para Tampa, a pesar del abismo competitivo entre ese salvaje Este y el mediocre Oeste.

item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cristopher Sánchez earned his major league-leading 18th win Sunday, leading the Philadelphia Phillies to a 7-2 victory over the New York Mets.
The Phillies (86-70), who salvaged a split of the four-game series, entered Sunday in the third National League wild-card spot, one game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four games clear of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Sánchez surrendered six hits — including Bo Bichette’s sixth-inning homer — and struck out six over 6 1/3 innings as he snapped a tie with the Boston Red Sox’s Sonny Gray for the big league lead in wins.
Join our family of readers starting at $5 for your first month and support local, unbiased journalism.
Already have an account? Log in to continue.
Otherwise, follow the link below to join.
| Please log in to continue |
The last Phillies pitcher to lead the majors in wins was Steve Carlton with 23 in 1982.
Justin Crawford had a three-run triple and Luis Arraez finished with two RBIs. Alec Bohm and Trea Turner each had run-scoring hits. Kyle Schwarber tied a career high with four walks.
Rookie Jonah Tong (2-2) gave up four runs and struck out five in 4 2/3 innings for the last-place Mets, who finished 36-45 at home — their worst record at Citi Field since the 2013 team went 33-48.
PIRATES 4, ROYALS 3
PITTSBURGH (AP) — Rafael Flores Jr. hit the go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth inning to help Pittsburgh to a win over Kansas City and complete a series sweep.
After Ryan O’Hearn led off with a single to center, Flores sent a slider from Nate Pearson (2-3) into the left-field bleachers for his 10th homer this season.
Pittsburgh rallied with a two-run homer in the eighth for a second straight day. Brandon Lowe had his 33rd of the season in a 6-5 win Saturday.
Carmen Mlodzinki (8-7) got the win. He allowed two runs and three hits in three innings. The reliever gave up a pinch-hit, two-run home run to Vinnie Pasquantino that gave Kansas City a 3-2 lead with two outs in the seventh.
Mason Montgomery earned his 16th save. He retired the first two batters in the ninth before Luke Maile hit a double and took third on a fielding error by Jake Mangum. Montgomery got Isaac Collins to fly out to right to strand Maile.
The Royals went ahead 1-0 in the first inning with three straight singles off Lake Bachar. Bobby Witt Jr. beat out a groundball to second baseman Lowe. He moved to third on a single to right from Jac Caglianone and scored when Perez shot one through the middle of the infield.
RAYS 5, RED SOX 1
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay crept closer to the AL East title with a victory over Boston.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Boston would have clinched a playoff spot with a victory. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25. They could still wrap up a spot Sunday with a Houston loss.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
CUBS 9, REDS 1
CINCINNATI (AP) — Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run as Chicago moved closer to clinching a postseason berth with a victory over Cincinnati.
Chicago (87-69) reduced its magic number to one and could wrap up a berth if the Diamondbacks lose to the Yankees later Sunday.
The Cubs began the day tied with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies for the top NL wild-card spot which would earn them home-field advantage in the wild-card round. The Cubs own the tiebreakers over the Diamondbacks, Padres, and Phillies.
Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman left Sunday’s game in the fourth inning after being struck in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch while standing near the on-deck circle.
Cubs left-hander David Peterson (9-8) allowed a run on three hits in seven innings with one walk and seven strikeouts.
The Cubs loaded the bases with one out in the third. Ian Happ singled in a run and Nico Hoerner walked to force in another to extend Chicago’s lead to 3-0. Pedro Ramirez’s two-run single made the score 5-0.
Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder (6-12) allowed five earned runs on six hits with three walks and three strikeouts.
CARDINALS 5, NATIONALS 3
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as St. Louis scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat Washington.
Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.
Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.
It was Herrera’s third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.
Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.
Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.
Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.
